decision_maker: Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee, Strategy and Resources Committee
content:
The Committee considered a report by the Works and
Recycling Manager (circulated previously) regarding Simple
Recycling – Soft Plastics trial update.
 
The Works and Recycling Manager outlined the report to the
Committee.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Works and
Recycling Manager advised the following:
 

·        
The majority of other
Devon Councils had decided to defer the implementation of the
collection of soft plastics in light of
Local Government Reorganisation and
following DEFRA’s decision to postpone the introduction of
soft plastics collections until April 2030.

·        
Some supermarkets were
collecting soft plastics for recycling. However, the soft plastics
were sent to the same reprocessing plant as the Council
used.  Supermarkets had to pay for the
disposal of the soft plastics.  50%
collected would be recycled and the other 50% would get incinerated
for energy from waste.  When the
recycling of soft plastics was rolled out across the country, it
was anticipated that supermarkets would no longer collect soft
plastics due to the costs incurred. 
Following the trial, 100% of residents would prefer to recycle
their soft plastics at the kerbside.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

Following Local Government Reorganisation, the new Devon Unitary Authority
would be delivering services in April 2028.  As part of this, discussions would need to take
place on the future infrastructure, vehicles and collections for
the waste and recycling service for Devon.  The Works and Recycling Manager would be part of a
working group and have input into these discussions and
considerations.

 
The Committee considered the following:
 

Expressed its disappointment that the Council
would not be able to roll out the collection of soft plastics at
this time due to DEFRA’s decision to postpone the
introduction of soft plastics collections until April
2030.  The Committee valued the trial
that had been undertaken and the feedback from residents and
thanked Officers involved in the trial.
Once the report had been considered by the
Strategy and Resources Committee, there would be a need to feedback
to those residents that took part in the soft plastics trial to
thank them for taking part and provide an explanation as to why the
Council had taken a decision to not continue with the collection of
soft plastics following DEFRA’s decision to postpone the
introduction of soft plastics collections until April
2030.

 
RESOLVED that Strategy and Resources
Committee be recommended that the implementation of Soft Plastics
collections is deferred until April 2030.

decision_maker: Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee, Council
content:
The Committee considered a report by the PMO Manager
(circulated previously) regarding the Programme Performance report for quarter 1 of
2026/27.
 
The Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
highlighted the key elements of the high
level update of the programmes
delivering the current Corporate Plan priorities and performance
measures for quarter 1 of 2026/27 as detailed in Appendix
A.  Appendix B provided the latest
update on process map reviews across services.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

KPI “B&B: Total number of households accommodated in leased /
B&B Accommodation” - B&B accommodation was used for temporary
accommodation.  Air B&Bs were not
used.
KPI “8b: Total number of properties registered as 2nd
homes each quarter” – the number of properties
registered as second homes had decreased as some houses had been
turned back into domestic housing or changed to business rates if
the property met the requirements of business rates and was let for
a set number of nights.
KPI “H&CS P:20 Ilfracombe Healthy Homes”
– The Council are applying for grant funding from Homes
England.  Council had previously
approved an amendment to the capital programme of
£1,259,000.  If there was a
funding shortfall in the project, then the Council would borrow
funds.  If there was no funding
shortfall then this would benefit revenue as there would not be a
requirement to borrow funds.
KPI “KR 8: No. of residential
properties (see 8a below) that have
been classed as empty for more than 3 months on the Council Tax
base” – the number of residential properties classed as
being empty for more than 3 months had increased which had been
partly as a result of houses on new developments not being
sold.  The Committee requested that the
Empty Homes Officer provide an update on the empty homes project,
the reasons why the number of empty properties was continuing to
increase and the work that was being carried out with housing
developers.
KPI “8a: Gross number of residential properties on the
Council Tax base” – once a property was including on
the Valuation list, then the owner of the property becomes liable
for Council Tax.  Once a property had
been completed and ready to be occupied, it would be included on
the Valuation list.  Once the property
was on the Valuation list, Council Tax would become payable
immediately. The Valuation Office determines the Council Tax band
for the property.  When a property
became liable for Council Tax, the Council sometimes place the
property on a temporary band which was based on similar properties
in the area whilst it awaits the Valuation Office confirmation of
banding. If the Valuation Office advised of a different banding for
the property, then the Council Tax band would be amended
accordingly.  The Committee requested
that the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive ascertain
the reasons as to why the Valuation Office had a backlog of valuing
properties to be included on the Valuation list.
KPI “H&CS P:16 Community Safety” – The
inclusion of Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) in other towns and villages would require
additional resources, funding and support from other partners to
enforce.  If there were any concerns
regarding the enforcement of the existing PSPOs, then these could be raised with the
Community Safety Partnership and the Crime and Disorder
Committee.
KPI “EE P:2C Management of our non-built assets” – an item
had been included on the agenda for the meeting of the Strategy and
Resources Committee on 14 September 2026 seeking approval to
purchase land for a new community woodland in Ilfracombe. This
would be funded by 50% from National Landscapes and 50% from the
Rural England Prosperity Fund. 
Following approval by the Committee, the land would be acquired by
the end of September 2026.
Process mapping
– some process mapping had not yet been started due to
waiting for other process mapping to be completed beforehand and
the capacity of officers to carry out all process
mapping.
Process map
“EH&H P:03 18+ Young Person
DCC Transition” – that an update be sought from the
Head of PMO and Environmental Health and Housing regarding a start
date for the 18+ Young Person.

 
RESOLVED that the recommendations be endorsed and
recommended to the Strategy and Resources Committee for
approval.

RESOLVED that the minutes of
the meeting held on 2 July 2026 (circulated previously) be approved
as a correct record and signed by the Chair.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Director of
Resources and Deputy Chief Executive (circulated previously)
regarding the Financial Management report for quarter 1 of
2026/27.
 
The Finance Manager presented the report to the Committee
and advised that since the publication of the report, the national
pay award for 2026/27 had been confirmed at 3.3%.  3% had been included in the original budget and
the additional £60,000 would be funded from the Budget
Management reserve and included as part of the Q2 Financial
Management report.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

The forecast that the
Trade Waste Service would generate a net budget surplus of
£122,000 was positive.  The
service was now generating favourable returns.  When the decision was taken by the Strategy and
Resources Committee to retain the Trade Waste service, the charges
had been increased by 46%.  These
increased charges were still considerably less than quoted by other
alternative providers.  It had been
presumed that the Council would lose a number of its customers,
however the Trade Waste team had worked hard to retain the customer
base.
The Strategic
Contingency Reserve was a reserve for one off items
only.  Additional funds had not been
placed in the Reserve for a number of years.  The Street Marshall Scheme had been funded through
this reserve for 2026-27.  At the end of
the last financial year, additional funding had not been placed in
the Strategic Contingency Reserve and had been placed in the Town
Centres reserve instead.  The Night Bus
scheme was a multi agency scheme and if it continued, then
consideration would need to be given as to how it would be funded
in the future.

 
RESOLVED that the recommendations be endorsed and
recommended to the Strategy and Resources Committee for
approval.

The Committee considered its work programme for 2026/27
(circulated previously).
 
In response to questions from the Committee regarding the
Pannier Market Working Group, the Director of Resources and Deputy
Chief Executive advised the following:
 

That the Council was currently in the process of
advertising for a Town Centre Venue Asset Manager which splits the
responsibilities for both the Pannier Market and Boutport Studios.
It was suggested that following recruitment, the new Manager be
invited to attend the Committee to provide an update on the future
plans for both venues.  A meeting of the
Pannier Market Working Group had not been arranged as it had been
difficult to find a suitable day and time for the
meeting.

 
RESOLVED that:
 
(a) 
 the work programme be amended as
follows:
 
                             
i.       
Public Transport be
removed from the work programme;
                           
ii.       
Empty Homes be added
to the work programme for December 2026 and that the
Empty Homes Officer be requested to provide an
update on the empty homes project, the reasons why the number of
empty properties was continuing to increase and the work that was
being carried out with housing developers;
                          
iii.       
Parkwood Leisure be added to the work programme for
January 2027 to provide an update to the Committee on the
performance of the leisure facilities, programmes, how they were
reaching out to stakeholders and the work that was being carried
out with GP surgeries and that a proforma be completed setting out
the purpose for the update;
                          
iv.       
Council Tax: reasons for the delays in valuations
being undertaken by the Valuation Office – that following
receipt of  further information and an
explanation of the reasons for delays being provided by the
Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive that if required a
proforma be completed by Councillor Bushell setting out the purpose
for an update being provided to a future meeting of the
Committee;
                           
v.       
Agricultural Working Group – that a proforma
be completed by Councillor Bulled setting out the reasons for the
re-establishing the working group and the remit of the
group;
                          
vi.       
Feedback from the Health Inequalities Working Group
following the collaborative event taking place during the Autumn
and any lessons learned be added to the work programme.

 
(b) 
a meeting of the
Pannier Market Working Group be convened as soon as possible and
that an update from the Working Group be provided at the next
Committee meeting and that following recruitment the Town Centre
Venue Asset Manager be invited to provide an update on the future
plans for the Pannier Market and Boutport Studies at a future
meeting of the Committee.

RESOLVED that the minutes of the meeting held
on 12 August 2026 (circulated previously) be approved as a correct
record and signed by the Chair subject to Councillor Bulled being
added to minute 26 as she had given her apologies.

The Committee considered a
report by the Planning Officer (JC) (circulated previously)
regarding planning application 81925.
 
The Planning Officer (JC)
advised the following:
 

·        
The receipt of a consultation response from
Environmental Health since the publication of the
report.  He read the consultation
response to the Committee which advised that “the Application
Form states hours of opening from 07:30 to 16:30 hrs Mondays to
Fridays (excluding Bank Holidays). Given the context of this
existing commercial site and the proposed opening hours, I do not
expect any unacceptable noise impacts to arise.  I recommend
consideration be given to including a condition restricting hours
of use on any permission such that use does not occur outside the
hours of 07:00 to 19:00 hrs daily (excluding Sundays and Bank
Holidays) to protect residential amenity.”  He advised that in his view that the condition
recommended by Environmental Health did not need to be implemented
as the Council had control of the hours and by not including this
condition would allow the Parks team to have more
flexibility.  The proposed change of use
would only permit the Council’s parks service team to use the
site.

·        
The flat was in an uninhabitable state.

·        
Planning application 37761 on 15 July 2004 included
a condition that the unit should be occupied by the owner, manager,
employee of the associated dairy or immediate family and that this
would prevent the occupation of the flat as it would be
unlawful.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Planning Officer (JC) advised the
following:
 

·        
The site was currently partly being used by the
Parks team.

·        
There was no condition previously imposed in terms
of the operation hours.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Building Surveyor (agent) advised the
following:
 

·        
The restriction of hours recommended by
Environmental Health was for standard working hours.

·        
The maisonette flat was located on the upper floor
and was uninhabitable due to mould and its condition.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Service Manager – Development Management
advised the following:
 

·        
As the maisonette flat could not be occupied, it
could, if required, be utilised for storage in conjunction with the
ground-floor area, which is also intended for storage.
 
RESOLVED (unanimous) that the
application be APPROVED as recommended by the Planning Officer
(JC).

Leaver left the meeting during the consideration of this
application.
 
Councillor Bishop took the
Chair for this item.

regarding planning application 82051.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Lead Planning Officer (North) advised the
following:

RESOLVED (unanimous) that the

The Committee considered a
report by the Planning Officer (circulated previously).
 
The Planning Officer advised
the Committee that the Officer’s recommendations for approval
were set out within the report. The application had been presented
to the Committee for decision as the applicant was a member of the
Planning Committee.
 
In response to questions by the
Committee, the Planning Officer advised the following:
 

Astro-turf was already in use at
the property, which is why it was not included in the
proposal.
Cladding was due to
be replaced at the time of the site visit. Any changes to the
finish of the main dwelling may require a separate
application.
The slate roof of the
proposed conservatory accords with the objectives of Policy
DM08A to reduce light spill in the Area
of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) and nearby Exmoor National
Park.

 
The Chair noted that the roof
specification was covered within condition 3.
 
RESOLVED (Unanimous) that the application be APPROVED as

Councillors Bishop and Leaver
rejoined the meeting.
 
Councillor P Leaver re-declared
his Disclosable Pecuniary Interest, and left the meeting for the
duration of the consideration of this planning
application.
 
Councillor Davies re-declared
his Disclosable Pecuniary Interest, and left the meeting for the
duration of the consideration of this this planning
application.
 
Councillor Bishop assumed the
role of Chair for this planning application, in the absence of the
Chair.
 
Councillor Williams made
reference to a potential interest as an owner of a camper van,
although not a visitor to the site in question
 
The Committee considered a
report by the Senior Planning Officer (circulated
previously).
 
The Service Manager
(Development Management) advised the Committee that the
Officer’s recommendations for approval were set out within
the report. The application had been presented to the Committee for
decision as the Chair, Councillor Davies, was the agent for the
application.
 
Mr B Seybold, Applicant,
addressed the Committee.
 
The Service Manager
(Development Management) recommended that the following condition
be added to the decision, if it were approved:
 
“No external lighting
shall be installed or erected on the site at any time, in the
interests of minimising landscape and visual impacts on the
National Landscape and local landscape character in accordance with
Policies ST09, ST04, ST14, DM04, and DM08A of the North Devon and
Torridge Local Plan.”
 
 
In response to questions by the
Committee, the applicant confirmed that the toilet and shower
blocks had their own LED downlights which were turned off
overnight
 
In response to questions by the
Committee, the Service Manager (Development Management) advised the
following:
 

The proposed,
additional condition, was in regards to any additional lighting,
and did not affect the existing lighting.
This was not a
permanent, year-round site. A previous appeal for a permanent
building on the site was refused. This was in order to protect the
landscape. The compromise was a seasonal site only and for the
building to be movable.

 
RESOLVED (unanimous) that the application be APPROVED as
recommended by the Service Manager (Development Management) subject
to the inclusion of the following condition:
 
(a) 
No additional external lighting shall be installed
or erected on the site at any time, unless agreed in writing from
the Local Planning Authority, in the interests of minimising
landscape and visual impacts on the National Landscape and local
landscape character in accordance with Policies ST09, ST04, ST14,
DM04, and DM08A of the North Devon and Torridge Local
Plan.

Councillor Lethaby rejoined
meeting.
 
Councillor P Leaver re-declared
his Non-Disclosable Interest, and left the meeting for the duration
of the consideration of this planning application
 
Councillor Bishop redeclared
his Non-Disclosable Interest, and left the meeting for the duration of
the consideration of this planning application.
 
The Committee considered a
report by the Lead Planning Officer (North)
(circulated
previously).
 
The Service Manager
(Development Management) advised the Committee that:
·      
The Officer’s recommendations for approval
were set out within the report.
·      
The application had been presented to the Committee
for decision as the Council was the owner and landlord of the
premises in question.
·      
Barnstaple Town Council had made a recommendation of
approval (since the publication of the committee
report).
 
Mr T Huggins (Representative of
the Applicant) addressed the Committee.
 
In response to questions by the
Chair, the Service Manager (Development Management) advised that
the restrictions on condition 3 were in place due to the
restricting parking and the site being within a Flood Zone
area.
 
RESOLVED (Unanimous) that the application be APPROVED as
recommended by the Lead Planning Officer (Major
Applications).

The Senior Planning Policy
Officer (NDC), presented the report to Committee, the purpose of
which was to seek approval for the necessary documentation to
undertake a scoping consultation in accordance with regulation 20
of the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England)
Regulations 2026.
 
Members were reminded that the
timetable for the new joint local plan was approved at the last
meeting and a Notice of Intention would be published on 30th June,
with the scoping consultation scheduled from 30th June to 11th
August.  As a result, Members were
advised their approval was being sought for the notice of scoping
consultation and relevant documents (attached with the agenda). The
Senior Planning Policy Officer further summarised the legal
requirements required and how the consultation should be
delivered.
 
Members were advised of the
consultees who should be invited to take part who would be (but not
limited to):
 

Specific
bodies  - Devon County Council, Parish
Councils, Environment Agency, Natural England, Infrastructure
Providers, Active Travel England
General bodies -
voluntary groups, groups with protected characteristic (As defined
in Equalities Act), bodies that represent business
interests
It was further stated
that any person able to take part in the consultation
process.

 
Councillor C Leaver and
Councillor Clayton (NDC) arrived at 10:10
 
It was explained that
Government guidance suggested a minimum of 21 days for the
consultation, but officers were proposing a six-week period to
allow for more meaningful comments, especially from parish
councils.
 
The Senior Planning Officer
noted the recommendations within the report, and advised that,
although there is only a requirement to publish the notice,
officers intended to also publish a supporting document to go
alongside the notice, which would provide further context for the
consultation and explain the Local Plan, whilst noting the impact
of LGR and explaining the intention / purpose of a scoping
consultation.
 
It was confirmed that close
collaboration with communication teams aimed to ensure a wide reach
and public understanding through social media and other media
channels, recognising the complexity of the process.
 
Members were advised that
officers were actively attending planning advisory forums and
meetings with other councils and MHCLG representatives to gather
best practise information due to limited detailed government
guidance. Recommendation 3 (delegated powers) was noted as a result
of this.
 
Further detail was provided
regarding the baseline report (Appendix 3), previously presented to
Committee in April, which had been updated with more local-level
analysis and a new "future section" with ONS projections. It was
confirmed that work was ongoing to improve the readability and
format of the document.
 
Councillor Crabb (NDC) joined
the meeting at 10:19
 
Members were also advised of a
requirement (through environmental legislation) to have a Strategic
Environmental Assessment (SEA) and its purpose was explained. It
was confirmed that the previous Sustainability Appraisal process
was now gone, but SEA was still required.
 
It was explained there was a
lack of government guidance on timescales and how to integrate the
SEA into the plan making process, now the Sustainability Appraisal
process was gone. As a result, officers have decided to conduct the
first SEA consultation concurrently with the local plan scoping
consultation. This involves consulting specific statutory bodies
(Natural England, Environment Agency, Historic England) on a
draught scoping report. It was confirmed that consultants have been
preparing this and a report should be avilable by the end of the
month, with delegated authority being sought to publish this
document once finalised.
 
Chair thanked the Senior
Planning Policy Officer (NDC) for summarising the report and noted
how officers were dealing with an ever changing, dynamic and
complicated situation.
 
Members were then provided the
opportunity to ask questions and the following discussion took
place.
 
Members asked for clarity
regarding the type of stakeholders included in consultation, and
whether it would include constituted community groups. The Senior
Planning Policy Officer advised that the aim was to reach as many
groups as possible.
 
Members raised the risks of
extreme weather in the future, the risk and impact of wildfires
specifically, and asked about how this would considered as part of
the plan building process, and the Planning Policy Manager (TDC)
advised that this was also on the agenda nationally.
 
Councillor Leather (TDC) joined
the meeting at 10:25
 
Members raised consultation
responses and requested a change to the wording of 2.7 to reflect
on types of responses available and the support / assistance on
hand for those who wish to respond. 
Officers agreed to take this away and members were asked to raise
awareness with constituents/communities.  Following a suggestion to use Libraries, officer
confirmed this had been the case in the past.
 
Members agreed that, while
recognising the findings of the Baselining Report, the vision and
consultation should focus less on nationally set housing targets
and more on the priorities identified through the Northern Devon
Place Story, particularly the economy, skills, wellbeing and other
identified issues. They also highlighted the impact of the road
network on businesses and tourism and suggested aligning the Local
Transport Plan and Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plans
to support a coordinated approach.
 
In response, officers confirmed
that the Local Plan would take these matters into consideration and
that communication on the consultation would also reflect the
issues raised. Following some feedback on readability of the data
in the baselining report, the Senior Planning Policy Officer (NDC)
advised that work was taking place to further improve the document
and advised that a version for the web would see some improvement
to readability too.
 
The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) also referred to the reports on the agenda, noting the work
that had taken place already to engage with infrastructure
providers regarding the progress of delivering infrastructure. The
timescales for preparing the report for the agenda had meant that
work to improve readability was limited, and it was suggested that
a more accessible version could be circulated outside of the
meeting.
 
Members asked about aligning to
the work being done by the Combined County Authority (CCA), noting
their responsibility for transport budget and Spatial Development
Strategy (SDS), whilst highlighting potential concerns for overlap
along with the risk of working in silos. The Planning Policy
Officer (TDC) advised that all areas were working together but
acknowledged the complexities of aligning with CCA and delivering
the SDS, noting the need for clarity on the geography of the SDS
and the challenging timescales, which were almost identical for the
SDS and the local plan. The need to work together across Devon was
recognised and work being carried out to ensure this was
summarised.
 
Members referred to the threats
listed on page 35 of the report and suggested technology (home
working, internet delivery) should be factored into defining
sustainability of places, given its impact on rural service
provision. The Planning Policy Manager (TDC) advised this would be
key consideration for defining sustainability.
 
There was a suggestion that the
SWOT analysis on page 36 of the report be circulated to Parishes to
raise awareness.  Additionally, members
asked about the online consultation format, whether it would
involve a series of open-ended questions, and if paper copies would
be available. The Senior Planning Policy Officer (NDC) confirmed it
would be online from 30 June, with open-ended questions and paper
copies at offices.
 
Following a query about the
ease of access and length of response the Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) stated the aim was for flexibility, encouraging full answers
but allowing short responses, with a relatively easy registration
process. The reasoning for encouraged online submissions were also
touched on in terms of efficiencies of managing
responses.
 
Members noted a lack of public
understanding of planning, particularly that housing numbers are
government-driven and local authorities have limited control. As a
result, it was felt there was a need for better public explanation
of planning realities in terms of what local planning teams can do.
In response the Senior Planning Policy Officer (NDC) confirmed FAQs
and a social media "myth-busters" campaign were being prepared to
address common public questions about housing numbers,
infrastructure, and planning context. Members were reminded of
their role in sharing these messages.
 
Members noted a typo on page
52, where bullet points were duplicated, officers advised this
would be corrected.
 
When asked about the target for
number of responses and estimated time for completion, the Planning
Policy Manager (TDC) stated there were no specific target, but the
aim was for a broad representative sample, and in terms of the
length of the questionnaire, the aim was to be concise and quick
for the public, but with scope for elaboration.
 
Members then queried the
potential of a Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL), the need for
housing that better meets local family needs, and the need to
recognise the area’s high-value industries within Local Plan
evidence base. In response, the Planning Policy Manager (TDC)
confirmed that Northern Devon Futures (NDF) Board is already
integral to the plan-making process, with the thematic working
group and NDF action groups aligned to help connect with those
industries and others. In terms of CIL, this would be explored but
it was explained how Section 106 agreements had benefited the area
through the last Local Plan. In response to housing needs, it was
advised that a new Housing and Economic Needs Assessment would
identify future housing requirements.
 
Following a question regarding
viability and highway infrastructure, it was also confirmed that
Devon County Council were actively involved in transport and
infrastructure planning for northern Devon, examples of this work
locally were provided for members. The importance of the FAQs and
myth busting was also noted here.
 
The Head of Planning and
Building Control (TDC) emphasised the importance of the piece of
work on lessons learned, particularly for strategic sites, ensuring
policy, phasing, and comprehensive approaches are right.
 
Members queried the doubling of
anticipated population growth rate compared to historical trends,
asking if this was government-led. The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) recognised there appeared to be a disconnect between
government's standard formula for housing requirements and the more
demographic projections, which had the potential to lead to more
housing than population growth might suggest – the rational
of Government was to provide more choice and competition. The
challenges of this locally were recognised however.
 
Chair reminded members of the
recommendations within the report. 
 
 
RESOLVED: that Members of the
Joint Planning Policy Committee (JPPC):
 

Approve the Notice of
Scoping Consultation (Appendix 1) and it being made available in
accordance with the regulation requirements, and a 6-week
representation period is commenced during which representations on
the matters contained within it may be received by the
Council.

 

Delegate authority to
the Head of Place Property and Regeneration (NDC) and Head of
Planning and Building Control (TDC) to finalise for publication the
formal Notice of Scoping consultation (draft provided at Appendix
1) including the making of changes to the wording, language, form
and layout to ensure legibility and compliance with legislation,
guidance and emerging best practice;

 

Delegate authority to
the Head of Place Property and Regeneration (NDC) and Head of
Planning and Building Control (TDC) to finalise for publication the
scoping consultation document (draft provided at Appendix 2)
including the making of changes to the wording, language, form and
layout to ensure legibility and compliance with legislation,
guidance and emerging best practice;

 

Note the content of
the updated Draft North Devon and Torridge Local Plan Baselining
Evidence Report, including the updated Infrastructure Delivery
Plan[SM1.1] review table  (Appendix 3)
and  delegate authority to the Head of
Place Property and Regeneration (NDC) and Head of Planning and
Building Control (TDC) to finalise for publication of the Report
including the making of changes to the wording, language, form and
layout to ensure legibility and compliance with legislation,
guidance and emerging best practice.

 

Delegate authority to
the Head of Place Property and Regeneration (NDC) and Head of
Planning and Building Control (TDC) to finalise for publication and
consultation the Strategic Environmental Assessment Scoping Report
in accordance with the Environmental Assessment of Plans and
Programmes regulations 2004.

The Principal Planning Policy
Officer (TDC) presented proposed updates to the HELAA methodology,
which was originally endorsed in 2020. It was explained that the
revisions align with draft Government guidance on identifying,
assessing and selecting sites for allocation, supporting the new
plan-making system and National Planning Policy Framework
(NPPF). Officers had also made minor
changes to improve clarity and reflect how assessments were
completed.
 
Some examples of the key
changes noted in the report were highlighted for members - the
introduction of a site categorisation process, as well as an
overall red, amber, green conclusion for each site assessment to
assist members during site selection.
 
The Principal Planning Policy
Officer (TDC) advised there were a number
of existing site assessments, published in autumn 2025,
which would be reviewed under the updated methodology. It was
stated that the assessment process itself would not fundamentally
change, although the presentation of results would be
revised.
 
In terms of timescales the
review would be part of the annual HELAA update in summer/early
autumn 2026, also alongside an update of the five-year housing land
supply position.
 
It was explained that
additional sites were being identified proactively through Land
Registry searches and direct contact with landowners, while the
ongoing Call for Sites remained open. The updated HELAA is expected
to support the site selection process in line with current Local
Plan timescales.
 
In response to a question
regarding the ability of sites to meet the increased housing
requirement, the Principal Planning Policy Officer (TDC) confirmed
that currently identified sites marginally exceed the requirement.
However, he noted that this provides limited flexibility. It was
explained that the Call for Sites was re-opened last year and
additional sites had come forward, and officers were also looking
at the proactive identification of further sites, to create a
broader pool of potential allocations and improve
choice.
 
Councillor Prowse noted his
role on the HELAA panel and reassured members about the ongoing
work of the panel. He emphasised the importance of distinguishing
the difference between the HELAA and its methodology and decisions
on potential allocations, with future public consultation before
decisions are made by members. The work undertaken by officers on
all three reports was highlighted and it was asked that this be
noted. It was stressed that no decisions on sites had been made,
and there was a need for clear communications when the updated
HELAA was published.
 
The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) encouraged members to identify and encourage landowners to
submit sites, stating that a larger portfolio would enable more
sustainable and appropriate site choices. Members were advised that
the teams would be writing out to landowners as part of the
proactive site identification process, with the caveat that there
were no guarantees of any sites being taken forward to be proposed
for development through the local plan.
 
Members asked whether site
assessments consider embedded carbon and biodiversity impacts,
noting the availability of tools that can help identify
lower-carbon development locations. The Principal Planning Officer
(TDC) advised that embedded carbon is not currently assessed
through the HELAA process. The Planning Policy Manager (TDC) added
that, while assessment tools were available, they did not always
produce significantly different outcomes for different sites and
the challenge of quantifying carbon impacts at this stage of the
process was explained.
 
Members asked about undeveloped
sites from the current plan and whether they would be removed. It
was explained that all existing allocated sites, whether developed
or not, were re-analysed and would go back into the "melting pot"
with newly promoted sites for review. The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) advised that with the significant housing numbers required,
difficult choices would be necessary.
 
Chair advised members of the
recommendations of the report.
 
RESOLVED That Members of the Joint Planning Policy Committee
(JPPC) Endorse the updated HELAA
Methodology as the basis for identifying and assessing potential
sites for development in the support of the local plan
process.

The Principal Planning Officer
(TDC) presented the report.  It was
explained that the settlement assessment was a first step towards
developing a spatial strategy for the local plan, providing an
up-to-date understanding of locations that were best suited to
promote growth. It would not directly determine what the hierarchy
or the spatial strategy would look like but aimed to provide an
up to date understanding of the role and
function of urban and rural settlements in northern
Devon.
 
Members were advised it
followed national policy and best practise, and officers had
broadened the traditional focus (shops, public transport) to
include a wider range of sustainability factors, more relevant for
rural areas.
 
It was explained that each
settlement would be scored out of 10 across the following six
assessment categories:
 

Service
Provision: Presence of key services and
additional services.
Accessibility: Public transport
availability/frequency, proximity to centres, quality of
infrastructure (including broadband).
Connectivity: Department for
Transport's metric on connectivity to a range of
services/facilities.
Economy and
Employment: Data sets on employment and
economic activity.
Environmental
Sensitivity: Air quality, flood risk,
heritage, landscape, ecology.
Community and
Housing:  Data
sets linked to social aspects of sustainability.

 
The Principal Planning Officer
(TDC) explained that the indicators (used for scoring) drew heavily
on census data and members were directed to the appendices for
further detail, additionally It was noted officers were able to
explain the methodology to members individually and via the
Thematic Working Groups.
 
Members were advised that the
scoring for settlements were an indication of sustainability and
for comparison, not absolute measures. It was also explained that
they were initial, unweighted scores and it was anticipated that
weightings would be used to emphasise importance / significance,
with members having a have a role on this.
 
After providing further detail
on scoring, and the next steps in the process, members were asked
for their questions.
 
Chair questioned an emphasis on
internet availability given that some rural access could be better
than in the towns. Following on from this, members highlighted the
issues experienced by farming families, especially young families
who wish to remain in rural areas, and how the changes in terms of
remote access to services meant that the sustainability definitions
needed to be reconsidered, helping to ensure people remained within
social networks if they wished.
 
Following a question regarding
some of the scoring of specific settlements within the report,
officers clarified that the existing local plan's categorisation
was shown, not the proposed one. 
Additionally, the current table orders settlements by unweighted
score, with weightings to be determined at a
later date.
 
Councillor James declared an
interest as a rural resident and went on to express concern that
the business register’s lowest figure for number of employees
was 300. This wasn’t felt to reflect rural employment,
potentially disadvantaging those in smaller rural locations.
Officers advised that these were objective assessments without
categorisation yet and thresholds would be set at a later date using the Thematic Working Groups to
help advise and develop the work further.
 
Members asked if suggestions
from a previous workshop (maps, new town possibility) were taken on
board. The Planning Policy Manager (TDC) confirmed all options for
growth were on the table, but noted that
any new settlements would take a very long time to deliver. The
next steps after scoping were explained, and the tight timescales
were noted.
 
Members reflected on the
experiences of the last plan and emphasised the importance of
parishes and members understanding the assessment process and the
relationship between settlements.
 
It was proposed by Councillor
Prowse and seconded by Councillor Leaver that a recommendation be
added. 
 
‘that a link to the report be
circulated to all members of both councils, inviting them to
feedback their initial views so the thematic working group can
consider individual councillors views.’ 
 
The work of Devon County
Council's Rural Deprivation Working Group and Public Health on
priority places was highlighted, it was
suggested that links be established with Public Health given that
their data could feed into the local plan.
 
RESOLVED That Members of the
Joint Planning Policy Committee (JPPC):
 

Endorse the
settlement assessment as the basis to inform the development of a
new settlement hierarchy for North Devon and Torridge.

 

Request that the
Housing and Infrastructure Local Plan Thematic Working Group (TWG)
considers the initial findings of the settlement assessment,
further develops the assessment approach by agreeing appropriate
assessment category ‘weightings’, and brings forward
initial suggestions for a settlement hierarchy, informed by the
outcomes of the assessment. 

 

That a link to the
report be circulated to all members of both councils, inviting them
to feedback their initial views so the thematic working group can
consider individual councillors views

The Committee considered a
joint report by the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief
Executive and Head of Place, Property and Regeneration (circulated
previously) regarding a potential building acquisition.
 
The Committee also considered a
minute extract of the Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee
held on 4 June 2026 (circulated previously) which had supported the
recommendations in the report.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, officers outlined the risks associated with the
potential building acquisition.
 
The Committee considered a
joint report by the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief
Executive and Head of Place, Property and Regeneration (circulated
previously) regarding a potential building acquisition.
 
The Committee also considered a
minute extract of the Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee
held on 4 June 2026 (circulated previously) which had supported the
recommendations in the report.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, officers outlined the risks associated with the
potential building acquisition.
 
In reaching its decision, the Committee set out that it
recognises its responsibilities with regard to impending Local
Government Reorganisation and the financial viability and
sustainability of any new incoming unitary authority, nevertheless
the Committee have also taken into account:
 

The significant public interest from the local
community and overwhelming desire for positive intervention by
North Devon Council to save these buildings.
The asset being prominent listed buildings in the
heart of the Sub Regional Centre and as such strong action is
likely to remain an ongoing corporate priority, for any new
authority in the longer term.
Waiting for the new authority ‘to bed
in’ would lead to further deterioration of the fabric of the
buildings.
The viability deficit is unlikely to be closed by
the private sector alone and the feasibility study (commissioned by
NDC with financial support from Historic England) suggests that
public sector funding would only be available to local
authorities.  This view is supported by
initial approaches to national bodies and confirmed in the officer
report.
At this stage there is no intention to commit the
capital funding, it was to ensure the saving of these buildings for
future use.
Enabling a mixed use to enhance the vitality of
Barnstaple and the wider North Devon community - bringing new
opportunities and high skilled employment to a sustainable
location.
Continuing the regeneration strategy that has
underpinned the Council’s priorities for some time, following
the purchase of Green Lanes Shopping Centre, the Future High
Streets Fund package, regeneration of Seven Brethren and the
Culture Fund interventions.

 
Taking these issues together, the Committee does not
believe that the decision to explore the possible acquisition of
the asset would prejudice the financial viability of any new
authority.  Furthermore, it is likely
that public ownership would lead to an exciting opportunity to win
inward investment for this asset.
 
RESOLVED:
 
a)        That authority be
delegated to the Head of Place, Property and Regeneration in
consultation with the Leader of the Council and Lead Member for
Regeneration, Economic Development and Planning to look to
negotiate the voluntary purchase of the buildings to secure them to
stem further deterioration and that a further report on the outcome
of the negotiations be brought back to the Committee for
consideration.  
b)        That the Council
work with other local and national partners, with an interest in
the retention and preservation of these listed
buildings.
c)         That the
Committee endorse the long-term aim of securing a regeneration
project for the re-use of the site.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to explore the acquisition of a building to save it from deterioration and secure it for future use.

content:
The Committee considered the
following notice of motion by Council on 22 April 2026 which had
been referred to the Committee for consideration:
 
“(a)      To actively
encourage partnerships with private and public sector organisations
to maximise the use of existing infrastructure for renewable energy
projects.
 
(b)       To call upon
government to develop policies that align with these priorities and
provide financial incentives for rooftop and car park solar
projects as and when funding becomes available.”
 
In response to questions by the
Committee, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised the following:
 

That the Council was
anticipating that Great British Energy would make available
potential funding for renewable energy projects on local authority
buildings.  In preparation for that,
South West Net Zero hub were in the process of collating details of
local authority projects.  The Council
would look to put forward projects at Green Lanes, Brynsworthy
Environment Centre, Barnstaple Pannier Market, Barnstaple Bus
Station, Tarka Tennis and solar on some car parks.
In relation to Green
Lanes, it was proposed to upgrade the LED lighting at a cost of
£100,000 and instal PV solar panels on the top deck of the
car park at a cost of £300,000 which would benefit retailers
and tenants through the service charges.  It would potentially generate energy savings by
reducing current annual lighting costs by approximately
£32,000 and energy costs of £37,000 following the
installation of PV panels which could achieve a total £70,000
savings per year and the costs would be repaid within six
years.  If external funding was secured,
the net costs would be reduced further. 
The project had been previously identified and funding for wider
capital improvements at Green Lanes had been allocated within the
Capital Programme. There may be potential to instal PVs on the
lower deck of the car park in the future.
As part of the
capital programme, the flooring at Green Lanes had been upgraded
and remedial works had been carried out on the roof.  The recent works to the roof would potentially
alleviate the need to carry out significant capital works to the
roof in the short term.

 
RESOLVED that the notice of
motion be adopted and that the Climate Action Team be requested to
look at the detail of how the Council can actively encourage
partnerships with private and public sector organisations to
maximise the use of existing infrastructure for renewable energy
projects.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to actively encourage partnerships for renewable energy projects, with a focus on maximizing the use of existing infrastructure.

content:
The Committee considered a
joint report by the Head of Environmental Health/PMO and Head of
Governance (circulated previously) regarding the Local Authority
Registered Providers (LARP) service specification and
policies.
 
The Head of Governance advised
the Committee of an additional recommendation “that contract
procedure rules be waived to formally appoint North Devon Homes as
the management agent for the Local Authority Registered
Provider”.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Head of Environmental Health/PMO advised the
following:
 

·        
North Devon Homes (NDH)
was already a trusted partner and intrinsically linked to the
Council and had a good reputation.  They
had been exceptionally helpful in terms of assisting the Council in
getting into a position to manage its social housing.

·        
A break clause would be included within the
management agreement.

·        
If the number of housing units increased,
consideration would be given to its operating model.

·        
NDH would manage allocations in accordance with adopted policies and
procedures.

·        
A local letting policy for Ilfracombe would be put
in place.

·        
That as Head of Environmental Health, she would be
the Senior Responsible Officer and her role would be to ensure that
the key performance indicators were adhered to, attend strategic
meetings and be the conduit with NDH.

·        
She regularly met with the Lead Member for Housing
and would provide guidance through the process.

·        
The number of social housing units was quite
small.  These properties were of good
quality and were quite new or had been refurbished. 

·        
All social housing units were subject to the same
rules in relation to right to buy.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Head of Governance advised the
following:
 

It was recommended
that the Service Specification for the provision of housing
management be approved in principle and that powers be delegated to
finalise the Management Agreement with NDH which would include the operative clauses that
enforce the Service Specification.
The proposed LARP
policies were based on NDH existing
policies which would enable NDH to
deliver housing services in line with their current
operations.
Some strategic
decisions, as the Landlord. would be retained and delegated to the
Senior Responsible Officer, rather than following the NDH policies. These would be set out within the
Management Agreement 
The Governance
Framework set out the shared governance arrangements, including the
new responsibilities of our committees in relation to the
LARP.

 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·        
Council owned properties would be less attractive to
right to buy due to the ceiling cost and it was less than
affordable than previously.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised the following:
 

·        
The recommended policies provided assurance of how
the properties would be managed.  If the
Council deviated from the proposed policies, it would be more
difficult for North Devon Homes to manage these properties and
would attract a potential higher management fee.

·        
Ownership of the social housing properties would
remain as a Council asset and future decisions on these properties
would remain with the Council.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The High-level aims and objectives of the LARP as
set out in paragraphs 4.2 to 4.8 of the report be
approved;

(b) 
Contract Procedure Rules be waived to formally
appoint North Devon Homes as the management agent for
LARP;

(c) 
The Service Specification for the provision of
housing management with North Devon Homes (Appendix A) be approved
in principle;

(d) 
The Performance Management Framework in Annex 1 of
the Service Specification, subject to any amendments agreed at the
North Devon Council and North Devon Homes Strategic Partnership
Meetings (Appendix B) be approved in principle;

(e) 
The North Devon Homes operational policies in Annex
2 of the Service Specification (Appendix C) be adopted;

(f)  
The LARP Rent Setting & Service Charge Policy,
Tenancy Management Policy as set out in Annex 3 (Appendix D) be
adopted;

(g) 
The Draft Site-Specific Information, including the
Local Lettings Plan for 36 & 37 Boutport Street, in Annex 5 (Appendix E) be
noted;

(h) 
The Draft Data Protection annex in Annex 6 (Appendix
F) be noted;

(i)   
The LARP Right to Buy Policy and Compensation Policy
will follow be noted;

(j)   
The Governance and Decision-Making Framework for the
LARP (Appendix G) be approved;

(k) 
Powers be delegated to:
a.   
The Head of PMO, Environmental Health & Housing,
the Head of Governance and the Senior Solicitor & Monitoring
Officer, in consultation with the Lead Member for Housing, to
finalise the Management Agreement with North Devon Homes, the
Tenancy Agreements, and to make any necessary amendments to

Devon Homes and the sign off process with the North Devon Homes
Board.
b.   
The Director of Resources and the Head of PMO,
Environmental Health & Housing, in consultation with the Lead

c.   
The Head of PMO, Environmental Health and Housing
and the Head of Governance, in consultation with the Lead member
for Housing, the power to make amendments and replacements to the
suite of policies set out in this report on an ongoing
basis

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
(circulated previously) regarding the transfer of community assets
expressions of interest.
 
The Director of Resources and
Deputy Chief Executive highlighted the following:
 

·        
The Marine car park public conveniences at Instow
– the car park was already controlled by Instow Parish
Council and the toilets formed part of the lease to Instow Parish
Council. The car park had planning permission in
perpetuity.  There were no risks to the
asset as part of Local Government Reorganisation.

·        
The expressions of assets had been considered in
accordance with the policy that had been approved by the Strategy
and Resources Committee and therefore consideration could not be
given to just recommending one asset transfer for each
parish.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised the following:
 

·        
There were 13 assets recommended to be considered as
a priority under phase one. 27 assets had been classified as
“Yes – non priority”.

·        
There was a need to consider the timing of the
proposed transfers and to balance the work alongside work required
as part of Local Government Reorganisation and the delivery of
current corporate priorities and projects.

·        
A number of
the assets recommended under phase one were public
conveniences put forward by Parish and Town Councils that had not
previously engaged with the Council in relation to the previous
review of public conveniences.

·        
There were 9 assets classified as “Further
consideration” whereby further information was required, some
of this from the Parish or Town Councils or from other
partners.  Following the receipt of the
additional information, consideration would then be given to
whether these should be included in the list for transfer to Parish
and Town Councils and if they should be prioritised.

·        
A risk assessment (RAG status) had been undertaken
in relation to assets that were being considered for transfer to
Parish and Town Councils.   Some
assets at Rock Park, Barnstaple had been categorised as “not
at risk” and others “potentially at risk” in
relation to the risk to the asset should it transfer to the new
authority and the impact on local council taxpayers should the
Parish/Town Council precepts need to increase to cover the costs of
the assets.  However, it was considered
that these assets should be considered at the same time and not in
piece meal.

·        
In accordance with the approved policy,
consideration would not be given to the transfer of income
generating assets such as car parks unless there were very strong
reasons for doing so.  All assets put
forward by Parish and Town Councils had been considered in
accordance with the policy. Assets would have previously been
transferred to the Council as part of the original Local Government
Reorganisation back in 1974.  If a
parish wished to purchase such an asset, this would be considered
separately.

·        
Once the list of assets to be considered under phase
1 had been approved, the next stage would be to discuss draft heads
of terms with the Parish and Town Councils to ensure that the
ongoing implications and the maintenance of the assets were
understood.  This would also include the
resources required and any such costs of transfer. There may be a
requirement to outsource legal work. 
Parish and Town councils could withdraw from the process at any
time up until the transfer of asset. 
Regular dialogue would be held with Parish and Town Councils and
updates would also be provided to the Committee.

·        
Where a Parish or Town Council had more than one
asset to be transferred, each asset would have a separate freehold
and there may be some efficiencies with the legal process and costs
minimised.

·        
If an asset had been categorised as a
“No” at this stage, if there were some changes to the
asset in the future then the asset could be potentially
reconsidered.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·        
As part of the initial communication that had been
sent out to Parish and Town Councils to gauge interest regarding
the transfer of assets, it had been made clear that by inviting
expressions of interest, the Council was not committing to
undertaking particular transfers  and
that the Council would need to consider the implications including
the resources on the Council undertaking such
transfers.  Consideration also needed to
be given to the resources required as part of Local Government
Reorganisation.

·        
Following the 85 requests received from Parish and
Town Councils, the report set out the process for prioritising the
transfer of assets and identified which assets should be considered
for transfer. If some assets were not transferred prior to vesting
day, then the new unitary authority could continue discussions with
those Parish and Town Councils.

·        
If there was a concern that there were assets that
had not been recommended to be determined under phase 1, a working
group could be set up to discuss these further and that the
decision to approve Appendix C should not be delayed. There was no
requirement to formally constitute as a working group and it could be set up at any time.

·        
The Devon Authorities were in the process of
appointing a consultant to map and identify all Council owned
cultural assets to enable these assets to be protected and managed
and to understand their importance within communities.  This information would be reported back to each
Council which was expected in August 2026.
 
Councillor Crabb read out a
statement on behalf of Councillor Maskell in relation to the Croyde
car park.
 
Councillors Clayton, Crabb, P.
Leaver, Williams and Wilkinson re-declared their Other Registerable
Interests and left the meeting prior to deliberations taking
place.
 
RESOLVED that Councillor Walker
be appointed to Chair the meeting.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The report and work undertaken to date in obtaining
expressions of interest from respective Town and Parish Councils
and the initial allocation of potential asset transfers against
approved policy as set out in Appendix A be noted;

(b) 
That the assessed RAG status shown for each asset as
set out in Appendix B be noted;

(c) 
That the priority phase one transfer of assets as
set out in Appendix C be approved and that the Head of Place,
Property and Regeneration be authorised to finalise the heads of
terms with the respective Town and Parish Councils and implement
the freehold transfer of the assets for phase one
transfer;

(d)  
A working group be set up to consider other
expressions of interests on an ongoing basis and any further
information received in relation to those assets put forward by
Town and Parish Councils detailed in Appendices A and B and the
Chief Executive approve the detailed composition of the working
group in consultation with the Leader of the Council.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the transfer of community assets expressions of interest to respective Town and Parish Councils.

content:
The Chair advised the Committee
that one of the objectors had requested that photographs of the
site be circulated to the Committee. 
This was a late submission and a copy had been provided to the
applicant. As it was a late submission, little weight could be
given to the photographs, these were circulated and the applicant
provided with a copy of the photograph pack.
 
The Committee considered a
report by the Lead Officer Development Manager (circulated
previously) regarding planning application 81320.
 
The Lead Officer Development
Manager advised that if the application was approved it was
recommended that a planning condition be included requiring a foul
drainage scheme to be submitted to and approved by the Local
Planning Authority.
 
The Senior Corporate and
Community Services Officer read out a statement on behalf Liz
Watkins (supporter), Stephen Jupp (objector) and Devon County
Councillor Richard Hopley.
 
Joshua Dunne (supporter), David
Barrow (supporter), Paula Roddy (objector), Martin Peake
(objector), David Morgan (objector), Gillian Vaux (objector),
Howard Tollie (objector), Emily Temple (agent) and Brian Symons
(Parish Council representative) addressed the Committee.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Lead Officer Development Manager advised the
following:
 

·        
Exmoor National Park Authority had raised no
objections to the application.

·        
If a local planning authority cannot demonstrate an
up-to-date 5 year supply of deliverable sites, the provisions in
paragraph 11(d) of the National Planning Policy Framework apply and
presumption in favour of sustainable development. Paragraph 11(d)
was therefore engaged.

·        
The Highways Authority had objected to the
application on the basis that the county roads providing access to
the site were by reason of their inadequate width, horizontal
alignment, condition and lack of footway/grass verge provision,
unsuitable to accommodate the increase in traffic likely to be
generated, with consequent risk of additional danger to all users
of that road, and interference with the free flow of
traffic.  The objection would also be on
the basis of the collision data. A condition was recommended
limiting parts of the site which may be used for any business
operations. In balancing the issues raised significant weight had
been given to the highways impact, however it had been slightly
reduced due to the limited overall movements likely from the site
and the number of pitches.

·        
In balancing the issues, limited to moderate weight
had been given to the pressure on local services. The site would
allow the applicant to access local services.   Limited to moderate weight had been given to
landscape and character impacts as there was not a significant harm
and impact on the landscape.  If there
was considered to be significant harm, this would be as a result of
special characteristics in the landscape which could not be
mitigated. In terms of visual impact, due to the site being located
on a gently sloping area of topography with well established
hedgerows, the wide ranging views were limited.

·        
Limited weight would be given to the application
being part retrospective.

·        
It had not been recommended that a personal
condition for the applicant being applied.  Condition 3 had been recommended requiring the
site not to be occupied by any persons other than gypsies and
travellers.  If the family moved, the
two pitches would remain on the site. 
It was not best practice to apply a personal condition, however
such a condition could be applied.  If
condition 3 was approved and the applicant sold the site, the site
would be sold at market rate for the provision of two pitches. If a
personal condition was approved, should the applicant move, then
the site would be restored to its original use.

·        
In terms of the location of local services, the
village of Brayford was located approximately 1 mile away which had
a primary school and village hall. 
There was a church located in Charles. 
The hospital was located in Barnstaple which was approximately 45
minute drive and the town of South Molton was located approximately
20 minute drive away.

·        
A condition requiring a lighting scheme to be
submitted and approved would achieve a more sensitive lighting
scheme as detailed in Condition 2. The condition would be
enforceable.

·        
The application was finely balanced. The table
provided in paragraph 8.11 was to provide a visual guide. The
balancing exercise undertaken was nuanced.

·        
The North Devon and Torridge Local Plan, policy ST20
stated that at least 15 pitches for permanent traveller
accommodation was required to be delivered during the period
2011-2031. 8 pitches had been delivered to date.  If this application was approved, a further 5
pitches would be required.

·        
Showed the location of the existing field gateway to
the southwest corner of the site located on the blue plan to be
blocked off.

·        
Each pitch would consist of one static caravan, one
touring caravan and one building to be used for the incidental
enjoyment of the pitch. The building would have a grey roof and the
touring caravans would be white.  It
would be difficult to condition the colour of the touring caravans
as they were not classified as buildings.

·        
There were generators on the site to provide
electricity. The applicant was currently in the process of
connecting to the grid. If a condition was imposed requiring
connection to the grid, there may be a time where the applicant
would be left without electricity.  As
the applicant lived on the site, it was in their interest that
there was minimal noise.  Environmental
Protection has not raised any objections regarding
noise.  If there was noise pollution in
the future, these can be reported to Environmental Protection who
could monitor and serve a noise abatement notice if
required.

·        
A condition was recommended requiring the submission
of detailed drawing in relation to fences, banks and other means of
enclosure.  It was proposed that
separations would be provided between the two pitches.

·        
Conditions were recommended to ensure that the final
details were approved by the Local Planning Authority, such as
landscape proposals.

·        
The application was for the provision of two pitches
(two homes).  Each pitch had two
caravans.  Due to the nomadic lifestyle,
a touring caravan needed to be located on the site.  Therefore there would be a maximum of four
caravans on the site.

·        
The applicant was a tradesperson, who would travel
to and from the site in a van.  No goods
were delivered to the site.  Goods were
delivered to customers.  A condition was
recommended requiring no goods to be stored on the
site.  The proposed condition 6 relating
to commercial activity including the storage of materials, plant
and equipment was appropriate.

·        
Recent Planning Inspectorate appeal taken in
relation to planning application 78493 whereby the Inspector had
included a personal condition and when it was no longer occupied
that the residential used permitted shall be
discontinued.

·        
A Noise Assessment had not been carried
out.

·        
The sizing of the caravans were within the
definition of the 1968 Caravans Act. 
The static caravans would remain on site.  The touring caravans would need to be
towed.  Two day rooms were proposed as
detailed in Condition 4.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Service Manager (Development Management) advised
the following:
 

·        
The provisions in paragraph 11(d) of the National
Planning Policy Framework applied and presumption in favour of
sustainable development.  However, it
would not apply if the site was located in a green belt, a National
Landscape, a National Park, designated heritage asset, and areas of
risk of flooding.  This site does not
fall within any of those designated categories.

·        
Officers were not recommending a personal
condition.  The agent had divulged
complex medical circumstances for the family.  A personal condition could be added limiting the
occupation to the applicant and his dependants due to the
exceptional personal and medical circumstances. If a personal
condition was included, the committee would need to consider
whether to also include condition 3.  If
condition 3 was not included, and the applicant ceased occupation
of the site then the site would be restored to its original use.
The personal condition would need to reflect this.

·        
Condition 4 provided details of what was included on
each pitch.

·        
Condition 10 provided details regarding the details
of the lighting being provided within 1 month of the
decision. 
 
Councillor Bulled, addressed
the Committee, in her capacity as Ward Member and had called in the
application for determination by the Committee.  She advised that she did not consider that she had
predetermined the application however, she had liaised with the
applicants, residents and the parish council and accordingly wished
to only speak on the matter as a Ward Member and would then will
leave the room for the deliberation and vote.  Councillor Bulled then left the room during the
consideration of the application.
 
RESOLVED that it being 11.43
a.m. that the meeting be adjourned for a comfort break and that it
be reconvened at 11.49 a.m.
 
RESOLVED (8 for, 4 against, 0
abstained) that the application be APPROVED as recommended by the
Lead Officer Development Manager subject to the
following:
 

(a) 
An additional condition being included to tie the
occupation of the site to the applicant and his family and that
condition 3 be removed;

(b) 
An additional condition being included requiring a
foul drainage scheme to be submitted to and approved by the Local
Planning Authority;

(c) 
That the trigger points contained within the
landscaping conditions be amended to reflect the correct seasons
and timings for planting;

(d) 
An additional condition being included in relation
to the use of the “Day rooms” being for incidental
use;

(e) 
That the drafting of the wording of the conditions
be delegated to the Service Manager (Development Management) in
consultation with the Chair of the Committee and Ward
Member.
