content:
The Senior Planning Policy
Officer (NDC), Elizabeth Dee, provided members with an update on
the Northern Devon Place Story, which was developed last year and
endorsed by both Councils, explaining the document’s
relevance to the development and drafting of the new Local
Plan.
 
It was explained the overall
purpose of the Northern Devon Place Story was to provide a
narrative about the area’s history, culture, community,
challenges, and future aspirations – and how this served as a
starting point for the Local Plan vision, which the new regulations
require.
 
Further detail was provided
regarding the required scope of the Local Plan vision, and the how
the content of the Northern Devon Place Story addressed these
areas.  Finally, the recommendations
were noted and a small typo addressed.
 
Members had a detailed
discussion, and the following points were made:
 

The value of this
document was noted in terms of Local Government Reorganisation,
Combined County Authority and attracting economic
investment.
The omission of
resilience and climate change adaptation was noted, along with the
omission of agriculture as a main industry.
It was confirmed by
the Senior Planning Policy Officer (NDC) that the baseline report
(item 11) would provide further evidence, including on
agriculture.

 
RESOLVED that Members of the Joint Planning Policy Committee
(JPPC) endorse the use of the Northern
Devon Place Story (Appendix 1) to inform the initial stages of
drafting of the vision for the new joint local plan.
topline: The Joint Planning Policy Committee has decided to endorse the use of the Northern Devon Place Story to inform the initial stages of drafting the vision for the new joint local plan.

content:
The Management Trainee for NDC,
Kit Ayers, presented the draft Consultation and Engagement Strategy
(attached with the agenda), explaining the purpose was to provide a
guide on the engagement work required for the new Local Plan to
ensure compliance and inform communities on how to get
involved.
 
It was confirmed this was a
first draft, which would be a working document amended through the
lifetime of the local plan development and to reflect updates to
Government guidance. It was explained that initial scoping
consultation would happen over the summer and would be an
opportunity to ask consultees about possible engagement methods,
with the aim to adapt based on feedback. 
 
The recommendations of the
report were noted and a verbal request for an additional
recommendation was made. The additional recommendation was for
delegated authority to the Head of Place, Property and Regeneration
(NDC) and the Head of Planning and Building Control (TDC) in
consultation with the Chair and Vice Chair of JPPC to prepare, approve and publish any
non-material changes to this strategy, including changes to the
wording, form and layout, to enable officers to enact those
expected applications mentioned above and to ensure compliance with
legislation guidance and emerging best practice.
 
The statutory requirements,
including the need to hold 3 consultations, were noted along with
the role of the thematic working groups, JPPC and district councillors in engaging and
communicating with the public on the importance of the local plan
was recognised.
 
Detail was provided on the on
the types of engagement work and the intended reach and work to
remove barriers to participation.  It
was confirmed that respective Communication Teams were developing a
communication plan to supplement the strategy, reinforcing key
messages and providing further structure – and examples were
provided (FAQs, myth-busting, social media polls).
 
In summing up the purpose of
the strategy was reiterated for Members, and it was explained this
would be a foundation on which to build engagement work for the
Local Plan. 
 
Members were asked for their
questions.
 
Members suggested that sessions
at community hubs could be arranged to assist young people or those
facing challenges with questionnaires, with advisors on hand to
answer questions and help was completion of feedback.
 
There was further discussion on
the need for engaging, shorter and focused online surveys, citing
the complexity of completing the recent Government consultation on
the national planning policy framework. The barriers presented by
complex consultations was recognised by officers and further detail
was provided on how engagement work would include more visual and
interactive forms of consultation.
 
Members noted the risk of AI
generated responses to online questionnaires. Officers acknowledged
this as a challenge and advised of potential sense checks, and the
use of AI to assist in the processing of responses.
 
There was interest in relation
to the myth-busting work, the challenge that members experience
when addressing concerns on housing numbers was noted, and it was
felt there was opportunity to raise awareness of impact of mandated
planning figures and the scope of the local plan in terms of the
meeting these requirements – managing
expectations.  This challenge was
recognised by officers, and it was confirmed housing numbers as one
of the key areas identified for this work.
 
RESOLVED that;
(a)   
Members of the Joint Planning Policy Committee
(JPPC) endorse the draft People and
Place Consultation and Engagement Strategy, and
(b)   
that, following a verbal recommendation requested in
the meeting,  delegated authority be
granted to the Head of Place, Property and Regeneration (North
Devon) and the Head of Planning and Building Control (Torridge), in
consultation with the Chair and Vice-Chair of JPPC, to prepare, approve, and publish any
non-material changes to the strategy (including wording, form, and
layout) to ensure compliance and best practise.
topline: The Joint Planning Policy Committee has decided to endorse the draft People and Place Consultation and Engagement Strategy for the new Local Plan.

content:
Eleanor Goodhead, Planning
Policy Officer (TDC), provided Members with a detailed presentation
on the draft baselining report. It was explained the purpose was to
build a picture of the plan area, showing current trends and future
scenarios, as a result this was a live document to be maintained by
officers. Detail was provided on the guidance the report was based
on and data collection sources that were used.
 
The key topics, listed below,
were highlighted and explained for Members in detail: 
 

Key
Features: Overview of area size,
population, natural/historic environment.
Population
Statistics: Changes over 20 years, ageing
population.
Changes Over Time
(Census 2011-2021): Household types, home
ownership, population density and context in terms of the national
picture.
Economy: Objectives from Economic
Strategy, core clusters (maritime, green energy), business
activity, deprivation indicators, digital connectivity.
Housing: Strategies, supply/delivery,
affordable housing, pressures (rents, house prices vs. income),
Gypsy and Traveller Accommodation Assessment.
Key Infrastructure
Delivery: Requirements, funding
statements, provision types, public transport, Infrastructure
Delivery Plan (85 requirements for main centres, 43 for local, 69
for villages).
Transport
Trends: Travel to work, car ownership
(high levels), work from home figures.
Connectivity: New government tool
(June 2005), showing differences between public transport and car
travel.
Environmental
Assets and Patterns: Flood risk, green
space, air quality, conservation, climate change
effects.
Future
Work: Local-level analysis, SWOT
analysis, interactive dashboard, further detail on health,
renewable energy, and heritage.

 
The next steps were explained
and Members were reminded of the recommendations in the report.
Feedback was welcomed whilst recognising that this was a working
document that would be added to over time.
 
Members noted that agriculture
was listed within the report as one of the five core clusters
– page 205, 4.3.
 
Members highlighted priorities
in the Devon Carbon Plan (rail connection, active travel) and the
need for Heywood Road roundabout improvements, enquiring about
Section 106 funding. Officers noted updates on Heywood Road
roundabout were referenced in the report appendix and the
Councillor was correct that more funding was required.
 
Members noted Table 7.7 in the
report – items not addressed – it was felt positive
that infrastructure had been reviewed and that Anchorwood cycling
bridge was noted in the report but queried a possible omission of
BARO2 (strategic Larkbeer connection) and BARO9 (Glenwood Farm
extension) from the table. Officers agreed to investigate these
potential omissions following the meeting (ACTION). 
 
Funding mechanisms and CIL
funding for larger projects was also noted – reflecting on
the need to prioritise how these projects were delivered,
connections at Roundswell were noted in terms of cycling routes,
including to Park School.
 
Members went on to thank
officers for a detailed report, noting it’s benefits as a
baseline report that would be built on over time. The need for
realistic plans that can be delivered was noted, along with the
benefits of the document in navigating a complex situation in terms
of planning.
 
Members welcomed the inclusion
of "working from home" and suggested further consideration of how
people access services in the new plan. For context, officers noted
potential COVID-era bias in census data used within the
report.
 
The Planning Policy Manager
added that future work would look to engage with infrastructure
providers and explore why some projects have not progressed, to
learn lessons from the previous plan.
 
RESOLVED that Members of the Joint Planning Policy Committee
(JPPC) recommend to:
1)   
Note the content of the Draft North Devon and
Torridge Local Plan Baselining Evidence Report (Appendix
1)
 
2)   
Note that this interim report will be used to
complete further analysis of the current information including
further statistical analysis at a local level. Officers can then
add more detail to the report and bring an update to a future
JPPC.
topline: The Joint Planning Policy Committee has decided to approve the Draft North Devon and Torridge Local Plan Baselining Evidence Report, outlining key features, population statistics, economy, housing, infrastructure delivery, transport trends, and environmental assets for future planning decisions.

content:
The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC), Ian Rowland, provided an update on the preparation of the
new Joint Local Plan for northern Devon. It was explained that
progress had previously been impacted by the national planning
reforms, but that the necessary secondary legislation came into
force on 25 March 2026, enabling formal commencement.
 
The Government’s proposed
timescales and the associated backstop dates were highlighted and
explained, alongside the Committee’s previously agreed
ambitions to progress locally at an accelerated pace alongside
Local Government Reorganisation. It was further confirmed that both
Councils had each successfully secured New System Plan Funding to
support plan preparation - approximately £108,000.
 
The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) advised Members on the requirement to prepare and publish a
Local Plan Timetable (Table 1, pages 12-13) and a Notice of
Intention to Commence Local Plan preparation, both of which are
required by legislation and must be published by 30 June 2026 in
prescribed formats (the publication of the Notice of Intention to
Commence by this date is a condition of the New System Plan
Funding). Subsequent to the agenda being published, Members were
advised the Government had issued further guidance on data
standards and an additional format would need to be published, it
was confirmed work was underway on this.
 
Further detail was provided on
the monitoring and review of the timetable, and it was confirmed
draft versions of both documents had been prepared and attached
with the agenda. Members were given a detailed summary of the
timetable and proposed deadlines, as well as the information
requirements set out in legislation – this was set out in
Appendix 1 of the report – and the requests for delegated
authority were noted and explained for Members in
detail.
 
Additionally, Members were
advised of a requirement for each authority to publish separate
timetables, however Officers will explore if a combined version can
be provided, recognising that this would be beneficial for the
public.
 
It was explained that no
Supplementary Plans were proposed at this stage and it was
suggested that the local plan would be known as the ‘North
Devon and Torridge Local Plan’, with a working title of
‘A Plan for Northern Devon’.
 
The Planning Policy Manager
(TDC) also outlined the next steps for early engagement, including
a proposed six?week scoping consultation, and provided an update on
project governance and programme management
arrangements.
 
An update was given on the
commissioning of the first tranche of technical evidence to support
the Local Plan, including a Housing and Economic Needs Assessment,
Gypsy and Traveller Accommodation Assessment and Level 1 Strategic
Flood Risk Assessment. It was confirmed that procurement processes
were underway, the challenges within the market were noted and it
was confirmed that further updates would be reported to the next
meeting.
 
Members were given an
opportunity to ask questions and the following was
discussed.
 
Members asked about the
potential impact of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and the
new authority, the Policy Planning Manager recognised this was
still an unknown, but noted Government guidance states that
Councils subject to LGR should continue to prepare local plans and
that new authorities should pick up existing work rather than start
from scratch.
 
Members raised concerns
regarding the timescales and whether there was adequate time to
engage with key stakeholders and gain their responses. The Planning
Policy Manager (TDC) confirmed that the timescales for formal
stages were set as minimums, and provided some detail on the
additional engagement work planned locally.
 
Members referenced the
milestones in Table 1 and asked for detail on the timing of
Highways evidence. The Policy Planning Manager confirmed that Devon
County Council had started work on a transport model for northern
Devon and advised on the type of data collection methods used to
form a baseline, how they would be used to map future scenarios,
and that the modelling would account for the seasonality of the
area. It was explained this modelling would allow for the
development of potential scenarios, which could inform the plan. It
was confirmed that updates would be provided at future
committees.
 
Members thanked the officer for
their work and reflected on the positives of such an ambitious
timetable. The recommendations were moved, but it was requested
that a date be added to the title of the new local plan to
establish it from the current plan.
 
There was a detailed discussion
and Members were advised of the reasoning for not adding a date at
this time, however it was felt important to differentiate between
the 2 plans for consultation purposes, and with this in mind it was
agreed the document name would be given further consideration
following the meeting and be brought back to the next meeting (both
suggested).
 
Members noted the importance of
the successful funding bid, in meeting the ambitious timetable,
especially given budget constraints. It was felt this could be put
to good use on the administration of the thematic working groups
and workshops.
 
Following a query regarding
Gateway reviews and decision-making processes it was confirmed that
the Joint Planning Policy Committee was constituted to take all
decisions related to the local plan, aside from the final decision
on whether to adopt the plan. 
 
Members noted that, following a
change of Committee membership, the thematic working groups should
now also be reviewed. 
 
RESOLVED that Members of the
Joint Planning Policy Committee (JPPC) recommend to:
 
1)   
Endorse the initial timetable for the preparation of
the new Joint Local Plan (Table 1);
 
2)   
Delegate authority to the Head of Place Property and
Regeneration (NDC) and Head of Head of Planning and Building
Control (TDC), in consultation with the Chair and Vice-Chair of
JPPC, to make changes to the dates in the initial timetable to take
account of detailed project programming and to finalise for
publication the formal ‘Local Plan Timetable(s)’ for
North Devon and Torridge (draft provided at Appendix 1), including
the making of changes to the wording, language, form and layout to
ensure legibility and compliance with legislation, guidance and
emerging best practice;
 
3)   
Delegate authority to the Head of Place Property and
Regeneration (NDC) and Head of Head of Planning and Building
Control (TDC) to approve and publish the final version of the
initial formal Local Plan Timetable(s) for North Devon and Torridge
on or before 30 June 2026;
 
4)   
Delegate authority to the Head of Place Property and
Regeneration (NDC) and Head of Head of Planning and Building
Control (TDC) to prepare, approve and publish necessary periodic
updates to the formal Local Plan Timetable(s) for North Devon and
Torridge;
 
5)   
Delegate authority to the Head of Place Property and
Regeneration (NDC) and Head of Head of Planning and Building
Control (TDC) to finalise for publication the formal Notice(s) of
Intention to Commence Local Plan Preparation (draft provided at
Appendix 2) including the making of changes to the wording,
language, form and layout to ensure legibility and compliance with
legislation, guidance and emerging best practice; and
 
6)   
Delegate authority to the Head of Place Property and
Regeneration (NDC) and Head of Head of Planning and Building
Control (TDC) to publish the final formal Notice(s) of Intention to
Commence Local Plan Preparation on or before 30 June
2026;
 
7)   
Agree that the Councils will not currently programme
the preparation of any Supplementary Plans; and
 
8)   
confirm the title by which the local planning
authorities will refer to the new joint local plan:
a)   
with it to be formally called the ‘North Devon
and Torridge Local Plan’, using the working title of ‘a
plan for northern Devon’ and that it is highlighted as being
prepared under the banner of the ‘people and place’
project; or
b)   
otherwise as agreed by the Committee.
topline: The Planning Policy Manager has decided to move forward with the preparation of a new Joint Local Plan for northern Devon, with approved recommendations for timelines, funding, and engagement strategies.

accommodation.

Understanding (MoU) with the MHCLG to secure LAHF Round 4 funding
in 2026/27 be approved;

(c) 
Authority be delegated to the Director of Resources
and Deputy Chief Executive and the Senior Solicitor and Monitoring
Officer, in consultation with Head of PMO, Environmental Health and
Housing to:
 (i) Finalise and sign the
MoU
(ii)Agree any
minor amendments required by MHCLG

The Capital programme be varied by £540,000
and that funds be released, subject to the signing of the
MoU;

(e) 
It be noted that delivery will be managed within
existing governance arrangements, with progress reporting through
established programme and capital monitoring processes.

Councillor Maskell presented

two of the notice of motion be referred to the Joint Planning
Policy Committee and points three and four be referred to the
Strategy and Resources Committee for consideration.

(a) 
That the following be referred to the Joint Planning
Policy Committee for consideration:
 
(i)           
To adopt a political stance, consistent with
planning law and the Local Plan, in favour of small, discrete,
solar panel installations, supporting their installation on:
-
a.   
Rooftops of commercial, residential and public
buildings.
b.   
Car parks through the development of solar
canopies.
(ii)         
To encourage the use of brownfield land for large
scale solar farms.

That the following be referred to the Strategy and
Resources Committee for consideration:

To actively encourage partnerships with private and
public sector organisations to maximise the use of existing
infrastructure for renewable energy projects.
(ii)         
To call upon government to develop policies that
align with these priorities and provide financial incentives for
rooftop and car park solar projects as and when funding becomes
available.
topline: The Council has decided to adopt a political stance in favor of small solar panel installations and encourage the use of brownfield land for large scale solar farms.

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Parks and Grounds Maintenance Manager (circulated
previously) regarding options for the Whiddon Valley
footbridge.
 
Councillor Rutty (Ward Member)
addressed the Committee in support of the replacement of the
bridge.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Parks and Grounds Maintenance Manager advised
the following:
 

·        
The transfer of the land forming part of the
cycleway and woodland from Pearce Construction which included the
eastern landing for the bridge was not required to enable the works
to be completed, as a works licence could be obtained.  There was no urgency for the transfer of the
land.

·        
The Council already maintained the area of land
which included cutting verges, inspecting and maintaining trees as
it was originally understood that the Council owned the
land.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised the following:
 

Given the position as
set out in the report, the transfer of the land should not present
a significant amount of additional work for the Legal
team
The Parks earmarked
reserve had accrued following the Parks service being brought back
in house.  This reserve was currently
used to replace machinery and equipment for the Parks
service.  Once the residual earmarked
reserve balance had been utilised, existing revenue budgets would
be used for the future replacement of machinery and equipment and
the Capital Programme for larger equipment needs.

 
It was suggested that the steel
framed bridge should be galvanised.
 
RESOLVED:
 

(a) 
That option three to remove the existing bridge,
steps and foundations and replace it with a new steel framed bridge
and associated foundations and steps be approved;

(b) 
That any associated cost be funded through the
Revenue Budget and the Parks earmarked reserve;

(c) 
That Legal Services investigate and undertake the
transfer of the land forming part of the cycleway and woodland
(edged in green) from Pearce Construction which includes the
eastern landing for the bridge. The land has been managed by the
parks team for many years.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to replace the Whiddon Valley footbridge with a new steel framed bridge.

The Committee considered a
report by the Head of Organisational Development and minute extract

2026 (circulated previously) regarding the Corporate Peer Challenge
report and action plan.
 
The Director of Resources and
Deputy Chief Executive outlined the discussions and minute extract
of the Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee meeting held on 9
April 2026.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised the following;
 

·        
The Lead Member for Regeneration covered the whole
North Devon area.  The Lead Member for
Coastal Communities included already the area of Ilfracombe as a
coastal community.  The action plan
included a recommendation that the role of the Lead Member for
Coastal Communities be expanded to specifically include Ilfracombe
and for the Lead Member to work in consultation with the Lead
Member for Regeneration.

·        
The recommendations were made following the
Corporate Peer Review and were not statutory. The action plan set
out the actions for each recommendation, some of which would evolve
alongside work undertaken as part of Local Government
Reorganisation. The timelines for the delivery of the action plan
would be considered alongside the Committee’s discussions
regarding reviewing the Council’s priorities.

·        
The Corporate Peer Review report alongside the
action plan would be published.

·        
The appointment of Lead Members was based on their
suitability and expertise in the subject matter.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, Councillor Prowse advised the following;
 

·        
Discussions had taken place with the Vice-Chair of
the Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee regarding developing
an evidence base for rural communities to help to inform the
proprieties of the new Unitary Authority.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Head of Organisational Development advised the
following;
 

·        
In relation to recommendation 3.5 of the Peer Review
“The Council must take proactive steps to address stretched
officer capacity before pressures escalate to unsustainable
levels”, discussions were taking place with the Committee
regarding identifying priorities for the next two years and to
review the action plan.
 
RESOLVED:
 

(a) 
That the LGA feedback report (the full report is
included in Appendix A) and the recommendations contained within be
noted and that the report be published on the Council’s
website;

(b) 
That the proposed Action Plan to take forwards the
LGA recommendations, as set out in Appendix B, be adopted subject
to reference to the role of Lead Member for Coastal Communities be
expanded and amended to “Lead Member for Coastal Communities
and Ilfracombe”;

(c) 
That the minutes and recommendations of the Scrutiny
and Policy Development Committee held on 9 April 2026 be
noted.

following:

Improvements to signage around the town centre
formed part of the Barnstaple Place Making project.  There was a need to review and consider areas to

·

to a future meeting of the Committee.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, Councillor Prowse advised the following;

A lot of work had been carried out in terms of

·

Lettings Agencies regarding fast tracking Flood Zone 3.  It was a priority to identify separate entrances

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Lead Planning Officer (Majors) (circulated
previously) regarding planning application 80058.
 
The Lead Planning Officer
(Majors) advised of the following:
 

Typographical
errors

Page 24 –
“A 30% policy compliant level…..” and not
“complaint);
Page 59 –
paragraph 5.44 – word “psychology” to be amended
to “ecological”;
Page 59 –
paragraph 5.45 – word “situation” to be amended
to “deciduous”;
Page 62 –
paragraph 6.7 phrase should read  ‘DCC have since confirmed there are
no technical objection to the access design proposed albeit no
detailed commentary of how this conclusion was reached has been
provided to the LPA.


A further three
letters of objection had been received since the publication of the
agenda, however did not raise any new
issues.
Technical matters had
arisen following a meeting that had taken place with the Highways
Officer of Devon County Council on 31 March 2026.  Safe walking routes to Roundswell Academy had been raised.  The Road Safety Officer had reviewed the route. A
previous planning application for development along Old Bideford
Road had secured works for the provision of a mini roundabout at
Tews Lane/Old Bideford Road. If this scheme did not come forward,
this application would need to secure the scheme.  The developer was in
agreement for a further condition to be include requiring
the submission of a scheme to secure a scheme for a safe walking
route north to the primary school.   The Highways Officer was present at the
meeting.
There was an ongoing
dialogue with the NHS regarding whether NHS contributions for Acute
Healthcare were justified as the earlier request  was not
currently compliant with CIL Regulation 122.  This had been challenged following recent case law
and further information had been provided.  Discussions had now taken place with the
developer and they had agreed to the
contribution of £398,226, as detailed in paragraph 9.1 of the
report, for Acute Healthcare. Further discussions would also be
taking place with colleagues at Torridge District Council
in regards to NHS acute care
contributions.

 
RESOLVED that it being 10.13 am
that the meeting be adjourned for a comfort break and that it be
reconvened at 10.18 a.m.
 
Councillor Lane re-declared his
non-registerable interest and left the room for the consideration
of the application.
 
The Senior Corporate and
Community Services Officer read statements from Darren Burnham
(objector), Geoff Hall (objector), Jennifer Dorey (objector), Kim
Ley (objector) and Linda Lee (objector) to the
Committee.
 
Mark Kidson (Chair of Horwood,
Lovacott and Newton Tracey), Claire Alers-Hankey (applicant) and
Andrew Pegg (agent) addressed the Committee.
 
Councillor
D. Knight, addressed the Committee in
his capacity as adjoining Ward Member.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Lead Planning Officer (Majors) advised the
following:
 

This planning
application and the previous planning application for 220 houses on
Old Bideford Road would be required to deliver and formalise and
provide the pavements and crossing point on Old Bideford
Road.  This scheme would provide a
footway and cycle link from Glenwood Drive. There was no plan to
provide a highway at Glenwood Road. 
This would require a separate planning application and change to
the access.
The developer was in
discussions with Stagecoach regarding the provision of a bus route
and it had been agreed that funding would be provided for the first
three years.  Discussions were taking
place between Devon County Council and Stagecoach regarding the
trigger numbers for the implementation of a bus route as part of
the section 106 process.
BAR09 had been implemented and
built out.  The dedication of land as
part of the section 106 agreement was designed to enable the future
delivery of the link scheme by Devon County Council as part of the
Transport Infrastructure Plan. As part of this application, only a
cycleway/footway would be provided on this land.
The developer had
based the signalised junction scheme on the Transport Assessment
and the number of traffic movements and had identified the
capacity.
There was an
aspiration for the provision of a park and change facility as part
of BAR10. 
The land was owned by Devon County Council.
The proposed housing
mix was not fixed and provided a buffer in the mix of types of
accommodation and would either be slightly higher or slightly
lower.
The timescales for
the delivery of the community centre would be considered as part of
the Section 106 agreement.
The gifting of land
to Devon County Council as part of the Glenwood Farm application
was a planning gain rather than a planning obligation. It future
proofed the land and the provision of a link road to come
forward.  Funding for a highway link
would be required as part of a future applications as no
s106 funds were taken as part of
BAR09 or BAR03 to deliver this link.
The capacity of the
existing highway network and wider strategic network had been
considered as part of the Transport Assessment.

 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Highways Officer, Devon County Council advised
the following:
 

Around 15 years ago,
it was proposed that a link road would be provided for Bickington Road to Fremington Road and the
A39.  The
land had been secured as part of the Glenwood Farm scheme. This
scheme had not received local support and had been removed from the
Local Plan.  There was no option
agreement in place to draw down and deliver this scheme. The scheme
was still included within the Infrastructure Plan, however was not a priority as there was no appetite
to deliver the scheme.
This application
would provide for a footway/cycleway scheme. In terms of walking
and cycling routes, the distances to the nearest facilities were
approximately 1.5-1.8 km.  These
distances were less than 3km which
would now be considered as being sustainable. The routes
were considered to be within suitable,
safe and convenient walking distances.
As part of this
application and previous applications, early discussions had taken
place with the Highways Authority regarding the provision of a
roundabout. At the early stage, a roundabout scheme was the
preferred option. However, the developer wanted to provide a
signalised junction. The developer had undertaken a detailed
Transport Assessment as part of the design concept for the
scheme.  A signalised junction would
accommodate traffic movements and had queuing capacity for both a
right turn or a left turn. This type of
junction would create natural breaks in traffic
movement.  During peak times, traffic
would be required to queue. There would be concerns if traffic was
being held up unnecessarily.  A
signalised junction would work better in terms of sustainability,
walking and cycling and crossing the A39.  There would be
more of an opportunity for vehicles get onto the Roundswell roundabout than there was currently. It
was considered to be acceptable in terms
of junction modelling.  There was no
justification to not accept a signalised junction
scheme.
The Transport
Assessment also took into account
current junction arrangements and the wider strategic network which
would also include the three key roundabouts at Lake, Roundswell and Barnhenge.  Manual
traffic counts taken in 2022 and updated in 2024 were taking into
consideration using industry standard software. Trip rates were
also taken into consideration.
Consideration was
also given to permissions granted as part of other planning
applications.
Tempo software was
also used which provided censor data which included projected
population growth, age of population and car demand.
The Highways
Authority considered peak traffic times to be week days between 8.00 – 9.00 am and 5.00 -
6.00 pm.  Outside of these times,
the majority of the time there was free
flowing traffic.
Schemes were
considered as a whole and not in isolation.
The park and change
facility as part of BAR10 would not be
coming forward at this stage.
Previously it had
been proposed that the development would have more than one access
out of the site.
Accidents occurred
which caused traffic gridlock, however
an application could not be refused on that basis. The design of
the junction was generous in terms of the number of lanes being
provided.  With the
exception of a serious traffic accident occurring, it was
expected that traffic would move freely.
There was no broad
strategic masterplan in place as the site was non-plan
led.  A masterplan was proposed as part
of the Larkbear planning application,
which was withdrawn, that included trigger points for delivery in a
timely manner.

 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Service Manager (Development Management) advised
the following:
 

The HEDNA mix sought a mix of types of accommodation to
meet the needs of the community and was not
prescriptive.
The Local Plan had
been adopted in 2018 which had been prior to consideration of the
Glenwood Farm application. We recognise in planning that things can
change and another technical solution (for example for a highway
access) may be presented in a formal planning application that
could be technically acceptable.
If the application
was appealed, the Planning Inspector would take into consideration
the technical Transport Assessment and view of the Highways Officer
that a safe junction would be provided for the number of traffic
movements identified.
Since consideration
of application 76293 in 2024, there had been a
number of wider changes including the Government
re-introducing mandatory targets for the delivery of 1,300
dwellings per year.  This application
was for a larger site, had better connectivity, provision of a bus
service, more mixed used and was sustainable.
If the applicant
raised concerns regarding viability, this did not have to be
considered for five years.  The delivery
of affordable housing would be a priority in any viability
challenge.
In terms of the
Larkbear application, section 106
contributions had been sought for the A361 link. 

 
Councillor Walker addressed the
Committee in her capacity as Ward Member.
 
RESOLVED (9 for, 4 against, 0
abstained) that the application be APPROVED as recommended by the
Lead Planning Officer (Majors).
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to approve planning application 80058, despite objections from local stakeholders and discussions on traffic management and community facilities.

to

to

to

54923

The Committee considered a report by the Head of Customer
Focus (circulated previously) regarding the Crisis Resilience
Fund.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
Customer Focus advised the following:
 

·        
The Council was
working alongside other Devon District Councils and Devon County
Council to finalise a unified Devon approach document.

·        
The Government had now
issued the management information return requirements.

·        
Not all arrangements
for the provision of resilience services would be in place by the 1
April 2026 and maybe limited at the start.  However, it was anticipated that all resilience
services would be in place by the summer.

·        
Not everyone would
qualify for a crisis payment, however may benefit from resilience
services.  A meeting had been arranged
with local organisations next week to discuss arrangements for the
provision of resilience support. 
Arrangements would also be in place for local organisations to be
made referrals into the Council.  Local
organisations would be offered free space at the Town Centre hub
and discussions had also taken place with Ilfracombe Town Council
regarding providing space for local organisations.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The contents of the report be noted;

(b) 
The final policy be approved by the Chief Executive,
as an urgent decision by the end March to ensure we have an
approved policy in place for 1st April 2026.

(c) 
The outcomes of the Equality Impact Assessment as
summarised in paragraph 6 of the report be noted.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the Crisis Resilience Fund policy for implementation by the end of March.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Director of
Resources and Deputy Chief Executive (circulated previously)
regarding a policy for the transfer of community assets.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·        
Consideration would be
given to the impact on teams within the Council in dealing with the
number of requests for the transfer of community assets and whether
any part of this process could be outsourced externally.

·        
Any lease obligations
on current community assets would be transferred with the
asset.

·        
A
number of assets were under the value of £100,000 and would not
require the consent of the Secretary of
State for land transfer when a structural changes order
comes into force for Local Government Reorganisation.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Chief
Executive advised the following:
 

·        
That in addition to
the impact on Council resources, consideration would also need to
be given to the impact on the community. The Government had issued
guidance which included a range of issues that would need to be
taken into consideration.

·        
As part of Local
Government Reorganisation, all of the Council’s assets would transfer to the new unitary authority as part of the
structural changes order.  This had
happened with other Local Government Reorganisations and there were many examples of
transfer of community assets to Parish and Town
Councils.  The transfer of Council
assets would form part of the conversations leading up to the
vesting day for the new unitary authority.

·        
The Section 24
structural changes order would set out the limits for land
transfer.  The limits were currently
unknown.

·        
The transfer of
community assets to Parish and Town Councils needed to take place during the lifetime of this
Council.

·        
If in the future
following the transfer of a community asset, circumstances changed
that there was a need for a release of covenant on the land, then a
request would need to be made to the new unitary
authority.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The report and work undertaken to date in obtaining
expressions of interest from respective Town and Parish Councils be
noted;

(b) 
The policy for the transfer of Community Assets as
set out in Appendix B be approved.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to approve the policy for the transfer of Community Assets.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Harbour Master
(circulated previously) regarding Council owned marine
assets.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Harbour
Master advised the following:
 

·      
It was recommended
that Fremington Quay was now removed from the scope of this project
and a separate capital bid would be prepared to support the works
required to make the site safe.  All of
the marine ladders and fenders would need to be removed.

·      
The works required to
be undertaken at Rolle Quay would be carried out in consultation
with the users of the quay.

·      
There would be no
change or impact on existing users of Fremington Quay for uses such
as fishing, recreational water users, walking and
cycling.

·      
There were no
timescales currently for works to be undertaken at Rolle and Castle
Quays, as further stage 2 investigation including intrusive
assessment and materials testing was required to be carried
out.

·      
The swing bridge was
owned by Devon County Council and was therefore outside of the
remit of the Council as a Duty Holder. 
However it played a role in the management system and the users had
good working relationship with Devon County Council.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Senior
Engineer advised the following:
 
·      
A separate business
case would be produced for works to be undertaken at Fremington
Quay due to its poor condition.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
Following the feedback from the public consultation,
the condition assessments and the initial findings from the
external Port Marine Safety Code (PMSC) audit:
a.    
It be noted that in accordance with paragraph 1.4.2
of the report that Fremington Quay was now removed from the scope
of this project and a separate capital bid will be prepared to
support the works required to make the site safe.
b.    
That Castle and Rolle Quay be retained as the named
Marine Facilities;
c.    
That a management and audit strategy for both Rolle
and Castle Quays be put in place to meet the requirements of the
PMSC;
d.    
That further stage 2 investigation including
intrusive assessment and materials testing be carried out for Rolle
and Castle Quays.

(b) 
The outcomes of the Equality Impact Assessment as
summarised in paragraph 6 of the report be noted.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to remove Fremington Quay from the project scope and prepare a separate capital bid for its safety works, while retaining Rolle and Castle Quay as Marine Facilities with further investigations and audits to be carried out.

The Committee considered a report by the Senior Planning
Officer (SE) (circulated previously) regarding planning application
80389.
 
The Senior Planning Officer (SE) advised that following the
site inspection on 10 December 2025, further consultation had taken
place clarifying that the application included parking for the
donor dwelling.  Following the
further  consultation, one
representation had been received from a neighbour in support of the
application and there had been no changes from any of the
consultees.
 
The Senior Corporate and Community Services Officer read
out a statement on behalf of Luke Mendham (supporter).
 
Allan Green (applicant) and Christopher Wilkinson (agent)
addressed the Committee.
 
Councillor Wilkinson, in his capacity as Ward Member,
addressed the Committee in support of the application.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Senior
Planning Officer (SE) advised the following:
 

·        
The removal of the
wall did not form part of this application.  If the wall was to be removed, it would need to be
included within the red line.  However,
the wall was outside of the red line.

·        
The red line had not
been changed.

·        
The further
consultation undertaken had been to clarify that the two parking
spaces would be retained for Blue Bay and that there would be
parking associated with the applicant’s dwelling.

·        
It was understood that
works would be undertaken to the gradient of the slope to the two
parking spaces.

·        
The applicant had not
amended the red line and wished to retain two parking spaces for
Blue Bay.  The description for the
planning application had been amended to reflect this
change.

·        
The Heritage and
Conservation Officer had calculated the floor area of the existing
garage was approximately 24 square metres and the proposed house
had a floor area of 192.8 square metres.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Service
Manager (Development Management) advised the following:
 

·        
That the description
of the planning application had been amended to include the
creation of two off road parking spaces for Blue Bay. Parking would
also be provided for the proposed dwelling.

·        
If the committee was
minded to approve the application, then a condition could be
included to retain parking to the east for residents and occupiers
of Blue Bay.

·        
Planning application
78702 which had been refused was refused on similar grounds as this
application.  She read out the reasons
for the refusal to the committee.

·        
Advised the committee
of another application whereby the Planning Inspector had
overturned the decision as it was considered that the application
enabled conservation and enhancement as it included the planting of
additional trees to protect the area.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Solicitor
advised the following:
 

·        
The Council as the
Planning Authority was responsible for taking planning decisions
which were lawful and robust.  Parish
Councils were consultees and were asked for their opinions on
planning applications. They were not bound the same way in terms of
legislation as Local Planning Authorities.

·        
If the Committee was
minded to approve the application, it would need to go through the
process of considering each reason for refusal and have clear
reasons which were policy based for going against the
officer’s recommendation of refusal.  It would need to provide reasons based upon
evidence.

·        
There had been two
applications on this site which had been refused.  Since these applications had been refused, there
had been a change in the Section 245
(Protected Landscapes) of the Levelling Up and Regeneration Act
2023.  This duty had now been
strengthened since the previous applications had been
refused.  The reasons for the previous
refusals had been under the previous test and when the duty was not
as robust.

·        
It was important that
the committee’s reasons for approval were robust to minimize
potential legal challenge.
 
RESOLVED (7 for, 2 against and 2 abstained) that the
application be APPROVED subject to the Service Manager (Development
Management) being delegated authority to attach the associated
planning conditions.
 
REASONS
 
The Committee took into consideration the design, that the
passive house would reduce carbon emissions, it was publicly
beneficial and that the proposal would significantly enhance the
conservation area through good design. It considered that the
proposal was acceptable and in accordance with the following
policies of the North Devon and Torridge Local Plan:
 

(a) 
Policy ST04 –
that the development was of high quality and a sustainable
design;

(b) 
Policy ST09 –
that the proposal did not conflict with policy 7 of ST09 and it was
an improvement and did not detract;

(c) 
Policy ST14 –
that the development protected and enhanced the natural
environment;

(d) 
Policy ST15 –
that the proposal does preserve and enhance the historic
environment;

(e) 
Policy DM04 –
that it was a good design in terms of a new development, creation
of places and responds to challenges of climate change;

(f)  
Policy DM07 –
that the proposal does conserve and enhance the setting of the
conservation area;

(g) 
Policy DM08 (a)
– that it protected the landscape by reason of its site,
scale, design and appearance and that the development would further
the purpose of conserving and enhancing the natural beauty of this
part of the protected landscape and thereby complying with the
statutory duty under section 245 of the Levelling Up and
Regeneration Act 2023.
 
In light of the above, the Committee considered that the
proposal accords with the policies of the North Devon and Torridge
Local Plan when read as a whole.
 
The Committee also considered that although there were two
previous applications for refusal on this site there were no
material considerations worthy of sufficient weight which would
indicate a decision other than that above.
topline: The Planning Committee has approved a new dwelling with parking spaces, citing design, carbon emissions reduction, public benefit, and conservation area enhancement as reasons for approval.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Service Manager
(Development Management) regarding planning application 80787
(circulated previously).
 
The Service Manager (Development Management) reported that
since the publication of the report, two further letters of
representation had been
received.  One of these representations
had been from the Environment Agency who had no objections and the
other representation had been from a neighbour who had raised concerns which had been
previously raised and included within the report.
 
Jason Hammond (objector) and Matt Steart (agent) addressed
the Committee.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Service
Manager (Development Management) advised the following:
 

·        
The Committee could
only consider the application that had been submitted and not
consider land beyond the red line.

·        
There was no formal
footpath towards public footpath 17, however the public footpath
could be accessed from the site.

·        
An informative could
be included requiring hedgehog friendly fencing to be
provided.

·        
A construction
management plan condition would have been part of the previous
outline planning permission.

·        
Use of mobile phones
whilst driving was a Police matter and could  not be considered
as part of this application.

·        
The original planning
application submitted in 2022 had originally been for the provision
of four dwellings, which was then reduced to two
dwellings.  It had been reduced to two
dwellings due to amenity issues and the proximity to other
dwellings.

·        
It was proposed that
four trees would be removed.  The Landscaping plan included planting on the top
of the hedge.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Highways
Officer (PY), Devon County Council advised the
following:
 

·        
In terms of the width
of the road, 4.1m would allow a
commercial vehicle and car to pass and two cars to
pass.  Large sections of the road were
wider at 6m which would also two large commercial vehicles to
pass.  The road would not be
adopted, however it was not far from an
adoptable standard.  The width of the
road was adequate and met the appropriate standards.

·        
Where the road
narrowed, this was positive rather than a
negative, as it would slow vehicles.  In his experience, this road was quite slow in
terms of speed of vehicles.

·        
The road would be used
by domestic vehicles and the occasional commercial vehicle, which
was not considered to be excessive.
 
Councillor Walker, in her capacity as Ward Member,
addressed the Committee.
 
RESOLVED (9 for, 1 abstained, 0 against) that the
application be APPROVED as recommended by the Service Manager
(Development Management) subject to the following:
 

(a) 
That the Service
Manager (Development Management) be delegated authority to include
one additional condition “that prior to occupation of
dwellings, that the widening of the road be undertaken in
accordance with the site plan” and an informative that
hedgehog friendly fencing is provided;

(b) 
That condition 13 (a)
and (b) be amended as
follows:
a) Monday -
Friday 08.00 - 18.00,
b) Saturday
08.00 - 13.00
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to approve a planning application for two dwellings with conditions related to road widening and hedgehog friendly fencing.

content:
Councillor Clayton briefly left the meeting and Councillor
P. Leaver took the Chair in his absence.
 
The Committee considered a report by the Director of
Resources and Deputy Chief Executive (circulated previously)
regarding the Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium
Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031.
 
Councillor Walker, Lead Member for Commercialisation and
Resources introduced the report to the Committee.
 
The Committee received a presentation by the Director of
Resources and Deputy Chief Executive and highlighted the
following:
 

Finance Policy Statement November 2025 –
outlining the key issues, leading Ministry of Housing, Communities
and Local Government proposal in consultation and the confirmed
policy position.
Finance Policy Statement November 2025 –
summary of transitional arrangements.
Draft 2026/27 Settlement.  In 2025/26 to 2026/27 there was a 5.7 increase in
core spending power across all Local Government.  In 2025/26 to 2028/29 that was a 15% increase in
core spending power across all Local Government.  This differed depending on which sector you were
in. Of £11.1bn growth in core spending power, £9.75bn
was from council tax or business rates (88%).  Of £11.1bn growth in core spending power,
£667m was from protection mechanisms (6%).
Core Spending power from 2026/27 to
2028/29.  Year on year change in core
spending power including Council Tax percentages.  Change in core spending power over the settlement
period percentages by type of authority.
Core Spending Power for North Devon Council which
included the Government grant and the ability to raise Council
Tax.  Cash reduction on the level of
resources to deliver services when inflation had currently been
running at 3% annually.  This assumed
Council Tax raising to the maximum threshold.  A real terms reduction over the 3-year period of
-10%.
Business Rates 2026/27 revaluation.  There was a periodic reassessment of market rents
to establish valuations. Nationally the valuations were supposed to
be net revenue neutral (i.e. so increasing or decreasing market
rents nationally does not change the cost to business of business
rates).  Therefore when valuations have
increased nationally the multiplier decreased
nationally.
Business Rates 2026/27 revaluation – 2026 by
region
Business rate 2026/27 revaluation – average
regional changes in 2026 compared to 2023.
Business rates multiplier from 2017/18 to
2025/26.
Business rates 2026/27 –
appeals.  Revaluation would trigger
business rates appeals. To compensate for this, nationally the
multiplier was not decreased by the same percentage as the increase
in rateable values.  An allowance was
made for the future loss in rateable values following
appeals.
Business rates multiplier with
rounding.
Business rates multiplier including new
multipliers.
Fair Funding Review 2.0 – business
rates.  A Business Rates event had been
scheduled to be held on 11 February 2026 at Node for local
businesses to attend.
Medium Term Financial Strategy approved in
February 2025 for 2025-2031. 
Summary budget position for 2026/27.
Green Lanes – 2021/22 to 2024/25 there was a
cumulative net return of (£972,600).  The 2025/26 budget included rates and net rent
reduction of £275,000 in line with the original net rental
cashflow presented in June 2021.
Council Tax – in 2025/26 increased Band D by
£6.29 (equivalent of 2.99%.  Rural
Councils could increase up to 3% or £5 (whichever
higher).  £6.48 would increase the
£216.68 to £223.16 (increase of 2.99%)
Draft Revenue Budget 2026/27 (Appendix
A).
Draft budget 2026/27 assumptions – 3%
increase on salary costs, 2.99% (£6.48) increase on Band D
Council Tax, garden waste subscription increased from £60 to
£65.  Grants as detailed in
Appendix B.
Reserves (Appendix C). 
The General Fund balance forecast level at 31 March 2027 was
£1.238m (6% of net budget).  The
recommended level was 5%-10%. Earmarked reserves – forecast
level at 31 March 2027 was £5.337m.  In compliance with the Local Government Act 2003,
the Chief Financial Officer assured members of the robustness of
the estimates and the adequacy of the proposed financial
reserves.
Medium Term Financial Strategy refreshed for 2026
to 2031 period – funding and costs (Appendix D).
Capital Programme – investment plans for
2025/26 to 2027/28 of £27.772m.
Draft Capital Programme (Appendix E).
Projected borrowing need.
Risks that could affect financial
plans.
Timeline for the approval of the
budget.
Future options to consider in relation to
commercial ventures and additional growth through Business Rates
Retention.

 
Councillor Clayton suggested writing a letter to Government
regarding the requirement for the Council to spend money preparing
for Local Government Reorganisation, which should be funded
centrally rather than local Council Tax payers having to
pay.
 
Councillor York addressed the Committee in her capacity as
Trustee of Age Concern, Barnstaple and North Devon in relation to
funding to be potentially awarded to the organisation and then left
the meeting.  She circulated a copy of
the Garfield Weston core funding application and leaflet detailing
the services provided by Age Concern.
 
RESOLVED that it being 1.00 pm that the meeting continue in
order for the remaining business to be transacted.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·      
That the £15,000
from the North Devon Community Lottery central fund had been
included within the budget.  The
Committee could take a decision on the allocation of this fund at
the meeting of Council on 25 February 2026 as other information may
be presented from other recipients of strategic grants.

·      
In relation to Local
Government Reorganisation, there would be a need to understand the
level of debt from other Councils that would move into the new
Unitary Authority.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Chief
Executive advised the following:
 
·      
Informal meetings of
the Strategy and Resources Committee would be arranged to start to
prepare for Local Government Reorganisation.  Part of these discussions would be in relation to
budgets, medium term financial strategy and borrowing.
 
RESOLVED that:
 
(a)
     the latest forecast
for Budget 2025-26 and the proposed contributions to earmarked
reserves be noted;
(b)
     the Chief Financial
Officer’s assurance on the adequacy of the reserves and the
robustness of the budget in paragraph 4.1.4.7 of the report be
noted;
(c)      the
Chief Financial Officer’s highlighted areas of risk
identified within the budget process set out in paragraph 4.1.4.8
and section 4.3 of the report be noted;
(d)
     the latest Medium
Term Financial forecast for 2026-2031 as shown in section 4.1.5 of
the report be noted.
 
RECOMMENDED that:
 
(e)      there be
an increase of 2.99% (£6.48) in the level of Council Tax
charged by North Devon Council for 2026-27 with a Band D Council
Tax level of £223.16
(f)      
the actions identified in sections 4.1.2 to 4.1.4 of the report,
which are required to ensure a balanced budget is achieved and
therefore recommend to Council the approval of 2026-27 General
Revenue Account Budget.
(g)      the
Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031 in section 4.1.5 of the
report be adopted as part of the Policy Framework.
(h)      the
Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2027-28 as highlighted in section 4.2
of the report be approved;
(i)
      Council
determine the allocation of the North Devon Community Lottery
central fund of £15,000.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to approve a 2.99% increase in Council Tax and allocate funds for the Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Sustainability
Officer (circulated previously) regarding the Local Nature Recovery
Strategy.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the
Sustainability Officer advised the following:
 

·      
The Devon Local Nature
Recovery Strategy was a strategic document and a tool that provided
guidance and an evidence base to inform Local Plans and planning
decision making.

·      
The legislation was
quite explicit in that it was not a constraint placed on planning
and the mapping would inform policy to be included within the Local
Plan.
 
RESOLVED:
 

(a) 
That Committee agrees as the Supporting Authority
that the draft Devon Local Nature Recovery Strategy be finalised
for publication in Spring 2026;

(b) 
That authority be delegated to the Supporting
Authority lead officer (Sustainability Officer) to make or approve
any amendments following comments received to the public
consultation (Oct 2025) materials and prior to
publication.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to finalise the draft Devon Local Nature Recovery Strategy for publication in Spring 2026.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Director of
Resources and Deputy Chief Executive (circulated previously)
regarding the Financial Management report for quarter 3 of
2025/26.
 
In response to questions, the Director of Resources and
Deputy Chief Executive advised the following:
 

The table detailed in paragraph 4.1.9 of the
report in relation to Green Lanes was the original table that had
been produced when the decision to acquire Green Lanes was taken in
2021/22.  . 
It was projected back in 2021 that the rental income would be circa
£1.1m for 2025/26.  There was an
expected reduction in cash flow, which had been
predicted.  It was hopeful that a new
tenant would be shortly moving into the vacant unit previously
occupied by River Island.  The net
income was still making a contribution to the Council and not all
of the external borrowing had been taken yet.
There were a number of reasons why the car parking
income had reduced.  Ringo was being
used by customers to pay for car parking for the time that they
were there.  Previously, some customers
would have paid more than the actual time using the car park. Ringo
provided the benefit of being able to extend the time of
parking.  Also an half hourly rate had
been introduced to encourage people to visit which was beneficial
for customers.  Less parking charge
notices were being issued, as customers were using Ringo for paying
for their stay in car parks.
The Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee had
set up a working group to review the Pannier Market’s
business plan.
Recycling sales were estimated to be down by circa
£80,000, however it was anticipated that following the
installation of the new baler, that the quality of the materials
would improve and the recycling sales would increase.

 
In response to questions, the Chief Executive advised the
following:
 
·      
That the Civil
Enforcement Officers were there to assist members of the
public.  They were not given targets for
issuing parking fines.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The contributions to/from earmarked reserves
(section 4.2 of the report) be approved;

(b) 
The movement on the Strategic Contingency Reserve
(section 4.3 of the report) be noted;

(c)  
The funds be released for the capital schemes listed
in section 4.4.8 2.5 of the report;

(d) 
The sections dealing with Treasury Management, Debt
Management and General Debtors (sections 4.5 to 4.7 of the report)
be noted.
 
RECOMMENDED:
 
(e) 
The variations to the Capital Programme 2025/26 to
2027/28 (sections 4.4.3 of the report) be approved.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to approve financial management decisions for quarter 3 of 2025/26.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Finance Manager
(circulated previously) regarding the review of fees and charges
for services 2026/27.
 
The Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised the following:
 

That further to the Committee’s earlier
decision today to continue with the Trade Waste collection service
for the collection of trade refuse and also schedule 2, there was a
requirement for the Committee to consider increasing the fees for
the collection of trade waste.  The
Committee was required to make a recommendation to Council on 25
February 2026 and to inform the budget report.  The fees needed to be increased to ensure that the
cost of the delivery of the service was recovered as a
minimum.
There was always a level of risk with setting fees
and charges.
The contracts for the collection of trade waste
were for a 12 month period.  If the
length of contract was reduced to enable fees to be reviewed, this
would have implications on the Finance team and there would also be
uncertainty for customers. If there was a surplus generated, the
committee could consider not increasing fees for the following year
2027/28.
Following the previous decision made by the
Committee all customers would be notified.  It was hoped that there would be some growth in
the number of customers following the positive public value being
placed upon the service.
When setting the fees for Trade Waste, there was a
need to take into account that small businesses were
struggling.
The Council benchmarked fees for non statutory
services to compare prices.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
Environmental Enhancement advised the following:
 

·      
That 82% of schedule 2
customers were commercial, but their trade waste recycling was
collected by domestic rounds.  Following
the decision made by the Committee, these customers would be
retained.

·      
There would be some
delay for businesses to decide whether to remain with the Council
or not.
 
RECOMMENDED that :
 

(a) 
There be a 3% increase in fees for 2026/2027
financial year, for the following services: (some
rounded)
a.    
Allotments – Appendix A
b.    
Building Control – Appendix B
c.    
Sports pitches – Appendix F
d.    
Pannier Market (Stalls and Events)) – Appendix
G
e.    
Pre-application Planning fees – Appendix
J
f.      
Event licence – Appendix L
g.    
Contractor Licence – Appendix M
h.    
Modification of S106 agreements – Appendix
N

 

(b) 
Council vary the remaining fees by the elements
outlined in sections 4.3 to 4.9 of the report;
 

(c)  
That the Trade Waste fees be increased by 46% based
upon a 40% drop off of customers.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to recommend fee increases for various services, including a significant 46% increase for Trade Waste fees in the 2026/27 financial year.
