content:
Councillor Walker requested that Council consider the
following recommendation “that
Councillors who represent Town or Parish Councils and/or the County
Council and which use the trade waste service be granted a standing
dispensation.  Such dispensation to be
limited to allow them to take part in the deliberation and vote on
the matter of the future service provision of the Council’s
trade waste and recycling service at Full Council and/or Strategy
and Resources Committee despite having a prejudicial Other
Registrable Interest as Town, Parish and/or County Councillors at
town and parish councils which contract with the District Council
for this service.  This is on the basis
that, in accordance with section 33(2)(c) and (e) of the Localism
Act 2011, such dispensation is in the interests of persons living
in the authority’s area and/or is otherwise
appropriate.”
 
It was moved by Councillor
Norman and seconded by Councillor Haworth-Booth that the
recommendation be adopted.
 
Councillors Bell (as member of
Braunton Parish Council and Devon County Council), Clayton (as
member of Barnstaple Town Council), Dawson (as member of Barnstaple
Town Council), Hunt (as member of Barnstaple Town Council), C.
Leaver (as member of Devon County Council), P. Leaver (as member of
Barnstaple Town Council), Lovering (as member of Barnstaple Town
Council), Orange (as member of Barnstaple Town Council), Patrinos
(as member of Lynton and Lynmouth Town Council), Quinn (as member
of Ilfracombe Town Council), Turton (as member of Ilfracombe Town
Council), Wilkinson (as member of Mortehoe Parish Council), York
(as member of Barnstaple Town Council) declared having a
prejudicial Other Registerable Interest as members of Town or
Parish Councils and/or Devon County Council and left the room
during the consideration of the recommendation.
 
Councillor Worden advised that
he would not be declaring an interest as South Molton Town Council
was previously a customer of the Trade Waste service provided by
North Devon Council, however they had now had another provider for
this service.
 
Councillor Bushell advised that
he would also not be declaring an interest as South Molton Town
Council was previously a customer of the Trade Waste service
provided by North Devon Council, however they had now had another
provider for this service.
 
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
Councillors who represent Town or Parish Councils
and/or the County Council and which use the trade waste service be
granted a standing dispensation;

(b) 
Such dispensation to be limited to allow them to
take part in the deliberation and vote on the matter of the future
service provision of the Council’s trade waste and recycling
service at Full Council and/or Strategy and Resources Committee
despite having a prejudicial Other Registrable Interest as Town,
Parish and/or County Councillors at town and parish councils which
contract with the District Council for this service;

(c)  
this is on the basis that, in accordance with
section 33(2)(c) and (e) of the Localism Act 2011, such
dispensation is in the interests of persons living in the
authority’s area and/or is otherwise appropriate.
topline: The Council has decided to grant standing dispensation to councillors with potential conflicts of interest to participate in trade waste service provision decisions.

content:
Council considered the report by the Works and Recycling
Manager regarding the Trade Waste Service Review that was
considered by the Strategy and Resources Committee held on 5
January 2026 (circulated previously).
 
Councillor Walker requested that Council consider the
following recommendation:
 
“To waive the council
procedure rules in the constitution to allow an additional three
members of the public who are representing businesses to be
permitted to speak for up to 5 minutes and that the council’s
debate on the petition be extended from 30 minutes to up to a
maximum of 1 hour”.
 
The recommendation was moved by
Councillor Jones and seconded by Councillor Orange.
 
RESOLVED that the council
procedure rules be waived in the constitution to allow an
additional three members of the public who are representing
businesses to be permitted to speak for up to 5 minutes and that
the council’s debate on the petition be extended from 30
minutes to up to a maximum of 1 hour.
 
Olly Seymour (petition
organiser) presented the petition regarding the North Devon Trade Waste Service
to Council (circulated previously).
 
Tudorel Vintila (Siam Bistro) addressed
Council.
 
David Hughes (Watermouth Valley
Camping Park) addressed Council.
 
Bill Bowen (Warkleigh Caravan site) addressed
Council.
 
It was moved by Councillor Clayton and seconded by
Councillor Topps that “Council
recognises that it cannot continue to run a loss making trade waste and recycling collection
service, subsidised by ordinary council taxpayers.  It also
recognises that the changes brought in by government as part of the
Simpler Recycling rules will make the service even more
unviable.  At the same time, council understands the pressures
faced for example by charities and small
scale holiday accommodation providers.  Council
recommends that Strategy and Resources committee look again at the
viability of continuing to provide a trade waste collection service
to these and other Schedule 2 customers on a full cost recovery
basis as a minimum”.
 
In response to questions, the Head of Environmental
Enhancement advised the following:
 

·      
That 20 businesses had
cancelled their contract for Trade Waste and confirmed that they
secured another supplier.

·      
South West Metals were currently in discussions with
approximately 300 customers.

·      
A business waste
broker was in the process of assisting approximately 50 businesses
to find an alternative supplier.

·      
The Trade Waste
collection lorry broke down on a regular basis.  It was now back on the road.  It was a specialist vehicle which was coming to
the end of life and it was expensive to
replace.  If the decision was taken to
continue with the collection of Trade Waste, the vehicle would need
to be replaced and there was an 18 month
lead in period.  Therefore, as an
interim measure there would be a requirement to hire in two loaders. 
This was an old vehicle that the Council had purchased. The Council
was now leasing all other vehicles.
 
In response to questions, the Senior Solicitor and
Monitoring advised the following:
 

·      
Schedule 2 waste was
classified as either household waste, commercial waste, or
industrial waste depending on its place of production, nature, or
the activity producing it. The Controlled Waste (England and Wales)
Regulations 2012 provide detailed classifications of waste types,
including Schedule 2 waste, and specify the circumstances under
which waste is treated as household, commercial, or industrial
waste. Schedule 2 waste is generally
treated as household waste under the Environmental Protection Act
1990, section 75(5), which defines household waste as waste from
domestic properties, caravans, residential homes, hospitals,
schools, and other similar premises.

·      
However, the
Controlled Waste Regulations 2012 further specify that certain
types of household waste may be treated as commercial waste for the
purposes of charging for disposal. For example, waste from domestic
properties used for business purposes, such as self-catering
accommodation, or waste from premises occupied by charities for
non-public purposes, may be classified as commercial
waste

·      
Accordingly there was not a general duty for local authorities
to collect Schedule 2 waste which constitutes commercial
waste.

·      
The Environmental
Protection Act allowed local authorities to find other means of
contracting out the collection of commercial waste.
 
An amendment was moved by Councillor Maskell and seconded
by Councillor Wilson:
 
“1. That Council asks Strategy and Resources to
review their decision in light of
updated pricing information.
2. That Council ask Strategy and Resources to consider
retaining the service for a minimum 12
month period, based on a new charging structure that will be
at least cost neutral to the council.
3. That the lead member prepares a regular report on the
finances and progress of the improvements”.
 
In response to questions, the Director of Resources and
Deputy Chief Executive advised the following:
 

·      
There were currently
two trade waste collection rounds and
one recycling round.

·      
82% of the waste
collected under schedule 2 were
collected by domestic rounds.  The
remainder was collected by the trade waste collection
rounds.

·      
The fees would need to
be increased for the service to break even.

·      
The Strategy and
Resources Committee at its meeting on 5 January 2026 had taken a
decision to stop the trade waste collection service.  At that meeting, it had
been discussed that if the trade waste refuse only collection service was to continue, the
fees would need to be increased between 7-8% based on the level of
customers at that time. Since that meeting, there was a potential reduction in the number of customers
of between 20-30%.  Therefore the fees would now need to be increased by
a higher percentage if this element of the service was
retained.
 
It was moved by Councillor Maddocks and seconded by
Councillor Bushell that the vote be taken by a recorded
vote.
 
RESOLVED that the vote be taken by a recorded
vote.
 
A
recorded vote was taken on the proposed amendment:
 
Voting for the amendment:
 
Councillors Bell, Bulled, Bushell, Crabb,
Haworth-Booth, Jones, Lethaby, Maddocks, Maskell, Milton, Patrinos,
Prowse, Quinn, Turton, Whitehead and Wilson.
 
Voting against the amendment:
 
Councillors Cann, Clayton, Coombs, Dawson, Hunt,
Jusef, D. Knight, R. Knight, Lane, C. Leaver, P. Leaver, Lovering,
Norman, Orange, Topps, Walker, Wilkinson, Worden and
York.
 
Abstained from voting:
 
None.
 
Totals: 16 For, 19 Against and 0 Abstained.
 
The amendment was lost.
 
Councillor Clayton agreed to amend his motion to take on
board Councillor Prowse’s comments and to delete the wording
“to these and other schedule 2 customers”.
 
An amendment was moved by Councillor Bushell “that
the decision be taken by full Council”.  There was no seconder.
 
The Chief Executive advised that the Council’s
petition scheme stated that if the matter was the responsibility of
the Strategy and Resources Committee, then the committee would take
the final decision, however Council could inform the
Committee’s decision.
 
A
further amendment was moved by Councillor Jones and seconded by
Councillor Bushell “that a survey of customers be carried out
to find out the current position, review the competition, identify
where there were gaps in service provision and pricing structure of
competitors.”
 
The Chief Executive advised that an email to survey existing customers could be carried out,
however, the Council would not be able to ascertain the pricing
structure of competitors.
 
Councillor Jones withdrew the amendment.
 
A
recorded vote was taken on the motion:
 
Voting for the motion:
 
Councillors Bushell, Cann, Clayton, Coombs, Dawson,
Haworth-Booth, Hunt, Jones, Jusef, D. Knight, R. Knight, Lane, C.
Leaver, P. Leaver, Lethaby, Lovering, Maddocks, Milton, Norman,
Orange, Patrinos, Prowse, Topps, Walker, Wilkinson, Wilson, Worden
and York.
 
Voting against the motion:
 
Councillors Bulled, Crabb, Maskell, Quinn, Turton and
Whitehead.
 
Abstained from voting:
 
Councillor Bell.
 
Totals: 28 For, 6 Against and 1 Abstained.
 
The motion was carried.
 
RESOLVED that:
 
(a) 
Council recognises that it cannot continue to run a
loss making trade waste and recycling
collection service, subsidised by ordinary council
taxpayers. 
(b) 
It also recognises that the changes brought in by
Government as part of the Simpler Recycling rules will make the
service even more unviable. 
(c)  
At the same time, Council understands the pressures
faced for example by charities and small
scale holiday accommodation providers. 
(d) 
The Strategy and Resources Committee look again at
the viability of continuing to provide a trade waste collection
service on a full cost recovery basis as a minimum.
topline: The Council's Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to extend the debate on the trade waste service review, considering the financial viability and impact on stakeholders.

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Planning Policy Team Leader (TDC) regarding the
Update on the Preparation of a New Joint Local Plan (circulated
previously). 
 
The Planning Policy Team Leader
presented the report to the Committee and confirmed
that:
 

The report provided
an update to the preparation of a new joint local plan, however, it
was tentative and based upon limited detail about planning reforms
and no firm understanding of the timing or nature of the new plan
making system. The authorities had now received some more detail -
although not the full picture.
Plan-making Guidance
(draft form) and details of what the Government expected to set out
as the process had been received - but not the actual regulations -
latest insight suggested would be issued on 30th
January.
It confirmed a
30-month plan-making and examination period, shouldered by a
'getting ready' pre-period and a post-adoption monitoring
period.  Importantly, the draft guidance
set out a lot of what was expected or required during the initial
'getting ready' period.
Appendix 2
consolidated some of the key guidance, focussing on the 'getting
ready' phase.
Getting ready phase
was a minimum of 4-months - predicated by the need to give formal
notice of commencing plan-making at least 4-months prior to the
formal start of the 30-month period. This would culminate in the
completion and publication of a Gateway 1 Self-assessment, which
triggers the commencement of the start of the formal 30-month
period.
In terms of the
getting ready phase - expected to make process in five
areas:

Local plan
timetable
Project management
and governance
Consulting and
engaging on the plan
Content of the
plan
Strategic
Environmental Assessment (SEA)


The required process
is to:

Prepare and publish
first version of local plan timetable
Publish formal notice
of intention to commence
Run a scoping
consultation


Expected to make
progress on a range of other activities including:

Project management
and governance arrangements, preparation of a Project Initiation
Document (PID)
Baselining
Begin evidence
gathering Availability of land, including a call for
sites
SWOT analysis of the
area and its context
Scope of the plan -
main areas and locally specific topic matters
Initial shaping of a
draft vision
Identifying
measurable outcomes
Likely levels of
development
High-level spatial
options and topics that might need policies
Scope and commence
SEA



 

Progress had already
been made on a number of these activities - with more work
ongoing.
PID - set out details
of programme, project management, resourcing, governance, etc. The
PID was now a mandatory requirement. The PID would be developed
over the coming months, with an expectation of a complete version
to be available by the time pass through Gateway 1
Self-Assessment.
PID sets out
indicative timeline. Including indication of publishing notice of
intention to start plan-making in June 26 and Publishing a Gateway
1 Self-assessment and commencing 30-month period in October 2026.
This fitted perfectly with a recently announced funding opportunity
- New System Plan Funding.
£14m was
available (in total) to support plan-making for any plans
deliverable by the end of the year. It was expected that
approximately £120k would be available to each Local
Authority. Each would have to submit a separate expression of
interest.

 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Planning Policy Team Leader advised:
 

The team had been
advised to continue with the works on the new plan, regardless of
the current Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) discussions. This
would then hopefully help to best secure the direction of travel
for the area going forward.
Neighbourhood Plan
funding had been withdrawn although the process, and legislation
was still in place.

 
Cllr Clayton arrived
(10:45)
 
RESOLVED that:
 
(a) 
the emerging detail of the new plan-making system
and associated guidance, be noted,
(b) 
Officers be enabled to update and continue to
progress activities deemed as necessary within the ‘getting
ready’ phase of plan-making, including the development of a
detailed plan making programme,
(c) 
the submission of an Expression of Interest by each
Council for New System Plan Funding be noted with the commitment to
work towards:
a.   
publishing the formal notice by 30th
June, and
b.   
publishing a Gateway 1 Assessment by 31st
October 2026, be supported,
(d) 
the initial draft of the People and Place Project
Initiation Document (PID) be adopted;
(e) 
the Update on the Preparation of a New Joint Local
Plan be noted.
topline: The Joint Planning Policy Committee has decided to progress with the 'getting ready' phase of updating a new joint local plan, including submitting an Expression of Interest for funding.

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Senior Planning Policy Officer (NDC) regarding the
Draft National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) Consultation
(circulated previously). 
 
The Planning Policy Team Leader
(TDC) presented the report to the Committee and confirmed the
following:
 

The NPPF proposed
reforms and changes to the planning system formed part of the wider
reforms of the planning system.
The consultation
comprised of the Draft NPPF and a wider consultation
document.
The consultation
would close on 10th March 2026.
The consultation had
225 questions which were to be answered which made the process
unworkable. In order to perform a more meaningful consultation the
joint authorities would need to focus their response; and
identify/target the more useful questions.
There was to be no
replication of the content of national decision-making policies in
our plans, nor were we to deviate substantially from policies, and
local areas were required to ‘do their bit’ towards UK
growth.
The presumption of
being in favour of development within settlements in that
‘development should be approved unless benefits are
substantially outweighed by the harms’ but ‘not at all
costs’.
The draft definition
of a ‘settlement’ being:

Including cities,
towns, villages and other predominantly built-up areas
Excludes hamlets and
scattered groups of houses.


Outside settlements
there was a closed list of acceptable developments, supported in
principle. If not on the list, it was only allowed in exceptional
circumstances.
Housing Delivery (or
lack of) would no longer trigger the ‘tilted
balance’.
There were clearer,
stronger rules regarding the viability and affordable housing. This
included stronger emphasis on social rent, and the inclusion of
military homes.
Within local plans
there was a stronger focus on allocations, and a need for 10% on
sites which were under 2.5 hectares (which was previously a
requirement only for those under one hectare).
There was a benchmark
that 40% of all new homes were required to be accessible and
adaptable.
Accessible homes,
parking, and green space standards were expected to be present in
the plans. This would ensure that developers were clear on what
they were required to attain when taking on new
developments.

 
In response to questions from
the Committee, Cllr Bell, the NDC Lead Member for Housing, agreed
that there was a real need for a percentage (possibly 5%) of the
adaptable housing to be created for those with need for
extreme-requirements (fully adaptable for severe disability rather
than more elderly/less mobile residents) in order to enable
residents to stay in their own homes.
 
Cllr Walker wished to emphasise
the importance of the fact that not all those requiring adaptive
homes would be elderly. The provision of adapted homes for those
under 55 was almost non-existent.
 
The Planning Policy Team Leader
advised the Committee of policy HC01 “Assessing the need for
homes” placed ‘older people’ front and centre,
(rather than disabled) although there was mention of ‘those
looking after children’, ‘specialist community-based
accommodation’.
 
The Chair noted that the
exclusion of hamlets and small villages from policies could make
exception sites difficult. He was concerned that larger could
continue to grow when smaller hamlets could
‘die’.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Planning Policy Team Leader advised,
that:
 
·        
There seemed to be limited opportunity to set
criteria to define the limits of places , and that it was more of a
binary policy. There would likely need to be boundaries created
around settlements.
·        
Biodiversity Net Gains (BNG) appeared to be the key
method of assessing and securing habitat conservation
on-site.
·        
Locations for development were not yet being
established, and locations/sites would be looked at in future. He
noted that 150+ sites could be required to meet the small sites
targets set through the proposals which seemed
unrealistic.
·        
There was a clear requirement to allocate land for
employment.
·        
There was a need to work with communities whilst
recognising the need to be adhering to the NPPF which could
constrain scope for what is possible.
·        
Local plans would continue to hold status and
existing Neighbourhood Plans would continue be considered in
decision making.
 
The Chair agreed that the draft
response to the consultation be shared with all members of both
councils.
 
Cllr Clayton left the meeting
(11:38)
 
RESOLVED that:
 
a)   
the report, the proposed changes to national
planning policy, and associated implications as set out in the
appendices, be noted.
b)   
the committee’s comments on the key aspects be
taken forward in the Councils’ formal consultation
response.
c)   
Officers be delegated authority, in consultation
with the Chair and Vice-Chair of the Joint Planning Policy
Committee, to prepare and submit a formal response to the
consultation on behalf of both Councils.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations in response to proposed changes to national planning policy, with a focus on key aspects for formal consultation response.

Councillor Davies re-declared his disclosable pecuniary
interest and left the room for consideration of planning
applications 80856, 80864 and 80969. 
 
Councillor Bishop took the Chair for these
applications.
 
Councillor C. Leaver re-declared her disclosable pecuniary
interest and left the room for consideration of planning
applications 80856, 80864 and 80969. 
 
Councillor Prowse re-declared his other registerable
interest and left the room for consideration of planning
applications 80856 and 80864.
 
The Committee considered a report by the Graduate Planning
Officer (MH) (circulated previously) regarding planning application
80856.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Graduate
Planning Officer (MH) advised the following:
 

·        
PVs could be placed on
buildings within a Conservation Area without planning permission in
some instances.  Planning permission was
required for the installation of PVs on a listed
building.

·        
Discussions had
previously taken place with the applicant regarding locating the
Solar PVs at the rear of the property, however this had now been
removed from the application.

·        
Solar PVs could be
located on northern elevations as these would still work and
provide the household with sufficient power. 

·        
In respect of this
application, the Conservation Officer did not support the
installation of solar PVs on the southern elevation, however this
did not exclude them being located in the garden at the rear of the
property.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Service
Manager (Development Management) advised the following:
 

·        
There was specific
policies within the Local Plan regarding the installation of Solar
PVs on listed buildings.  Policies
ST15 and DM7 in the Local Plan protected the historic
environment and conserved heritage assets.

·        
The proposed location
of the PVs were on the front of the roof, which required planning
permission as it fronted the road.  It
was not proposed that the Solar PVs were located at the rear of the
property.  Planning permission would not

The Committee considered a
report by the Head of Place, Property and Regeneration, regarding
the Future High Streets Update.
 
The Director of Resources and
Deputy Chief Executive presented the report and advised the
Committee:
 

The capital programme
required a virement of £100,000 from the Cultural Development
Fund project budget, and £675,000 from the recently awarded
Homes England Affordable Homes capital grant to the Capital
Programme.
Construction costs
had generally risen by over 20% over the last six
years.
Boutport Street had a
number of provisional sums within the contract.
The budget position
was clearer since the car parks works had been completed on phase 1
and phase 2.
The report covered
the challenges faced on the project – this included
inflation, fire safety management, contamination, the structural
condition of no.36 Boutport Street, programme extension, and the
administration of the Structural Engineers (Clarke Bond), and the
subsequent appointment of a replacement contractor.

 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
advised that:
 
·      
Improved signage for the Central car park when
coming into the town centre, would be looked at.
·      
The accommodation at Boutport Street comprised of a
mix of 1/2/3 bedroomed dwellings.
·      
NDC had invested some of its own funds to the
project alongside the various funding streams.
 
RECOMMEND:
 
(a) 
That the capital programme be varied by
£775,000 – to be funded by capital virement of
£100,000 from the Cultural Development Fund project budget
and £675,000 be funded from Homes England Affordable Homes
capital grant recently awarded the North Devon Council.
 
(b) 
That the remaining £525,000 Homes England
Affordable Homes capital grant be utilised and reduce the already
approved borrowing requirement for the Future High Street project,
as outlined in sections 4.21 and 4.26 of the report.
topline: The Council has decided to vary the capital programme by £775,000 to address challenges in the Future High Streets project.

content:
Cllr P Leaver declared a
non-registerable interest as he was a Director of a company that was a trade waste
customer. 
 
Cllr C. Leaver declared a
non-registerable interest, as her spouse had declared a
non-registerable interest as a Director
of a company that was a trade waste customer. 
 
Both Councillors P Leaver, and
C Leaver, left the room during the consideration of this
item.
 
The Committee considered a
report by the Waste and Recycling Manager regarding the Trade Waste
Service Provision (circulated previously).
 
The Waste and Recycling Manager
addressed the Committee and advised:
 
·      
The report considered the continuation of the
existing trade waste service and set out the costs
involved.
·      
The service could be split into two sections to
consider: Trade Waste, and Trade Recycling.
·      
External organisations;
Newberry, and Veolia, had expressed interest in taking on the
existing customers.
·      
Mid-Devon District Council had also approached the
Council in relation to the service in the south of the NDC
area.
·      
Trade customers would not be left without
replacement services as there were alternative contractors
available to provide a service to them.
·      
A price increase of 25% would be needed in order for the existing service to break-even. It was currently running at a
loss.
 
The Chair read the following
statement from the Lead Member for Waste and Recycling:
 
The report has clearly shown
that Mark Kentell and his team have spoken to businesses who use
the trade waste service. From the responses it's clear to me that
for the vast majority there would be little problem in changing to
an alternative supplier. However, there remain a very few rural
businesses who think that they might have a problem - but they
have not made specific enquiries to be sure. Mark and Paul have
talked to other providers in the local area, and
it looks as though there are alternatives for our existing
customers and that there wouldn't be any businesses left high and
dry. 
 
So, we have
to look at whether the council want to continue subsidising
a service that is not statutory and will just get more
expensive for ordinary council taxpayers when changes to
regulations come into force. 
 
When the multi-year funding
settlement was released just before Christmas, North Devon was
shown to be one of only 2 districts in Devon who will receive a
real term cut of more than 10% in spending power over the three
years of the settlement. 
 
It's within that context that
we have to consider which of our
non-statutory services are the best value for a dwindling budget
and which do the most to support our farmers and small businesses.
I don't think that continuing to subsidise Trade Waste and
Recycling by up to £200,000 is good value for money.
Personally, I think that we would be better off
targeting support for rural employment through business advice
services, such as those delivered through North Devon Plus, or by
targeted support for farmers such as the discount on planning
pre application fees. 
 
It's clear to me that other
providers are available for the few rural businesses who will be
most affected by the proposed removal of the service and that it is
not the best use of council taxpayers' money to continue to
subsidise it.
 
In response to a question, the
Chair advised that he had spoken to some of the staff, but was not
certain who the Lead Member had spoken to on the matter.
 
The Committee Members noted
that:
 
·      
Current trade customers had expressed their concerns
to Councillors – many citing that they would be happy to pay
an increased charge as the service provided by NDC was deemed to be
excellent, and better than that from alternative
providers.
·      
The alternative providers currently charged
approximately 20% more than NDC.
·      
There could be problems in sourcing alternative
providers in the more rural areas.
 
The Waste and Recycling Manager
advised that the 25% increase could only break-even if the existing customer-base continued
with NDC and did not go elsewhere. So it
could not be guaranteed.
 
In response to a question, the
Chief Executive advised that as the Trade Waste & Recycling
service was a commercial activity there was no
‘contract’ which could be sold on. Therefore other commercial companies could not pay a
sum to take on the customers.
 
The Director of Resources and
Deputy Chief Executive advised that should the separate trade
recycling service not be continued, the remaining main trade refuse
service would require a 7-8% price increase to customers. The
additional costs with the recycling service were due to the cost of
vehicle replacement. Any price increase would need to be immediate
for 2026/27, rather than phased, in order
to prevent a resulting ongoing budget-gap.
 
The Waste and Recycling Manager
advised that not all contracts with the individual trade customers
currently ran from 1st April.  Some of the existing contracts continued into
2026/2027.
 
RESOLVED that the Trade Waste and Recycling Service by North
Devon Council be ceased in full.
 
Councillor P Leaver, and
Councillor C Leaver, rejoined the meeting.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to cease the Trade Waste and Recycling Service provided by North Devon Council.

The Committee considered a report by the Lead Environmental
Health Officer – Commercial Regulation (circulated
previously) regarding the Hackney Carriage Fare Tariff
Review.
 
The Lead Environmental Health Officer – Commercial
Regulation provided the Committee with background information
regarding the review:

 
·      
The Local Government
Act 1976 set out the maximum fares chargeable. The hackney carriage
drivers were able to charge less than the set figures.
·      
The most recent review
had taken place in July 2022.
·      
Consultation had taken
place, and the results were provided in appendix E. It was noted
that there was disparity in responses.

 
The Committee discussed the issues created by both
increasing the maximum fares, or leaving
them as they were.

 

RESOLVED:

 
(a) 
That the Lead Environmental Health Officer
Commercial Regulation undertakes further informal consultation with
the licensed taxi trade on the specific proposals within options 2
and 14 on appendix F:

 
o  
Option 2: Trade
£3.50 flag / no other increase.

 
o  
Option 14: CPI (13.7%) flag only and rounded up to
nearest 10 pence on tariff one and four only.

 
It should be borne in mind that
rates may need minor adjustment for them to be compatible with a
taximeter, and
 
(b) 
that the above
consultation included the following proposals:

 
o  
retain the current valet charge at £100 in
line with comments at paragraph 4.24 (suggested
£100)

 
o  
increase the fare for non-motorised vehicles from
£2.00 to £2.40 a minute (resultant tariff if relevant
CPI increase is applied and the tariff is rounded up to the nearest
10 pence) (suggested £2.40)

 
o  
increase waiting time from £0.25 per minute,
in line with comments at paragraph 4.28 (suggested
£0.30)

 
o  
continue including a fuel surcharge within the
tariff. If so it, would be a necessity to amend its current wording
to reflect south west average fuel oil
prices being unavailable. Suggested to amend the wording
to:
o  
a surcharge of 10p be
added to the fare when published Government weekly road fuel price
for ultra-low sulphur diesel exceeded £1.75 per litre with a
further 10p added for each subsequent
increase of 10p per litre.

 
o  
include any additional extras charge to cover
unexpected bank holidays. Whilst infrequent these were currently
uncatered for. A suggestion would be to propose a £0.50 extra
charge in the event of an extra public holiday being announced in
the life of the tariff with the additional charge being added to
the meter for each hiring on the new public holiday.
topline: The Licensing and Community Safety Committee has decided to undertake further consultation on potential changes to the Hackney Carriage Fare Tariff, including adjustments to various charges.

Councillors C. Leaver and P. Leaver re-declared non

The Committee considered a report by the Waste and
Recycling Manager (circulated previously) regarding the Trade Waste
Service provision.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Waste and
Recycling Manager advised the following:
 

·      
It was considered that
there were a sufficient number of
private companies that collected trade waste. There were a few
companies that also collected recycling and food waste.

·      
Four other District
Councils in Devon did not provide a trade waste service.

·      
The current costs
charged by the Council for the collection for trade waste
was considered to be quite low and
following discussions with other District Councils, the current
charges were low in comparison.

·      
The costs charged by
private companies could be higher than the Council
charged.

·      
There may potentially
be an opportunity to work with Mid Devon District Council in the
future for the collection of trade waste. There had previously been
an arrangement in place with Mid Devon whereby they had collected
trade waste on behalf of the Council in areas such as
Witheridge. 

·      
The Council had
previously undertaken collections on behalf of Torridge District
Council.

·      
In
order for the trade waste collection service to break even
financially, the charges would need to be increased by 20%
and that the current level of customers
did not decrease.

·      
The recent changes in
legislation had come into effect in 2025 which meant that all
businesses with 10+ employees were required to recycle food
waste.  For smaller businesses with less
than 10 employees, this requirement came into effect from April
2027.

·      
The onus was upon
businesses to find a trade waste food collection
service.

·      
The vehicles would
need to be replaced in April 2026.  The
current vehicle was off the road on a regular basis due to
break downs. If the Council kept this
vehicle, there would be an increase in the time that the vehicle
was off the road and the Council would
not be able to provide the same level of trade waste collection
service.

·      
The Council lost 5% of
its customers following the requirement to collect food
waste.

·      
There were currently
no plans to consult with the remaining business customers in
addition to the recent sample of customers contacted. 

·      
The ordering of a
replacement vehicle would take between 5-6 months.  If consideration of the trade waste collection
service was deferred until January 2026 and it was decided to
continue with the service, the replacement vehicle would not be in
place by April 2026.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
Environmental Enhancement advised the following:
 

·      
With the exception of Mid Devon District Council, the Council
had spoken to the other four District Councils who currently
provided a trade waste collection service.  They were all in the process of reviewing this
service and considering the level of charging.

·      
The trade waste
collection service was not a statutory service.

·      
Other District
Councils that had rural locations were coping without the provision
of a Council trade waste collection service.

·      
The Scrutiny and
Policy Development Committee had recommended that the Committee
consult with its existing customers.  20
local businesses had been contacted and asked for their views on
whether they would continue to use the service if the charges were
increased by 20%.  Some customers had
advised that they would absorb the increase in costs, whereby
others had advised that they would consider alternative
options.  There had not been an opportunity to contact all of the 800 customers.  Those businesses that had been contacted
were located in rural and urban areas.
Two businesses had been contacted in the Witheridge area and they had not advised that it would impact
the future viability of their businesses. There had been a mixed response from
businesses.  No businesses had advised
that it would have a major impact.  Some
smaller businesses with less than 10 employees already had a food
waste trade collection service in place when they were not currently required to do
so.  The results of the consultation
could be shared with the Committee.

·      
If the Council
continued to provide the trade waste collection service, then it
would need to collect food waste and invest in infrastructure and
vehicles to collect the food waste. There was also insufficient
space in the waste transfer hall to tip the food waste.  The Council also needed to expand the collection
for recycling for domestic properties to include tetra
plastic.

·      
There were currently 6,500 registered businesses in North
Devon.

·      
The recent changes in
legislation had come into effect in April 2025 which meant that all
businesses were required to recycle food waste. 

·      
The Council
did not currently collect food waste
from businesses. If businesses put food waste in with trade waste,
the Council could refuse to collect. There was a potential for the Government to require local
authorities to start checking trade waste in the future.

·      
The Council
already collected food waste from
domestic properties and had informed businesses that we were
currently unable to collect food waste and advised them to find a
collection service.

·      
If the prices were
increased by 20% and a number of
businesses stopped using the Council’s services, the service
would not break even.

·      
Contracts were in
place with trade waste customers and the Council would be required
to provide a minimum of two months’ notice for any changes to
the service to its customers. 

·      
If the trade waste
service ceased, the Council would help to support businesses
with finding alternative collection
services.

·      
If the trade waste
service continued, the largest lorry would need to be replaced due
to its age and two split loader lorries would be required.  The costs were detailed within the
report.  The Council had a contract with SSF for the lease of vehicles.
Prior to this arrangement, the Council procured vehicles, many of
which were old and broke down on a regular basis.  The annual maintenance costs for vehicles
was very high.  The current vehicle would need to be replaced next
year with a leased vehicle if the Council continued to provide the
trade waste collection service. The vehicle was old and likely to
break down on a regular basis.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·      
That the drop in
income of approximately £90,000 for 2023/24 had been as a
result in a decrease in the number of customers.  There had been a
corresponding reduction in the number of agency staff employed and
number of staff required for the rounds.  The key information to consider was the net costs
of both income and expenditure.

·      
The financial figures
included on pages 22 and 23 included the assumption of replacing
vehicles.  To break even in 2026/27, the
prices would need to be increased by 19.76%.  These costs did not include central support
costs.

·      
Paragraph 4.8 detailed
the costs for the vehicle which was bought in 2018 for
£190,000 and the current maintenance costs which were
£19,000 per year.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Chief
Executive advised the following:
 

·      
Businesses located in
rural areas had a duty to find a food waste collection service, as
the Council was not able to provide this
service.

·      
If the Council took
the decision to cease the trade waste collection service, it would
work with businesses to provide support in finding alternative
providers and provide all businesses with a two
month notice and would continue to work with businesses up
until April 2026.

·      
For those businesses
who were required to have a food waste collection service, they may
consider having one provider to collect all trade waste.

·      
If charges were
increased, the Council may lose business customers as a
result.

·      
If the Council took
the decision to continue with the trade
waste collection service, then the service must be financially
sustainably and have no impact on the Council’s budget by
either breaking even or making a profit.
 
RESOLVED that consideration of the decision for the future

the Committee on 5 January 2026 for further information and that

any questions to the Waste and Recycling Manager by the end of this

consultation with businesses be presented to the Committee for
consideration.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Head of
Environmental Enhancement (circulated previously) regarding the
Parks Team depot.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
Environmental Enhancement advised the following:
 
·      
Informal discussions
had taken place with Barnstaple Town Council regarding relocating
some of its works equipment to the site.
 
Councillors Clayton, Hunt and P. Leaver declared an
interest for transparency reasons as Members of Barnstaple Town
Council.
 
Councillor Milton left the meeting.
 
In response to further questions from the Committee, the
Head of Environmental Enhancement advised the following:
 

·      
As detailed in
paragraph 5.5 of the report, the total spend for the areas of work
required within the next 12 months was estimated to be between
£103,000 and £168,000.

·      
The Parks Team did not
require all of the space, therefore there was potential to generate
income for the remaining areas.

·      
The location of the
depot near to the town centre provided benefits of working with the
Waste and Recycling team, the ability to respond quickly and to
also work with partners.

·      
There was potential to
bring the flat back into use in the future.  The proposed works were to stop the flat
deteriorating further.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 
·      
The options for the
Parks Team to have a permanent base at Gaydon Street Dairy or to
lease an alternative site which would cost approximately
£30,000 per annum.  The costs for
renting an alternative site for just over five years would pay for
the up-front costs for the works to be undertaken at the
Dairy.  There would still be an
opportunity to consider developing the site in the
future.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
Place, Property and Regeneration advised the following:
 

·      
That she had been
involved with the project and was mindful of opportunities that
working in partnership would bring. There was potential storage
opportunities and this would be identified once the project bid had
been finalised.

·      
It was not an easy
site to develop, however it was located within the development
boundary. 

·      
The site provided
commercial opportunities.
 
RESOLVED that the Gaydon Street Dairy
becomes the permanent base for the Parks Team and that it be noted
that a separate capital funding (PAG) bid would follow to fund
associated works once costs had been finalised.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to make the Gaydon Street Dairy the permanent base for the Parks Team, with potential income generation and future development considerations.

·      
The Council had delegated a number of functions to
Lynton and Lynmouth Town Council for the administrative area of

taken to ensure that performance against the 14 review

and Monitoring Officer, to agree the terms of the new agency
agreement with Lynton and Lynmouth Town Council;

agreement with Lynton and Lynmouth Town Council with effect from 1

content:
Council considered a report by the Chief Executive
(circulated previously) regarding Local Government Reorganisation
(LGR).
 
Council received a presentation by the Chief Executive who
outlined the context for LGR; Government criteria and further
guidance that had been provided; the timetable for LGR;
“Reimagining Devon” case for change  appraisal of the 8 options as detailed in the
Executive Summary; the financial case; future Councillor numbers;
the 4:5:1+ model; Torbay’s proposal; Plymouth/Exeter
proposal; and Devon County Council’s proposal.
 
It was moved by Councillor Clayton and seconded by
Councillor Worden that the recommendations be adopted.
 
An amendment was moved by Councillor Prowse and seconded by
Councillor Patrinos that the recommendations be adopted and subject
to the inclusion of the following:
 
“This Council urges Government to adopt a unitary
model for local government in Devon that continues to promote the
unique identity, culture and community of Northern
Devon.  In discussions and negotiations
over the final form of unitary local government, North Devon
Council will seek guarantees that promote the continued
distinctiveness of our region, in particular:
 
·        
Recognising the
separate Northern Devon economy by an early commitment to endorsing
and promoting the North Devon & Torridge Economic Strategy
underpinned by the 5 core clusters identified.
 
·        
Taking forward a Local
Plan for Northern Devon that focusses on the strong sense of
belonging, highlights the central role of the Biosphere, and the
importance of the Barnstaple-Bideford corridor to providing future
growth, and ensures the continuing provision of the current broad
range of retail and cultural opportunities in northern
Devon.
 
·        
An endorsement of
‘A Place Story for Northern Devon’ that symbolises what
makes North Devon special with its own Economy, Housing Market and
housing needs.  Supporting an emphasis
on the importance of the sub-regional role of greater Barnstaple
which currently offers a wide range of professional careers and
encourages higher skills training to combat the exodus of
young.
 
·        
A commitment to keep
decision making close to people through the implementation of an
area/neighbourhood structure that is meaningful and not merely
consultative.  Securing a continued
substantive presence in Barnstaple for the delivery of services to
the public and local members.  Seeking
the maximum number of elected councillors (to replace the existing
50) in North Devon with wards that represent real
communities.”
 
It was moved by Councillor Jones and seconded by Councillor
Bushell that the vote be taken by a recorded vote.
RESOLVED that the vote be taken by a recorded
vote.
 
RESOLVED that it being 8.00 pm that the meeting adjourn for
a short comfort break and reconvene at 8.04 pm.
 
A
recorded vote was taken on the proposed amendment.
 
Voting for the amendment:
 
Councillors Bell, Bishop, Bulled, Bushell, Cann, Clayton,
Coombs, Crabb, Dawson, Davies, Haworth-Booth, Hunt, Jones, Jusef,
D. Knight, R. Knight, Lane, C. Leaver, P. Leaver, Lethaby,
Maddocks, Maskell, Milton, Norman, Patrinos, Prowse, Quinn, Rutty,
Spear, Topps, Turton, Walker, Whitehead, Wilkinson, Williams,
Wilson, Worden and York.
 
Voting against the amendment:
 
None
 
Abstained from voting:
 
None
 
Totals: 38 For, 0 Against and 0 Abstained
 
The amendment then became the substantive
motion.  No further amendments were
put.
 
Voting for the substantive
motion:
 
Councillors Bell, Bishop, Bulled, Cann, Clayton, Coombs,
Dawson, Davies, Hunt, Jusef, D. Knight, Lane, C. Leaver, P. Leaver,
Lethaby, Norman, Quinn, Rutty, Spear, Topps, Turton, Walker,
Whitehead, Wilkinson, Williams, Worden and York.
 
Voting against the substantive
motion:
 
Councillors Bushell, Haworth-Booth, Jones, R. Knight,
Maddocks, Patrinos and Prowse.
 
Abstained from voting:
 
Councillors Crabb, Maskell, Milton and Wilson.
 
Totals: 27 For, 7 Against and 4 Abstained
 
The substantive motion was therefore carried.
 
 
 
RESOLVED:
 
(a) 
That Council endorse the submission of the
“Reimagining Devon” Case for Change as the
Council’s response to the invitation to submit final
proposals in respect of local government reorganisation in
Devon;
(b) 
That Council supports proposing the 4:5:1+ option as
set out in Appendix 1 of the case for Change to the Secretary of
State as a modification to extend the current boundaries of
Plymouth City Council;
(c) 
That delegated power be given to the Chief
Executive, in consultation with the Leader:
a.   
 to make minor changes to the
Case for Change in conjunction with the other councils who have
worked in collaboration, and
b.   
to submit a covering letter accompanying the Case
for Change to government including wording to give effect to the
suggestion in 4.19
(d) 
That this Council
urges Government to adopt a unitary model for local government in
Devon that continues to promote the unique identity, culture and
community of Northern Devon.  In
discussions and negotiations over the final form of unitary local
government, North Devon Council will seek guarantees that promote
the continued distinctiveness of our region, in
particular:
a.   
Recognising the
separate Northern Devon economy by an early commitment to endorsing
and promoting the North Devon and Torridge Economic Strategy
underpinned by the 5 core clusters identified.
 
b.   
Taking forward a Local
Plan for Northern Devon that focusses on the strong sense of
belonging, highlights the central role of the Biosphere, and the
importance of the Barnstaple-Bideford corridor to providing future
growth, and ensures the continuing provision of the current broad
range of retail and cultural opportunities in northern
Devon.
 
c.   
An endorsement of
‘A Place Story for Northern Devon’ that symbolises what
makes North Devon special with its own Economy, Housing Market and
housing needs.  Supporting an emphasis
on the importance of the sub-regional role of greater Barnstaple
which currently offers a wide range of professional careers and
encourages higher skills training to combat the exodus of
young.
 
d.   
A commitment to keep
decision making close to people through the implementation of an
area/neighbourhood structure that is meaningful and not merely
consultative.  Securing a continued
substantive presence in Barnstaple for the delivery of services to
the public and local members.  Seeking
the maximum number of elected councillors (to replace the existing
50) in North Devon with wards that represent real
communities.
topline: The Council has decided to endorse the submission of the 'Reimagining Devon' Case for Change and support the 4:5:1+ option for local government reorganisation in Devon.

content:
Council considered a report by the Chief Financial Officer
(circulated previously) regarding the Statement of Accounts for
2024/25 and the recommendation of the Governance Committee held on
11 November 2025.
 
The Chief Financial Officer advised the
following:
 
o  
The draft Statement of Accounts (SOA) for year ended
31 March 2025 had been signed by Chief Financial Officer on
19th June 2025.
o  
It was recommended that the Statement of Accounts
for 2024-25 (post audit) be approved and be formally signed and
adopted.
o  
The statutory back stop date for all SOAs to be
signed-off for the 2024-25 financial year was 27th
February 2026.
o  
The External Audit of the Accounts had been carried
out by Bishop Fleming.  The majority of
the audit of financial statements took place through
August/September, there were some areas still to be
finalised.
o  
The Audit Completion Report had been presented to
the Governance Committee on 11 November 2025 and reported an
Unqualified Opinion on the Financial Statements.  There were two recommendations, one medium and one
low which compared to four recommendations last year,following Key
Findings which had been accepted by management.
o  
The Narrative Report identified the
challenges that the Council was facing and how it
aimed to address those challenges together with the review of the
previous financial year 2024-25.
o  
The Council recognised that the impact the world
economic conditions  had on public
finances would continue well beyond 2024/25 and the imbedded effect
of high inflation over the last few years would continue to place
considerable additional strain on the Council in the medium
term.
o  
The Review of the 2024/25 position on page 75
detailed the quarter three position which reported a forecast net
surplus of (£9k).  The net,
favourable variances seen in the last quarter, most notably
additional income from Business Rates, resulted in the final
outturn position achieving a net budget surplus of
(£322k).  The table on page 76
detailed the main variances.
o  
The Options for the (£322k) surplus, was to
contribute the following amounts to earmarked reserves:

Ø 
Repairs Fund Reserve - £140,000 –
provide funds for Capital bids approved quarterly throughout the
year
Ø 
Strategic Contingency Reserve - £100,000
– potential future funding for Street Marshalls
scheme.
Ø 
Budget Management reserve – This replenished
the reserve by £82,000 and helped to mitigate the annual
contribution to the base budget.

o  
Green Lanes Shopping Centre – Council
approved in June 2021 to proceed with the
acquisition of Green Lanes Shopping Centre which the Council
completed the purchase in November 2021.  The purchase of
Green Lanes Shopping Centre was a once in a lifetime opportunity to
acquire this strategic asset and complement other significant
regeneration improvements being delivered within the Barnstaple
town centre through the Future High Streets
project. 
o  
The financial outturn for the Centre produced a net
return for: 2021/22 year of (£243,600); 2022/23
(£291,000); 2023/24 (£237,000), although this did
include £150,000 from the income volatility reserve due to
the financial impact of losing Wilko in August 2023; and 2024/25
(£196,000).  This was still
producing a positive return for the Council and was in line with
our original forecasting.
o

recommendation of the Governance Committee held on 10 June 2025
Governance (circulated previously) regarding the Annual Governance

The Chief Financial Officer highlighted the
following:
 

·      
The Annual Governance Statement (AGS) formally
recorded and published the arrangements that were in place to
ensure that the Council’s functions were carried out
effectively, based on the core principles of the governance
framework. This gives the reassurance that the Council’s
decisions were lawful, public money was safeguarded and resources
were used to their best potential. 

·      
The framework included the work of the Strategy and
Resources Committee and Full Council in setting budgets, strategies
and corporate objectives; the work of the Governance Committee on
Risk Management and reviewing audit report alongside the Senior
Management Team and the Corporate Risk Group.

The Internal auditors, Devon Assurance Partnership,
carried out 23 audits during the 24/25 and their overall assessment
was that the Council generally have sound system of governance,
risk management and control in place.

·      
The external auditors, Bishop Fleming, have recently
completed their value for money review and again concluded that the
Council have proper arrangements to secure economic, efficient and
effective use of our resources. In connection to their governance
review they found no significant weaknesses in the Council’s
arrangements.

There were some areas that the Council had

(b) To consider the following question submitted by
Councillor Rutty to the Chair of the Licensing and Community Safety
Committee
 
“Nighttime safety and
spiking is one of my top concerns as a young person. How
do we ensure people are safe when they enjoy their nights
out?”
 
It was noted that the a

In response to a supplementary

that she would contact the Lead Officer for Licensing regarding

the Council’s website.
 
(c) To consider the
following question submitted by Councillor Rutty to the Leader of
the Council
 
“With the decline of our
hospitality industry especially in winter what are we as a Council
doing to ensure our hospitality trade not only survives but thrives
in all seasons especially winter?"
 
Councillor Clayton, Leader of
the Council provided a response to the question and advised that
“he was aware of the pressures on our hospitality sector
across North Devon. The Government’s increase in national
insurance contributions and inflation have made trading very
challenging at the moment. There were however some relief
available. For example, the Retail, Hospitality and Leisure Relief
provided relief from Business Rates for certain businesses and so
far 890 business within North Devon have taken advantage of
this.  The total relief for 2025/26 was
£3,433,777.36.  Small business
relief was also available which provided 100% relief from business
rates for those business that qualify. North Devon+ was a local
authority owned company that provides business support.  It has provided free business support to many
businesses including those form the hospitality and tourism
sectors. As a Council, we have also provided grants to assist in
tidying up business shop fronts in our towns and we were also
currently giving grants to communities and organisations to hold
cultural events. The Council had also invested in capital projects,
in both Barnstaple and Ilfracombe town centres with a view to
making the centres more vibrant and attractive. Furthermore,
Barnstaple and Ilfracombe now enjoy the presence of the Street
Marshals that make the centres a safer and reassuring place to
visit. Obviously the Council would welcome any ideas, initiatives
that Councillors and residents believe would further enhance our
town centres.”
 
There was no supplementary
question.
topline: The Council has decided to provide relief and support to the hospitality industry in North Devon to ensure its survival and prosperity, especially during the challenging winter season.

Councillors Cann,

The Committee considered a
report by the Senior Electoral Services Officer regarding the
Community Governance Review (CGR) (circulated
previously).
 
The Head of Governance
addressed the Committee and advised that:
 

Appendix A of the
report contained the responses and feedback from the first round of
consultation on the initial draft proposals.
The CGR recommendations should be compliant with
three legals test:

1.   
Do recommendations reflect the identities and
interests of the area under review.
2.   
Do the recommendations support effective, convenient
local government.
3.   
Has account been taken on other arrangements for
community representation and engagement

Appendix B contained
the draft proposals which had been updated following the results of
the initial consultation. These were the proposals which were being
considered for presentation to the public, as part of the second
round of consultation.
These would then go
out to consultation shortly, up until the end of January
2026.
The results of the
second round of consultation would then be presented to Governance
in March 2026, then on to Full Council.

 
The Senior Electoral Services
Officer presented each proposal, in appendix B, to the Committee,
with the view that each would be considered in turn.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Chief Executive advised that:
 

The levels of precept
and council tax paid in the parishes was not relevant to the
proposed reorganisation, and that the changes were primarily
concerned with the identity, and interests of, the local
communities.

 

As Barnstaple was a
sub-regional centre it was expected that people from across the
other wards and parishes would visit and benefit from the
facilities there.

 
Councillor Cann noted that her
parishioners were unhappy with the prospect of paying a larger
precept as part of their Council Tax.
 
The Committee was advised that
those taking part in the second round of consultation would be
asked to confirm their postcode and the ward in which they
lived.
 
         
RESOLVED that:
 
(a) 
The draft recommendations as detailed in Appendix B
of the report be approved;
 
(b) 
The proposals as detailed in Appendices C, D, E and
F be approved and used for the second consultation;
 
(c) 
That the outcomes of the Equality Impact Assessment
as summarised in paragraph 6 of the report be noted.
topline: The Governance Committee has decided to approve draft recommendations and proposals for a Community Governance Review, potentially impacting local government arrangements and council tax payments.
