Councillor R. Knight returned
to the meeting.
 
The Committee considered a
report by the Senior Planning Officer (JJ) (circulated previously)
regarding planning application 79478.
 
John May (applicant) addressed
the Committee.
 
Councillor Biederman, Devon
County Councillor, addressed the Committee in support of the
application.
 
Councillor Coombs, as Ward
Member, addressed the Committee in support of the application and
then left the meeting during the consideration of the
application.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Service Manager (Development Management) advised
the following:
 

·      
At this time the Council was not able to demonstrate
a five year housing land supply.  This
means that the housing policies within the Local Plan carry less
weight.  It was considered that Policy
DM18 still holds weight, as this is not
a housing policy.  Therefore Paragraph
11(d) does not apply for this planning application. 

·      
There were currently approximately 2000 on the
housing waiting list.  She had spoken
with the planning agent who had confirmed that the units would not
be affordable units, but would be for open market
rental.

·      
There was evidence from Planning Inspectorate appeal
decisions of the requirement for compelling evidence to demonstrate
that there was no longer a demand for these properties as holiday
accommodation.  There had been a missed
opportunity in the applicant not providing compelling evidence of
marketing that had been carried out as this may have shown that
there was no-one coming forward.

·      
A temporary permission for a three year period,
could set a precedent for future applications although each
application was taken on its own merits. A temporary permission
would be still be a departure from Policy DM18.

·      
Tourism would be reviewed as part of the review of
the new Local Plan.

·      
Reason 1 was the main reason for recommending
refusal and the applicant had failed to provide compelling evidence
to demonstrate that the occupancy condition restricting the
existing properties to use as holiday accommodation only was no
longer justified.
 
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Senior Planning Officer (JJ) advised the
following:
 

·      
The Council was acutely aware of the housing needs,
however there was a need for tourism to contribute towards the
rural economy and that tourism was a key driver.  It was important to protect uses where they were
making a valid contribution to the rural economy.  If the units were not making a contribution, then
there was a requirement for the marketing of the properties as
holiday accommodation for a minimum of 12 months to ascertain
whether there was a demand from the market for them as holiday
accommodation.  It was considered that
they were still making a valid contribution and the guest reviews
reflected that.

·      
A temporary permission for a three year period would
still be a departure from Policy DM18.  Consideration
would need to be given as to the material considerations for
departure.

·      
In terms of a sustainable location, the use of the
properties as holiday accommodation was different to permanent
residential use. It was considered that for residential use, the
properties were located in an unsustainable location as it was
unclear how future occupiers would utilise sustainable transport
modes.  The travel patterns for
residential use would be different to holiday use as it would
include travel for employment and retail purposes.

·      
Applications for the conversion of redundant
buildings were by nature located in rural locations.  Government guidance advises that consideration of
the location of buildings in rural locations for Class Q
applications should not be taken into account.

·      
Evidence had not been provided as to the financial
viability of the holiday accommodation as this information had not
been submitted by the applicant. He referred to the supporting text
of Policy DM18 paragraph
13.109.  The applicant had provided
evidence of booking records.

·      
The report that was presented to the previous
Committee meeting included two Planning Inspectorate appeal
decisions which related to holiday accommodation which had less
bookings than for this application.
 
Following debate by the
Committee, the Solicitor advised that although the Committee had
considered that the Local Plan was not fit for purpose, it was a
legally binding document.  Lawful
decisions taken by the Committee have to be in accordance with the
Local Plan unless the Committee considered that there were material
considerations to go against the Local Plan. The officers had
provided advice of what was compelling evidence and if the
Committee went against the recommendation, it needed to specify
what evidence it had seen that the officer had not
considered.
 
RESOLVED (unanimous) that the
application be APPROVED FOR A TEMPORARY PERIOD OF THREE
YEARS:
 

(a) 
to allow the applicant to undertake marketing of the
properties for a period of 12 months to enable evidence to be
provided at a later date and that the method of marketing be agreed
in advance with the Service Manager (Development Management);
and

(b) 
that the Service Manager (Development Management) be
delegated authority to apply appropriate planning conditions in
relation to amenity for the temporary approval.
 
In determining this
application, the Committee considered that in this case the
properties were an integral part of a working farm and the
intention of the owner was not to sell on due to the relationship
with the farm and that the accommodation would provide housing for
a family member and the temporary change of use would allow a
family member to occupy the accommodation.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to approve a planning application for a temporary period of three years to gather evidence through marketing of properties.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Senior Planning
Officer (SE) (circulated previously) regarding planning application
80389.
 
The Senior Planning Officer (SE) advised that since the
publication of the agenda:
 

·      
The applicant had
submitted additional drawings on 9 October 2025 which provided an
update on the context of the site.

·      
Four letters of
support had been received.
 
The Heritage and Conservation Officer addressed the
Committee to outline the reasons for the comments that she had made
as a consultee.
 
Lewis Andrews, representing the North Devon Coastal
National Landscape addressed the
Committee to outline the reasons for the comments that he made as a
consultee.

The Committee noted a typographical error on page 95 of the agenda,
whereby reference was made to “Councillor J Patrinos, Lynton
and Lynmouth Ward” who was consulted in error.
 
Allan Green (applicant) and Christopher Wilkinson (agent)
addressed the Committee.

The Senior Corporate and Community Services Officer read out
statements in support received from Johnny Clark, Luke Mendham,
Simon Lea and Kevin Gaskell.
 
Councillor Wilkinson, in his capacity as Ward Member,
addressed the Committee in support of the application.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Senior
Planning Officer (SE) advised the following:
 

·      
Reference to public
benefit was in relation to how the public would benefit such as
social or economically to the District
or locally.

·      
The floor area
included the garage.

·      
The scale of the
development had an impact on the built area.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Heritage
and Conservation Officer advised the following:
 

·      
It was proposed that
the single story garage would be
replaced with a two story 3 bedroomed house which was a large
increase in size on the built form.  It
was not possible to hide a building of that size within the
landscape.

·      
The development would
be seen from different viewpoints.  At
present the density was very low. The applicant had provided
viewpoints and viewpoints were also included within the
Conservation Appraisal.

·      
The approval of this
development may result in incremental development.  It was not considered that the development would
preserve or enhance the significance of the Conservation
Area.
 
The Solicitor advised the Committee that in relation to
National Landscapes the Council now had a strengthened duty to
consider the application under Section 245 of
the Levelling Up and Regeneration Act 2023, previously there was a
requirement to have ‘due regard’. She referred to a
recent Planning Inspectorate appeal decision in relation to this
new duty.
 
RESOLVED (unanimous) that the application be DEFERRED FOR AT LEAST TWO CYCLES PENDING A SITE
INSPECTION to assess the impact on the Conservation Area and
National Landscape and that the Heritage and Conservation Officer
be invited to attend.
 
Councillor Haworth-Booth left the meeting.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to defer a planning application for at least two cycles pending a site inspection to assess the impact on the Conservation Area and National Landscape.

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Lead Planning Officer (Major Applications)
(circulated previously) regarding planning application
80681.
 
The Lead Planning Officer
(Major Applications) provided the following update:
 

·      
Since the publication of the report, the new five
year housing land supply statement had been published which
confirmed that the figure was now 4.61 years, which was a slight
decline from the statement that was published last
year.  Therefore, the Council did not
have a five year housing land supply.

·      
No new representations or consultation responses
have been received since the publication of the report.

·      
Stephen Reed Senior Historic Environment Officer
from Devon County Council Historic Environment Services, Catherine
Marlow from Historic England and Simon Prideaux, Housing Enabling
Officer from North Devon Council were present at the
meeting.
 
The Committee received a
presentation by Stephen Reed, Senior Historic Environment Officer,
Historic Environment Team, Devon County Council regarding Devon
County Council’s Historic Environment Teams objections to
this application.
 
The Committee received a
presentation by Catherine Marlow, Development Advice Team Leader,
Historic England regarding Historic England’s objections to
this application.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Senior Historic Environment Officer, Devon
County Council advised the following:
 

·      
The site formed part of the setting of the open
field formed by the enclosure of former open strips.

·      
For its survival it should be given the same status
as a scheduled monument. There were only three open fields in
England which were formed this way.

·      
Similar open strip fields were located in Sheepwash
and Combe Martin, which were protected.

·      
The open field was not being strip
farmed.

·      
The site was part of a medieval open field system
which were protected and form part of the historic
landscape.

·      
In terms of architectural evidence that had been
considered, the open field looked like other medieval strip fields
sites.

·      
The Great Field was unique in Devon and virtually
unique in the country.  He illustrated
the loss of the Great Field on the north west corner of the
site.  The setting of the strip fields
lied underneath the housing estate to the North of the site and the
farm and holiday cottages adjoining the site.

·      
At Combe Martin, by developing on the edge of the
strip fields, it was starting to lose its character.
 
Steve Crowther (representative
from Heanton Punchardon Parish Council), Councillor Graham Bell
(supporter), Mark Cann (applicant), Karen Evans (Director of the
CLT), Val Cann (Secretary of the CLT) and Steve Crowther
(representing CPRE supporter) addressed the Committee.
 
Councillor Maskell, in her
capacity as Ward Member, addressed the Committee in support of the
application.
 
The Senior Corporate and
Community Services read out a statement received from Councillor
Maddocks, in his capacity as Ward Member, in support of the
application to the Committee.
 
Councillor R. Knight
re-declared his non registerable interest and left the meeting
during the remainder of the consideration of this
application.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Lead Planning Officer (Major Applications)
advised the following:
 

·      
The farm located adjoining the site was owned by a
third party and was not part of this application.  No conditions or planning constraints could be
imposed on this property.

·      
The tenure of the housing would be secured at the
technical stage. The description of the application stated it was
for social/local connection rental properties.

·      
In response to a question regarding further
developments on the Great Field, the Lead Officer advised each
planning application needed to be determined on its own
merits.

·      
In terms of extant planning applications, the only
site in Braunton was for 12 affordable dwellings at
Velator.  In terms of Heanton, in
accordance with the housing waiting list there was a need for 44
dwellings.  Two dwellings were currently
underway, 59 units at Chivenor 18 of which were affordable and at
the Chichester site 80 units of which 24 dwellings were
affordable.

·      
She did not have the figures for the number of
affordable units built last year.

·      
There was no specific use class for agricultural
buildings in relation to the barns on the adjoining farm. The use
was in accordance with the definition of agriculture in section 33
of 6 of the Town and Country Planning Act.  It was understood that the farm was a mixed use of
livestock and arable activities.

·      
The proposed site had been rotated to mimic the open
field strip system.  The use of the
buildings had been considered. One building had alternative use
permitted by an extent consent.  All
uses of the buildings were noise generating.  The holiday lets located at the farm were not
lived in 365 days of the year.

·      
Showed the location of the public rights of way
along the great field on the aerial plans.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Housing Enabling Officer advised the
following;
 

·      
The Service Lead (Affordable Housing) had emailed
the applicant on 3 November 2025 confirming the numbers on the
housing waiting list for Braunton.

·      
In terms of finding sites for affordable housing,
the CLT took the lead on finding a suitable site. The Council
proactively searched for suitable sites.  The need for affordable housing in Braunton was
significant.  He was unaware of any
alternative sites that could be brought forward by the
CLT.  Ongoing negotiations were taking
place in relation to two other potential sites.
 
RESOLVED (9 for, 1 against, 0
abstained) that the application be REFUSED as recommended by the
Lead Planning Officer (Major Applications).
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to refuse a planning application for a housing development on a site with historical significance.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Director of
Resources and Deputy Chief Executive (circulated previously)
regarding the Financial Management Report for Quarter 2
2025/26.
 
The Finance Manager highlighted the following:
 

·      
The revenue budget for 2025/26 approved at Council
on 26th February 2025 at £18,072,800.

·      
As at 30 September 2025,
the latest forecast net budget was £17,954,800, which
produced a budget surplus of £118,000. Details are shown in
“Appendix A – Variations in the Revenue
Budget”.

·      
The original budget for 2025/26 included a forecast
to achieve £250,000 worth of salary vacancy savings. The
current position forecasts would achieve £106,000 based on
known vacancies to date, but it was anticipated that the budget of
£250,000 would be achieved by the end of the financial year,
however there was a risk this may not be fully achieved. (Rather
than being a target to aspire to, the £250,000 was an
estimate of the natural savings that will be achieved due to the
time it takes to recruit for vacant posts.)

·      
The National pay award for 2025-26 had been agreed.
The pay award exceeded the budgeted 3% included in the original
budget by 0.2%, the £40,000 shortfall had been funded from
the Budget Management reserve, the estimated 2025-26 year balance on this reserve was now
£529,326.

·      
The Planning fees for quarter 2 had been reviewed
and it was now estimating the income to be favourable by an
additional £150,000 compared to the base budget, volumes and
larger applications continue to be up on 2024/25 levels. We will
continue to monitor the income and will feed any changes into the
quarter 3 report.

·      
Pannier market income was down by £65,000,
officers have been reviewing the events income element, and it was
hoped that quarters 3 and 4 would see a partial
recovery.

·      
Pay and Display income was down by around 3% on
budgeted volumes, resulting in an estimated £120,000 less
income compared to budget, this was partly offset by increased
carpark permit income.

·      
Recycling sales were still currently down by circa
£41,000, the new baler commodity prices are still filtering
through, and we will revise this figure further in the quarter 3
report.

·      
As at 31 March 2025 the
Collection Fund reserve balance held was
£777,321.  This reserve included a
net (£138,021) deficit balance that would be utilised in the
current year (£233,222) and 2026/27 £95,201 surplus, to
mitigate timing differences of business rate reliefs awarded in
2024/25 that from an accounting perspective impact over the next
two financial years; There was also £89,000 transfer to the
Strategic Contingency reserve thus leaving the fund reserve with a
residue future balance of £550,300 (£455,099 +
£95,201) protection against future volatility.

·      
At the 30 September 2025 total external borrowing
was £12,000,000. The timing of any future borrowing was
dependent on how the authority manages its treasury
activity.  Since the publication of the
report, there was a requirement to borrow an additional
£2m to support our treasury
position.

·      
The 2025/26 Capital Programme was detailed in
“Appendix D – Capital Programme
2025/26”.

·      
Overall variations of (£2,964,162) were
proposed to the 2025/26 Capital programme. The variations to
schemes and slippages in funding as detailed in paragraph 4.4.3 of
the report.  This also includes the
additional £2m for temporary
accommodation.

·      
The overall revised Capital Programme for 2025/26 to
2027/28 taking into account the budget variations was
£26,306,015.

·      
The Programme of £26,306,015 was funded by
Capital Receipts/ Borrowing (£13,480,036), External Grants
and Contributions (£11,001,589) and Reserves
(£1,824,390).

·      
The proposed funds to be released for capital
schemes as detailed in paragraph 4.4.8 of the report.

·      
Treasury Management as detailed in paragraph 4.5 of
the report.

·      
Debt Management as detailed in paragraph 4.6 of the
report.

·      
General Debtors as detailed in paragraph 4.7 of the
report.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·      
The car park income
last year had dropped by 7%, which had been partially as a result
of the works being undertaken to the Barnstaple central car park
and the car park being closed for a period of time.  This decrease had now started to improve for
2025/26.  Some volatility had been
factored in for the works to the central car park.  The decrease had now reduced to 2% which was a
much smaller variance. 

·      
Data of usage was
collected for each car park.  The
general overview was that the usage of car parks had increased
compared to last year, some of this increase was attributable to
the central car park.  The usage and
ticket sales had increased since last year.  If car parks were offered free of charge,
residents would use the car parks and would therefore reduce spaces
available for visitors to the town.

·      
As part of the
Barnstaple pannier market capital programme project, growth in income had been
included.  There was currently a decline
in this projected new income source.  A
plan was in the process of being prepared to identify areas to
generate additional income.  This
plan along with more detailed budgetary
income and business plan would be presented to the Scrutiny and Policy
Development Committee for consideration.  It was anticipated that the income would recover
through additional events being held at the market.  The scoping paper for the review would be
presented to the next meeting of the Scrutiny and Policy
Development Committee on 13 November 2025.
 
In response to questions, the Head of Place, Property and
Regeneration advised the following:
 

·      
The Pannier Market
business plan projected additional income following the completion
of the works.  The
reduction in income being reported was in relation to the projected
income in the Business Plan and not an overall reduction from last
years income.
 
 
RESOLVED:
 

(a) 
That the contributions to/from earmarked reserves be
approved (as detailed in paragraph 4.2)

(b) 
That the movement on the Strategic Contingency
Reserve (as detailed in paragraph 4.3) be noted.

(c)  
That funds be released for the capital schemes
listed in paragraph 4.4.8.

(d) 
That the sections dealing with Treasury Management,
Debt Management and General Debtors (paragraphs 4.5 to 4.7) be
noted.
 
RECOMMENDED:
 
(e) 
The Council approve the variations to the Capital
Programme 2025/26 to 2027/28 (as detailed in paragraph 4.4.3 of the
report).
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to approve contributions to/from earmarked reserves, release funds for capital schemes, and note movements on the Strategic Contingency Reserve in the Financial Management Report for Quarter 2 2025/26.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Sustainability and
Climate Officer (circulated previously) regarding the 2025 Update
to the Council’s carbon footprint.
 
The Lead Member for Climate and Biodiversity introduced the
report to the Committee.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the
Sustainability and Climate Officer advised the
following:
 

·      
The sales of diesel at
Ilfracombe harbour had increased.  If it
was being sold by another supplier, this would not do anything to
improve the environment, as the diesel was still being sold and
used.

·      
It would be costly for
the Council to scope emissions through purchasing.  It was more beneficial to reduce carbon
emissions.  The Council had previously
produced a calculation for carbon footprint for
purchasing.  However, this had been
based on the cost of purchases and was not accurate in relation to
the carbon footprint.

·      
The electricity usage
had increased since 2022/23 for the Council due to increase in
costs. The increase was also due to the Defra Greenhouse gas
conversion costs.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·      
The Council’s
approved Procurement Strategy incorporated to purchase locally to
support the local economy and reduce carbon outputs.  There was a need to balance the reduction in the
carbon footprint with financial factors and recognise where it
could be reduced.

·      
A number of teams at
the Council already shared lifts to and from work. Vehicles were
also shared when attending meetings. 
Hybrid working had resulted in the use of the car park being busier
on some days than others.  There was
still more that the Council could do to reduce the use of
vehicles.
 
RESOLVED:
 

(a) 
That the Climate and
Environment Grant scheme for smaller Parish and Town Councils be
reintroduced to be funded by the residual balance in the earmarked
reserve for Climate and Environment Grants and that the scheme be
brought to the meeting of the Committee on 1 December 2025 for
consideration;

(b) 
That the results of the carbon audit be
noted.

(c)  
That the options for reducing these emissions be
noted.

(d) 
That this report provide a basis for discussion for
members on our way forward.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to reintroduce the Climate and Environment Grant scheme for smaller Parish and Town Councils to address the Council's carbon footprint in the 2025 Update.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the PMO Manager
(circulated previously) regarding the Performance Report 2025/26
Quarter 2.
 
The Head of PMO, Environmental Health and Housing
outlined the key elements of Appendix A as outlined
in paragraph 4.2 of the report which provided a high level update in relation to the programmes
delivering the Corporate Plan priorities and performance measures
for Quarter 2 2025/26.
 
In addition to the report, the
Head of PMO, Environmental Health and Housing provided the
following updates since the publication of the
report:
 

Positive feedback received from the Local
Government Association Peer Challenge which had recently taken
place in relation to programme
management.
Homes England Investment Partner status has been
achieved, providing the first tranche of
funding of £1.2m that had been
received for 36/37 Boutport Street,
which forms part of the Future High Street project..
Following the previous meeting of the Committee, a
table detailing all the external funding for that has been drawn
down for those programme projects had now been
included within Appendix A.  However,
this did not include the Homes England funding of
£1.2m which had been recently
announced noted above.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
PMO, Environmental Health and Housing advised the
following:
 

Total number of households accommodated in leased
or our own temporary accommodation – last year there was a
higher number accommodated in leased/bed and breakfast
accommodation.  This number had reduced
this year as a result of an increase in
Council owned property.  The Council was
continuing to be proactive with the procurement of further
accommodation to be used for temporary accommodation and was
looking to purchase further properties in Barnstaple, South Molton
and Ilfracombe.
The Customer Focus team analysed repeat complaints to identify causes and
were able to interrogate the data and report back the outcomes. The
number of missed bin collections had
reduced significantly as a result of
this process. A number of collection
rounds had been disrupted last year due
to a number of changes, however this had not
happened this year as there has been a planned approach to
only make small incremental efficiency changes.
The Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) enabled everyone to work from home or
elsewhere. ICT are now in the process of rolling out new
assets.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Chief
Executive advised the following:
 

In terms of celebrating success for programme projects, it was also important to make
sure that the profile of North Devon was highlighted on a regional
basis.  This was highlighted during
discussions with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local
Government.
The Peer Review report would be published in
January 2026.  An action plan would be
produced.  Any suggestions for inclusion
within the action plan to be drawn up were welcomed.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

The percentage of household waste sent for reuse,
recycling and composting had reduced compared to last
year.  This had been as a result of the new baler being installed and
during this period some material were
sent off site to be processed and could not be included within the
Devon County Council data. It was anticipated that the percentage
would increase for the next quarter.

 
RESOLVED that the actions being taken to ensure
performance is at the desired level be noted.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to note the actions being taken to ensure performance is at the desired level.

content:
Councillors Milton and Patrinos declared other
registerable interests in this item, but
remained in the room during the consideration of the item as it was
in relation to the endorsement of the Exmoor National Park
Management Plan.
 
The Committee considered a report by the Senior Planning
Officer (circulated previously) regarding the endorsement of the
Exmoor National Park Management Plan.
 
The Head of Place, Property and Regeneration highlighted
the following:
 

·      
The Exmoor National Park Authority had adopted a new
Management Plan: Exmoor National Park Management Plan 2025 -2030 -
The ‘Partnership Plan for Exmoor’ in July 2025 and have
requested that their key partners, including North Devon Council,
formally endorse the Plan.

·      
As a ‘relevant authority' there was a legal
duty on the Council to further the purposes of the National Park
when making decisions or carrying out activities relating to or
affecting land within the National Park (section 245 (Protected
Landscapes) of the Levelling Up and Regeneration Act 2023. In
addition, government guidance also states that relevant authorities
should consider participating in the preparation, review and
implementation of the management plan.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Head of
Place, Property and Regeneration advised the following:
 
·      
That the Economic
Development Team worked closely with Exmoor National Park Authority
and would raise the issues discussed by the Committee in relation
to Lynton and Lynmouth’s reliance on tourism,  limited
employment opportunities and reduction in population.
 
RESOLVED:
 

(a) 
That the Exmoor National Park Management Plan 2025
– 2030 be endorsed.

(b)  
That the Council work with the Exmoor National Park
Authority to ensure appropriate input from them and appropriately
consider the impact on Exmoor during the review of the North Devon
and Torridge Local Plan.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to endorse the Exmoor National Park Management Plan 2025-2030.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Lead Environmental
Health Officer (Environmental Protection) (circulated previously)
regarding the adoption of the Air Quality Strategy.
 
The Lead Environmental Health Officer (Environmental
Protection)  highlighted the
following:
 

·      
North Devon Council revoked its single air quality
management area in Braunton in June 2023 and is therefore required
to produce an air quality strategy. This strategy must be formally
adopted by the Council and included in the Annual Status report to
DEFRA.

·      
The formal consultation on the draft air quality
strategy had been undertaken for a period of 6 weeks.

·      
The consultation responses and draft strategy had
been considered by the Scrutiny and Policy Development Committee at
its meeting on 11 September 2025. 
Following the consultation and consideration by the committee,
minor amendments had been made to the strategy.

·      
Following the adoption of the strategy, other bodies
such as Devon County Council Highways and Director of Public Health
were required to have regard to the strategy.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Lead
Environmental Health Officer advised the following:
 

·      
The Annual Status
report submitted to DEFRA would include details of the successes
and what had been achieved such as the spend of Section 106
fund.

·      
Gaseous ammonia was
seasonal, however there was a slight upward trend in measurements,
however currently there was no impact locally.  A lot of work had been done in other countries,
such as Holland, in relation to using the good waste on the
ground.  The Council was now carrying
out annual monitoring of ammonia emissions.   There was a number of external factors that
affected the data.

·      
It was important to
make sure that farmers were supported and networks were in place to
provide support.

·      
The Environmental
Health Team were consulted on proposals for slurry pits.

·      
The air quality in
North Devon was relatively clean.  There
were some spikes in areas such as Braunton.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director

following:

That officers met

officers.
 
RESOLVED
 

(a) 
That the Council’s Air Quality Strategy be
adopted.

(b)

as summarised in paragraph 6 of the report be noted.

content:

Committee considered a report by the Head of Governance (circulated
previously) regarding the Mid Year Treasury Management report
2025/26.
 
The Head of Governance highlighted the
following:
 

The capital programme had increased by circa
£2.5m since the original strategy
was agreed, but this had been offset by capital grants and  reserves
contributions resulting in a limited impact on the  underlying need to
borrow.
The forecast borrowing remained at
£22m. The current position for
borrowing as at 30 September 2025 was
£12m. 
In October 2025, there was a requirement for further borrowing of
£2m from the Public Works Loan
Board which would increase the current total borrowing, excluding
finance leases, to £14m. 
There may be a requirement to borrow
a further £8m by the end of the financial year depending on
the variations of the capital programme
and cash flow.
The
Council held £6.45m of
investments as at 30 September 2025
(£1.2m at 31 March 2025) and the investment portfolio yield
for the first six months of the year was 4% against the benchmark
7 day average SONIA rate of 4.20%. The
Council’s budgeted investment return for 2025/26 was
£400,000. Investment interest of £189,000 was earned in
the half-year period.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the
Head of Governance advised the following:
 

The increase in capital expenditure for
the Environmental Enhancement service reflected the variations to
the capital programme which had been
included within the Financial Management report for Quarter 2
2025-26.
In terms of borrowing rates, the Council
was waiting to see the impact from the Government’s budget in
November 2025.  The interest rate
forecasts were detailed in Appendix A, paragraph 3.2. .The Council’s borrowing strategy was to
undertake short term borrowing to wait
for the interest rates to decrease and then fix for a longer period.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the
Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

The majority
of capital expenditure for the Environmental
Enhancement Service last year had been
as a result of the change of
infrastructure and installation of the new baler within the Waste
and Recycling service.

 
RECOMMENDED:
 
(a) 
That the changes to the prudential indicators be
approved.
(b) 
That the report and the treasury activity be
noted.

content:
Also present: The Driver, and
Corporate and Community Officers G Turnbull, and C Brayley
(observing)
 
The Chair introduced herself
and invited those present to introduce themselves.
 
The Licensing Officer confirmed
all requirements had been met in relation to this
application.
 
The Legal Officer outlined the
hearing process, explaining that the Licensing Officer would begin
by presenting her report; the Sub-committee could then ask
questions. The Driver would then be able to present his case, and
the Sub-Committee would ask questions. If there was a witness the
Driver could call for them to present a case. Once all questions
had been asked the Licensing Officer would sum up followed by the
Driver. All public and press would then be asked to leave so that
the Sub-committee could take legal advice to formulate its decision
(although none were present). Everyone would be readmitted to the
meeting whereby the proposed decision would be read out, and then
be voted on. A copy of the decision notice would be given to the
Driver and the Chair would call the meeting to a close.
 
The Driver confirmed he
understood the process.
 
It was agreed that the
Sub-committee would inspect the vehicle following the presentations
by the officers and the driver.
 
The Driver presented his
case.
 
The Driver gave the following
responses to questions:
 

The vehicle had been
owned by the applicant for some time and had not been purchased
specifically for business use.  The
vehicle had been the family vehicle (as they were a family of
eight).
The applicant
preferred to apply for a hackney licence (over a private hire) as
would be more flexible for his work.
The applicant had
other vehicles which were used for the business.

 
The Sub-committee Members, the
legal and licensing officers, and the clerk viewed the vehicle with
the driver.
 
The Sub-committee noted that
although the V5 logbook stated the vehicle had nine seats, it did
actually have eight as the front seats had been updated to two
separate seats (one of which was a ‘captain’s chair).
The previous arrangement had three front seats. 
 
The Sub-committee notes that
the amendment to the seating incurred no changes to the side
mounted seat belt mechanism, which remained unaffected in its
original position.
 
The Sub-committee further notes
that the standard of the vehicle both internally and externally was
excellent and in line with that vehicle inspection report provided
as part of the report for consideration.
 
The driver confirmed the
vehicle had been an eight-seater when he purchased the
vehicle.
 
The Driver summed up
 
RESOLVED that everyone be excluded from the meeting with the
exception of the Members, Legal Officer, and Corporate and
Community Services Officer in order for the Sub-Committee to
receive legal advice in accordance with paragraph 5 of Schedule 12A
of the Local Government Act 1972.
 
That it being 11.45 all public
and press be readmitted to the meeting.
 
The Chair asked the legal
officer to read out the proposed decision and the reasons for the
proposed decision.
 
 
RESOLVED that a Hackney Carriage Proprietor’s Licence
(vehicle licence) with standard conditions as stipulated in the
Council’s Hackney Carriage and Private Hire Licensing Policy
2023 be granted to Hackney Carriage Licence ref V.01, and further
the official amendment as to number of seats in respect of the V5
Logbook be registered with the DVLA within 28 days and that any
future adaptation is appropriately registered and meet legally
required safety standards.

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Place Manager (Town Centres) (circulated previously)
regarding the Street Marshal Scheme 2026.
 
The Place Manager (Town
Centres) highlighted the following:
 

·      
The current contract for the Street Marshal scheme
ended on 31 December 2025.  There was a
need to consider whether to continue provide funding for the
provision of a Street Marshal scheme for a further year to December
2026.

·      
Street Marshals were first introduced in
2020.

·      
The scheme remained the same and provided a highly
visible presence within Barnstaple and Ilfracombe and worked as
part of a multi-agency team.   The
aims of the scheme were detailed in paragraph 4.7 of the
report.

·      
Since March 2024 the scheme had been funded by the
council with contributions from the Office Police Crime
Commissioner and Barnstaple Town Council.

·      
The Hotspot funding and contribution from Barnstaple
Town Council enabled the current contract to be awarded based on 9
days, seven days a week in Barnstaple two days in
Ilfracombe.  This was an increase from
five days a week in Barnstaple and two days in
Ilfracombe.

·      
Anti social behaviour and incident data analysis as
detailed in paragraph 4.11 of the report which had been provided by
the current supplier.

·      
Hotspot funding comes to an end on 31 March 2026 and
to date there had been no commitment to any ongoing funding from
the Office of the Police Crime Commissioner.

·      
Barnstaple Town Council had agreed a further
contribution of £38,000 towards the 2026 street marshal
scheme. 

·      
Ilfracombe Town Council had agreed a contribution of
£8,000 towards the 2026 street marshal scheme.

·      
Resource implications as detailed in paragraph 5 of
the report which outlined the costs including a reduced
service.
 
In response to questions from
the Committee, the Place Manager (Town Centres) advised the
following:
 

·      
Flexibility was built into the contract to allow for
a response to be made should a hot spot develop.

·      
Incidents of anti social behaviour needed to be
reported.  If Councillors were aware of
incidents, then they should report them direct to the
Council’s Anti Social Behaviour officer.

·      
The contract was for seven hours a day and the core
hours of operation were 10 am to 5 pm. 
However, the shift pattern changed when there were spikes in anti
social behaviour.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The Contract Procedure Rules be waived and approval
be given to enter into a new 12-month contract up to 31 December
2026 with the existing provider (subject to agreeing terms) on the
basis that they have been delivering the service for the last 5
years, have established practices in place and have built trusted,
invaluable contacts and relationships with NDC staff, Police,
businesses, Town Council and the wider community;

(b) 
The level of Street Marshal provision continue at
the existing levels of service;

(c)  
The cost of the Street Marshal scheme be funded from
the Town Centre Management earmarked reserve, Strategic Contingency
Reserve and financial contributions from Barnstaple and Ilfracombe
Town Councils as set out in Section 5 of the report;

(d) 
The outcomes of the Equality Impact Assessment as
summarised in paragraph 6 of the report be noted.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to continue funding the Street Marshal Scheme in Barnstaple and Ilfracombe for another year.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Ilfracombe Harbour
Master (circulated previously) regarding Ilfracombe Harbour Sea
Pool.
 
The Director of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive
highlighted the following:
 

·      
That an internal
health and safety advice report by the Health and Safety Advisor
had been circulated to the Committee and had been published as a
supplementary document.  The report
included key considerations to be taken into account such as:
hazards; should the pool be capable of being permanently flooded
and emptied; profile; water quality; and lifeguarding. It also
included options to consider such as: opening the sea pool area for
public swimming and recreation; opening the sea pool area for
structured, organised and competent
groups only; continue to prohibit the sea pool as a swimming
area.  Lifeguards were required to be
position no more than 20 seconds from the furthest point requiring
intervention.

·      
The location of the
pool as detailed in the photograph on page 69 of the
report.

·      
The Ilfracombe Sea
Pool project had been given approval in June 2023.  Since then an in-depth study of the safety
measures necessary to mitigate the remaining risks of creating a
retained sea pool and to clarify the assets owner’s liability
had been undertaken seeking advice from the Royal Life Saving
Society (RLSS), Independent
specialised legal counsel (Bevan
Brittan) and specialised marine
infrastructure experts Teignmouth Maritime Services
(TMS).

·      
The study was now
complete and form the basis for the formulation of options for
consideration.  The study also
highlighted that the funds secured for this project were
insufficient for the updated advice and recommendations.

·      
Since June 2023 there
had been an incident where a girl had been swept into the sea and
also unauthorised activities such as
tombstoning had continued to take place which the Harbour Master
had to respond to.

·      
There were a number of
hazards in the area which included variable water depths,
underwater obstructions, limited exit points and consideration
would need to be given regarding the provision of
lifeguards.

·      
Legal advice had been
sought from Bevan Ashford which was detailed in Appendix 2 (NOTE:
not for publication as under
Section 100A (4) of the Local
Government Act 1972 it contains exempt information as defined in
Paragraph 5 of Part 1 of the Schedule 12A of the Act (as amended from time to time),
namely information in respect of which a claim to legal
professional privilege could be maintained in legal
proceedings).  If the Committee wished
to consider in more detail, then the committee would be required to
exclude the public and press from the meeting.

·      
Royal Life Saving Society (RLSS) report which was detailed in Appendix
1.  The question of requiring lifeguards
had been raised and an extract from the report was detailed in
paragraph 6.1.2 of the report.  There
was no specific regulation that required sea water pools to have
lifeguards however there was guidance from the Health and Safety
Executive Managing Safety in Swimming Pool HSG179.  The
RLSS report recommended that the pool
should only be open to groups and not to the public.  Lifeguards would not have full visibility of the
sea pool.  It could be opened up to the
public if the identified hazards were removed, a standard depth of
water and accessible entry to the pool.

·      
The benefits of having a sea pool were detailed in
paragraph 4.6 of the report.

·      
The legal position and
summary from the Bevan Brittan advice notice as detailed in
paragraph 5.2 of the report.

·      
Photographs shown on
pages 77 and 78 of the report showed underwater obstacles and
entrapment.  Some material had occurred
from when the harbour had been
reconfigured previously.

·      
It was a working
harbour.

·      
Consideration would
need to be given on how to manage the area when lifeguards were not
on duty as the pool could not be closed as it would have an impact
on the working harbour.

·      
There was a concern as
to whether all of the risks could be mitigated.

·      
Cold water swimming
currently takes place on the other part of the harbour by the Watersport centre.

·      
The costs for the
project were detailed in paragraph 7 of the report.  The costs to proceed with the project had
increased considerably since 2023 and there would be a requirement
for the Council to fund the projected cost of £118,000, which
would result in an annual borrowing cost to the revenue budget of
£12,000 per year.  The estimated
costs for the provision of one lifeguard was approximately
£30,000 per year and it was anticipated that there would be a
requirement for more than one lifeguard which would increase the
annual revenue costs further.

·      
If the decision was
taken to not proceed with the sea pool, there was still a
requirement for the Council to undertake some works such as the
removal of hazards, provision of additional signage and improved
lifesaving equipment.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Harbour
Master advised the following:
 

·      
If the sea pool was
open to organised groups, Bevan Brittan
advised that the Council would still be required to mitigate
risks.  The Harbour team would not be
able to prevent the public from using the sea pool.  Based upon the advice given, in her view the only
options were to either open the pool to the public and put in place
all of the mitigation measures required or not open it to
anyone.

·      
If the decision was
taken to not proceed with the sea pool, works would still be
required to mitigate the known risks, these would be to remove old
construction debris, fill in the entrapment risks on the old Pier
foundations, clear signage to show the area is out of bounds
displayed and upgrading the life saving
appliances in that area. These works could be undertaken at the
original costs.

·      
There were benefits to
having a sea pool, however these benefits did not outweigh the
ongoing risks and costs.

·      
This area currently
floods twice a day and was currently considered as a hazardous
area.

·      
It was not reasonably
practicable to proceed with opening a sea pool based upon the
information that had been provided.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Director
of Resources and Deputy Chief Executive advised the
following:
 

·      
If the decision was
taken not to proceed with the sea pool, there was still a
requirement for the Council to undertake works to remove hazards in
addition to providing signage.

·      
Even if investors were
sought for the pool, the Council would still have
responsibility.

·      
The costs for
provision of lifeguards was difficult to determine as it would
depend upon the use of the pool and would result in additional
revenue costs for the Council.

·      
Further communications
would be made advising not to swim in the harbour area.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Health and
Safety Advisor advised the following:
 
·      
If the decision was
taken to proceed with the sea pool, the Council would become a
“pool operator” in accordance with the Health and
Safety Executive Guidance.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a)  
The advice provided by the RLSS as set out in Appendix A of the report be
noted;

(b)  
The legal advice provided by Bevan Britton as set
out in Appendix B of the report (please note that this advice is
provided in Part B of the Agenda) be noted;

(c)  
The material changes since the resolution in June
2023 (scope, cost, risk appetite) be noted;

(d)  
The financial changes since the resolution in June
2023 as set out in Section 7. 2 of the report be noted;

(e)  
Having regard to the information set out in this
report and having considered (a) to (d) above, that the area
remains as it is at present with additional signage, identified
hazards clearly publicised and the removal of debris and
areas of entrapment to
mitigate risks as referred to in the
report.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to keep the Ilfracombe Harbour Sea Pool area as it is at present, with additional safety measures in place.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Head of Place,
Property and Regeneration (circulated previously) regarding an
update regarding Lynbridge car park, Lynton.
 
The Head of Place, Property and Regeneration highlighted
the following:
 

·      
In April 2022 a report
was taken to Strategy and Resources Committee to consider the
future of Lynbridge car park following the closure of the car park
in February 2022 on health and safety grounds.

·      
At the Committee
meeting in April 2022, Members resolved that the Council proceed
with option 4 (in the original report) and offer the land to the
Town Council or community, disclosing the concerns with the
structure and that if after a 6 month period it was clear that were
was  no interest in the land that the
report be brought back to the Committee.

·      
Over the last three
years, there had been intermittent contact from the Town Council
but no solution had come forward and was not expected to do
so.  No party wished to take
responsibility for the car park going forwards.

·      
The Engineers team had
reinspected the car park on the 21 August 2025 and noted that it
was continuing to deteriorate.  They
were able to see that the slop on which the structure stands
was  now appearing to wash out and some
of the material was sliding down the slope.  They also observed that some of the concrete beams
supporting the slabbed surface appeared to be bowing and so no
further load should be imposed upon it.

·      
Demolition of the
structure continued to be the preferred option, particularly now
that confirmation had been received that neither the residents nor
the Town Council wished to take it on. However, having observed tha
the slope and the adjacent highway would be unsupported once the
structure was removed, it was something that would need to be
considered as part of any demolition project and a solution found
that does not undermine it.

·      
There was the
potential for a further failure of the structure should we
experience a harsh and stormy winter.

·      
Councillor Patrinos
had been consulted on the report.
 
RESOLVED that:
 

(a) 
The car park be
permanently de-commissioned and that the exact nature of this be
delegated to the Head of Place, Property and Regeneration in
consultation with the Ward Member to ensure the optimum solution
was found that keeps the entire area safe and minimises the cost to
the Council;

(b) 
The outcomes of the
Equality Impact Assessment as summarised in paragraph 6 of the
report be noted.
topline: The Strategy and Resources Committee has decided to permanently decommission Lynbridge car park in Lynton due to safety concerns and lack of stakeholder interest.

content:
The Committee considered a
report by the Head of Place, Property and Regeneration (circulated
previously) regarding Barnstaple work programme.
 
The Head of Place, Property and
Regeneration highlighted the following:
 

·      
The report set out an update of recent work that the
Council had carried out in the town both alone and in collaboration
with partners such as Barnstaple Town Council,and through the
Barnstaple Place Partnership Board.

·      
The adopted Barnstaple Vision continues to form the
strategic context for the Council’s work in Barnstaple town
centre.

·      
In February 2022, the High Street Task Force
announced that 68 Local Authorities would receive a package of
expert advice and support, helping to deliver long term
transformation to towns and cities in England. North Devon was
announced as one of those Local Authorities and the Council
nominated Barnstaple as the town to receive this
support.

·      
Three workshops were held with a range of
stakeholders and facilitated by the High Street Task
Force.  As a result of these stakeholder
workshops, the High Street Task Force developed a Place Making
Programme and action plan.  The
conclusions of the action plan as detailed in paragraph 4.3 of the
report.

·      
The Governance arrangements for the Barnstaple Place
Partnership Board as detailed in paragraph 4.4 of the report. The
Terms of Reference and governance structure for the Barnstaple
Place Partnership Board were detailed in the
appendices.  Individuals were expected
to report back regularly to their own organisations and
networks.

·      
Key achievements and priorities of the Barnstaple
Place Making Action Plan as detailed in paragraph 4.4.

·      
The larger regeneration projects currently being
worked on in relation to the Future High Street Fund and others as
detailed in paragraph 4.5 of the report.

·      
Following the award of the Cultural Development
Fund, the culture projects and activities being undertaken as
detailed in paragraph 4.6 of the report.

·      
Following the award of Safer Streets funding,
Community safety projects being undertaken as detailed in paragraph
4.7 of the report.

·      
Housing related projects being undertaken as
detailed in paragraph 4.8 of the report.

·      
Parks and Leisure projects being delivered as
detailed in paragraph 4.9 of the report.   The Tarka Leisure Centre had recently
received its 1 million visitor.

·      
In collaboration with partners, the UK Shared
Prosperity Fund had enabled small scale investment in employment
and skills with significant results. 
The projects being undertaken were detailed in paragraph 4.10 of
the report which included the Barnstaple Work Hub.

·      
An update on Council owned assets as detailed in
paragraph 4.11 of the report.

·      
Next steps and performance monitoring as detailed in
paragraph 4.12 of the report. 
Performance on projects would be included within the quarterly
performance management reports to the Committee together with the
minutes of the Place Partnership Board.
 
In
response to questions from the Committee, the Head of Place,
Property and Regeneration advised the following:
 

·      
The Oliver Buildings were in private ownership.
There was an awareness that the buildings formed a gateway to the
town.  Whilst planning permission had
been granted for the buildings, the permission is not viable to
deliver..  Historic England have part
funded  a feasibility study.  There was a need to understand the best use of
buildings, viability and regulation. 
The report was expected by the end of November 2025 and would then
be in a better position to advise. 
Discussions had taken place with the owners in terms of how we
could support and enforcement.

·      
Details of external funding secured for projects
would be included within future performance management
reports.

·      
Officers were continuing to work with the Exeter
Science Centre in relation to their Science, Technology,
Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) project and discussions were
taking place regarding temporary accommodation for them.

·      
In relation to business rates, the Council could
only control the rates for its own assets.

·      
There was a need to encourage people to shop locally
to support local businesses.

·      
North Devon+ provided advice to small
businesses.

·      
S215 notices could be served on businesses regarding
condition of their properties.  
Letters had been sent to local businesses requesting work to be
undertaken to their properties. 
Previously the Council had looked into the option of using a cherry
picker to clear guttering of properties in the town centre, however
there would be a need to gain consent of the owners and there was
also an issue regarding liability for insurance
purposes.
 
In
response to questions, the Director of Resources and Deputy Chief
Executive advised the following:
 

·      
When projects came forward, the project breakdown
costs and contributions were calculated.  It was identified at this stage how projects were
to be funded i.e. internal or external funding. How projects were
funded could also be included as additional context within the
quarterly performance management reports.

·      
Small businesses may quality for business rate
relief. The Council work with businesses in their own assets, such
as Butchers Row, Green Lanes and Barnstaple pannier market traders
and provided help and support.

·      
Business rates was a national scheme.  The Council was not able to change it to a local
scheme unless the Government changed the parameters of the
scheme.  There were currently no plans
for the Government to change the scheme.
 
In response to questions, the
Head of PMO, Environmental Health and Housing advised the
following:
 

·      
The quarterly performance management report would be
amended to include an additional column identifying where external
funds had been drawn down.

·      
Councillor Prowse declared a disclosable pecuniary
interest for transparency reasons as a trustee of the Barnstaple
Bridge Trust.
 
RESOLVED that the report be
noted.

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Parks, Leisure and
Public Open Space Officer (circulated previously) regarding the
allocation of S106 public open space funds to projects in Bishops
Tawton and Braunton.
 
The Head of Environmental Enhancement highlighted the
following:

Project to extend
Braunton football club car park as detailed in paragraph 4.1 of the
report.

·      
Project to add a new
swing set at Stanley Verney play area, Bishops Tawton as detailed
in paragraph 4.2 of the report.

·

be used for the provision of bicycle racks at the club, however the

(a) 
Section 106 public

content:
The Committee considered a report by the Senior Planning
Officer (DJ) (circulated previously) regarding planning application
79684.
 
The Senior Planning Officer (DJ) advised the Committee that
the report referred to policies within the Braunton Neighbourhood
Plan in error and that all references to this Plan should be
disregarded as they were irrelevant to the determination of this
application.
 
The Senior Corporate and Community Services Officer read
statements received from Daniel Hill (objector), Abbey Hopkins
(objector) and Councillor Bell (as an individual - objector) to the
Committee.
 
Stephen Crowther (objector) and Claire Howes (agent)
addressed the Committee.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Senior
Planning Officer (DJ) advised the following:
 

·      
The provision of a
community hub had been included within the outline planning
permission 55214 and was not part of this site allocation or
covered by policy BRA01. This application did not prejudice the
delivery of a community hub in the future and the delivery of the
hub was in the hands of the land owner. 
This application needed to be considered on its own
merits.

·      
Policy BRA01
specifically related to business and employment opportunities and
did not specify use classes.

·      
On balance, there was
a degree of conflict with the outline planning
permission.

·      
The proposed use
generated significant employment and was broadly
compatible.

·      
The Highways Officer
was present to respond to any questions in relation to parking and
access.

·      
The land use located
at the south east of the site on the location plan was a pumping
station.

·      
The landscaping plan
indicated that screening would be provided inside of the
site.  The substation was not shown on
the proposed site plan and was located outside of the site and not
within the control of the applicant.

·      
The majority of the
green open space was located around the eastern edge of the site
which was adjacent to the existing area of public open
space.

·      
There was a reasonable
expectation that residents would benefit from the existing public
open space located to the east of the site.  There were no breaks in the hedgerow as it was a
secured site, therefore residents would be required to access the
public open space by walking along the pavement at the front of the
site.

·      
The units for
residents were not self contained and would accommodate residents
with various degrees of care need. Residential (extra care) homes
were more self contained with a small kitchenette area.  Care homes tended to have bedrooms with ensuite
facilities, community facilities and meals provided.

·      
A Travel Plan had been
submitted, however given the level of objections raised in relation
to parking and access to the site, a condition was recommended
requiring a revised Travel Plan to be submitted in consultation
with the Highways Authority.

·      
It was recommended
that Biodiversity Net Gain would be secured via a condition with
associated monitoring fees secured via a section 106
agreement.

·      
A drainage strategy
had been submitted.  It was not viable
to provide infiltration on the site. The drainage strategy included
site attenuation.  The parking would be
on an impermeable service with catchment pipes which would take
water to the drains.  The size of the
attenuation tanks were appropriate to the development as a whole.
Existing drainage easement located on the south east corner of the
site.

·      
No objectives have
been received from the Environment Agency or Lead Local Flood
Authority in relation to drainage. A condition was recommended
requesting the provision of final detailed drainage drawings which
the Lead Local Flood Authority would be consulted.

·      
The space standards
for the bedroom sizes of 12.5 square meters indicated single
occupancy. The occupancy would be a decision of the
operator.

·      
In relation to whether
the guidance in the “Care Homes for Adults – The Design
Guide” had been considered, a communal balcony was provided
on the east side of the site and included areas that were paved and
gardens which provided access to break out areas. The private
bedrooms did not have balconies.  There
was a glazed communal area at the end of each floor, however
residents could not directly access external space from their
private rooms.  The provision of
balconies had been discussed with the agent, who advised that this
provision was not commonly provided due to health and safety and
operational reasons. 

·      
The design of the
building had significantly improved following
negotiations.  An additional condition
had been recommended requiring the submission of material details
to ensure that the quality of materials were suitable.
 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Highways
Officer (PY) advised the following:
 

The application was supported by a robust
Transport Statement and Travel Plan which considered traffic
generation and parking requirements.
The traffic movement was broadly in alignment with
the standard movements of 12 vehicle movements peak time in the
morning and 15 vehicle movements peak time in the
afternoon.
It was noted that over the past 10 years, there
has been significant improvements made to the highways, footway and
cycle link in the area.
In terms of determining car parking requirements,
it was relevant that this site was in a sustainable location with
access to a full range of sustainable travel options.
The pedestrian and cycle links from the site
linked to Braunton, Wrafton and Barnstaple.  The pedestrian link was 250 meters from the site.
The cycle link was a long distance route.
In terms of public transport to the site, during
peak times there was a bus every 30 minutes and at weekends it was
between 30-60 minutes.
There was no approved standard within the Local
Plan in relation to car parking provision.  Based upon historical guidance on car parking
standards, 32 spaces would be recommended, however this proposal
included 25 spaces In terms of a nursing/residential home,
historical guidance provided for one space per eight
residents.  In the worst case scenario,
if there were 24 members of staff travelling by car to work, that
this figure together with eight spaces for residents provided the
total of 32 spaces.  However, not all
members of staff would drive to the site and would either car
share, walk, cycle or travel by bus. 
Wrafton and Braunton were within reasonable cycle distances and
there was a frequent bus service travelling from Barnstaple.
Sustainable travel was considered in the following order:
pedestrian, cycle, good public transport and then finally
car.
A condition was recommended requiring an updated
Travel Plan to be submitted.
The Highways Authority considered the scheme to be
acceptable.
The Highways Authority were aware of the ongoing
problems with the condition of the road and raised ironworks which
had been a result of mixed residential and commercial uses. There
was a section 38 agreement in place for the adoption of the
road.  Discussions had taken place
between the Highways Authority and the developer regarding the
adoption of the road and he would provide an update on the
situation to Councillor Ricky Knight.

 
In response to questions from the Committee, the Service
Manager (Development Management) advised the following:
 

·      
The Local Plan did not
include a car parking standard, however it had been included within
the previous Local Plan.

·      
In relation to parking
provision, she read policy DM06 to the Committee.

·      
The Highways Officer
had looked at the site in terms of public transport and access to
the site and would have taken into account policy DM06.

·      
Biodiversity Net Gain
would be secured via a section 106 agreement over a 30 year
period.
 
Councillor Ricky Knight, in his capacity as Ward Member in
support of the application, addressed the Committee.
 
RESOLVED (5 for, 2 against, 0 abstained) that the
application be APPROVED as recommended by the Planning Officer
(DJ).
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to approve a planning application despite objections from local stakeholders.
